1:1.headline: חזון, "vision": the harshest of ten words for prophecy
1:1.body: Rashi says the Bible has ten words for prophecy, and חזון is the harshest. The book uses it here because what follows is hard rebuke.

sources.quote: קְרָאָם חָזוֹן, שֶׁהוּא קָשֶׁה מֵעֲשָׂרָה לְשׁוֹנוֹת שֶׁנִּקְרֵאת נְבוּאָה
sources.says: Rashi says these rebukes are called חזון because it is the harshest of the ten words for prophecy.

sources.quote: ועש״ז נקרא הנביא בשם חוזה כי רואה במראה הנבואה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says this is why a prophet is called חוזה, a seer.

1:2.headline: Isaiah swaps Moses' words for heaven and earth. Why?
1:2.body: Moses told heaven האזינו, "give ear", and earth שמע, "hear"; Isaiah reverses them. Rashi says now both witnesses have been called with both words, so their testimony matches; Radak adds a midrash that Moses was close to heaven and Isaiah close to earth.

sources.quote: מֹשֶׁה אָמַר ״הַאֲזִינוּ הַשָּׁמַיִם וְתִשְׁמַע הָאָרֶץ״
sources.says: Rashi notes that Moses said "give ear, heavens" and "hear, earth".

sources.quote: בָּא יְשַׁעְיָה וְחִלֵּף אֶת הַדָּבָר, נִמְצְאוּ שְׁנֵיהֶם מְעִידִים בִּלְשׁוֹן הַאֲזָנָה וּבִלְשׁוֹן שְׁמִיעָה
sources.says: Rashi says Isaiah switched them so both witnesses testify with both words.

sources.quote: לפי שהיה משה קרוב לשמים לפיכך אמר האזינו השמים
sources.says: Radak brings a midrash: Moses was close to heaven, so he said "give ear" to it.

sources.quote: והנה אין הפרש על דרך הפשט בין שמעו ובין האזינו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says that on the plain meaning there is no difference between the two words.

1:3.headline: The ox knows its קונה: its buyer, or whoever raises it?
1:3.body: קונה usually means a buyer. Radak says here it is whoever raises and feeds the animal, as God is called Israel's קונה; Rashi says it is the one who trains the ox to plow.

sources.quote: ואין פירוש קונהו קונה אותו בדמים לבד אלא המגדלו ועושה לו צרכיו תמיד וכן אביך קנך
sources.says: Radak says קונהו is not only the one who paid for it, but the one who raises it and meets its needs.

sources.quote: קֹנֵהוּ. מְתַקְּנוֹ בַּחֲרִישָׁה בַּיּוֹם
sources.says: Rashi says it is the one who trains it to plow by day.

1:4.headline: הוי: a groan of grief, or a call to listen?
1:4.body: Rashi says almost every הוי in the Bible is a groan, like "alas", but a few are a loud call. Metzudat Zion says it is a call that can carry sorrow or joy.

sources.quote: כָּל הוֹי שֶׁבַּמִּקְרָא לְשׁוֹן קֹבֶל וְקִינָה
sources.says: Rashi says every הוי in Scripture is a word of complaint and lament.

sources.quote: אֶלָּא שֶׁיֵּשׁ מֵהֶם מוּעָטִין שֶׁהֵם לְשׁוֹן צַעֲקַת קְרִיאַת קוֹל
sources.says: Rashi adds that a few are a loud call.

sources.quote: המלה הזאת היא ענין קריאה בין לצער בין לשמחה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the word is a call, whether in sorrow or in joy.

1:4.headline: נזרו: they drew apart like a nazir, or became strangers
1:4.body: Rashi says the root נזר always means to hold apart, as with a nazir: they drew back from God. Radak also offers the root זר, "stranger": they became strangers to Him.

sources.quote: אֵין נְזִירָה בְּכָל מָקוֹם אֶלָּא לְשׁוֹן פְּרִישׁוּת
sources.says: Rashi says נזירה everywhere means separation.

sources.quote: נסגו מענין זר
sources.says: Radak offers a second reading: they turned away, from the word זר, stranger.

1:6.headline: A טריה wound: crushed, or fresh and still oozing?
1:6.body: The Targum, cited by Rashi, reads it as a crushed wound. Menachem and Metzudat Zion read it as moist, like the "fresh" jawbone in Judges: Radak says a wound that never dries is one that will not heal.

sources.quote: תִּרְגֵּם יוֹנָתָן: ״מְרַסְסָא״, כְּתוּתָה וּמְרוּסֶסֶת
sources.says: Rashi cites the Targum: a crushed, battered wound.

sources.quote: מְנַחֵם פֵּירֵשׁ לְשׁוֹן לַחוּת, כְּלוֹמַר: לַחָה וְרְטוּבָה, תָּמִיד נוֹבַעַת
sources.says: Rashi reports Menachem's reading: moist and wet, always oozing.

sources.quote: טריה. לחה כמו לחי חמור טריה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means moist, like the fresh jawbone of a donkey.

sources.quote: וזה סימן למכה שאין לה רפואה
sources.says: Radak says a wound that stays moist is the sign of one that cannot be healed.

1:6.headline: לא זרו: not dusted with medicine, not healed, or not drained?
1:6.body: Rashi says no doctor sprinkled healing powder on the wounds. Menachem, cited by Rashi, reads it as "healed", from מזור, a cure; Ibn Ezra reads it as "pressed out", like wringing a fleece.

sources.quote: הַנְּגָעִים הָאֵלֶּה לֹא זוֹרוּ עַל יְדֵי רוֹפְאִים אַבְקַת סַמָּנֵי תַחְבּוֹשֶׁת
sources.says: Rashi says doctors did not sprinkle the powder of bandage medicines on these wounds.

sources.quote: וּמְנַחֵם פֵּרֵשׁ לְשׁוֹן רְפוּאָה
sources.says: Rashi reports that Menachem read it as healing.

sources.quote: כי המכה לא תרפא עד שתוזר הליחה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says a wound does not heal until the fluid is pressed out.

1:7.headline: "Overthrown like זרים": by strangers, or by a flood?
1:7.body: The verse ends "desolate, as overthrown by זרים". Radak compares it to Sodom, a people "strange" to the fear of God; Radak and Ibn Ezra also read זרים as זרם, a flood that sweeps the land.

sources.quote: כמהפכת סדום ועמרה שהיו זרים מיראת האל
sources.says: Radak says it is like the overthrow of Sodom and Gomorrah, who were strangers to the fear of God.

sources.quote: ויש מפרשים זרים כמו זרם מטר
sources.says: Radak reports a reading of זרים as a rainstorm flood.

sources.quote: ויתכן היות זרים מגזרת זרם
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says זרים may come from זרם, a flood.

1:8.headline: Why a hut in a cucumber field is a מלונה, a night-lodge
1:8.body: Rashi says a vineyard guard lives in his hut day and night, against birds and thieves, so it is a סוכה. Cucumbers are too hard for birds, so that guard comes only at night, and his hut is a מלונה, from לון, "to spend the night".

sources.quote: זוֹ שֶׁבַּכֶּרֶם קְרוּיָה סֻכָּה, לְפִי שֶׁהוּא גָּר שָׁם יוֹמָם וָלַיְלָה
sources.says: Rashi says the hut in the vineyard is called a סוכה because the guard lives there day and night.

sources.quote: לְפִיכָךְ נִקְרֵאת מְלוּנָה עַל שֶׁהִיא לִינַת הַלֵּילוֹת
sources.says: Rashi says the cucumber-field hut is called מלונה because it is only for the nights.

1:9.headline: "A tiny remnant" or "almost like Sodom"? The accents decide
1:9.body: Rashi joins כמעט to what follows: we were almost like Sodom. Ibn Ezra says the accent marks join it to the words before, "a very small remnant", and that keeping to the accents is a great rule.

sources.quote: כִּמְעָט כִּסְדֹם הָיִינוּ. כֻּלָּנוּ כָּלִים
sources.says: Rashi reads it as "we were almost like Sodom": all of us destroyed.

sources.quote: כמעט. דבק עם שריד בעבור טעם המפסיק, כי עיקר גדול הו' לשמור דרך הטעמים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says כמעט goes with "remnant" because of the accent, and following the accents is a great principle.

1:10.headline: They said "almost like Sodom"; the prophet answered "rulers of Sodom"
1:10.body: In verse 9 the people said they were nearly like Sodom. The Talmud says the prophet took them at their word and called them "rulers of Sodom", and Rashi draws the lesson: do not open your mouth to the Satan.

sources.quote: כִּמְעַט כִּסְדוֹם הָיִינוּ״, מַאי אַהֲדַר לְהוּ נָבִיא — ״שִׁמְעוּ דְבַר ה׳ קְצִינֵי סְדוֹם
sources.says: The Talmud says: they said "we were almost like Sodom", and the prophet answered "hear, rulers of Sodom".

sources.quote: אַל יִפְתַּח אָדָם פִּיו לַשָּׂטָן
sources.says: Rashi says from here the sages taught that a person should not open his mouth to the Satan.

sources.quote: זאת תשובת הנביא בעבור שאמרו הם כסדום היינו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says this is the prophet's answer to their saying they were like Sodom.

1:16.headline: "Wash yourselves" opens ten calls to return
1:16.body: Rashi counts ten commands from רחצו, "wash", to לכו, "come", in verse 18, and matches them to the Ten Days of Repentance. Radak says the washing is of the heart.

sources.quote: עֶשֶׂר אַזְהָרוֹת שֶׁל לְשׁוֹן תְּשׁוּבָה יֵשׁ כָּאן, כְּנֶגֶד עֲשֶׂרֶת יְמֵי תְּשׁוּבָה
sources.says: Rashi says there are ten commands of repentance here, matching the Ten Days of Repentance.

sources.quote: רחיצת הלב וזכותו
sources.says: Radak says it means washing and cleansing the heart.

1:17.headline: חמוץ: the robbed man, or a ruling left to rise like dough
1:17.body: Rashi and Radak read חמוץ as "robbed", from a verse in Psalms. The sages read it from חמץ, leaven: happy is the judge who lets his ruling sit and does not rush.

sources.quote: חָמוֹץ. גָּזוּל
sources.says: Rashi says חמוץ means robbed.

sources.quote: ורבותינו פירשו לשון חמץ ואמרו אשרי הדיין שמחמץ את דינו
sources.says: Radak says the sages read it from leaven: happy is the judge who lets his ruling ferment.

sources.quote: ורבי' פרשוהו שיחמצו הדין, והטע' שלא ידינו מיד
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the sages took it to mean the judges should not rule at once.

1:17.headline: אשרו: strengthen, guide, or set straight the wronged?
1:17.body: Rashi says it means "strengthen" the robbed man, from a Talmudic word, or "guide" him on the right path. Metzudat Zion reads it as ישרו, "set straight".

sources.quote: אַשְּׁרוּ חָמוֹץ. הַחֲזִיקוּ אֶת הַגָּזוּל
sources.says: Rashi says it means strengthen the robbed man.

sources.quote: לָשׁוֹן אַחֵר: הַדְרִיכוּהוּ בִּנְתִיב אֱמֶת
sources.says: Rashi's second reading: guide him on the path of truth.

sources.quote: אשרו. מל׳ ישר
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it comes from ישר, straight.

1:18.headline: Red as worm-dye: why wool here, and snow before?
1:18.body: Rashi says תולע is red dye from grains with a worm in each. Radak's father noticed the pairs: sins only somewhat red turn white as snow, deep-red sins turn white as wool, which is less white.

sources.quote: צֶבַע שֶׁצּוֹבְעִים בּוֹ אָדוֹם, גַּרְעִינִים הֵם, וְיֵשׁ תּוֹלָעִים בְּכָל אֶחָד וְאֶחָד
sources.says: Rashi says it is a red dye made from grains, with worms in each one.

sources.quote: ואם יהיו אדומים מאד כתולע אז יהיו כצמר שאינו לבן מאד כמו השלג
sources.says: Radak says, citing his father, that very red sins become like wool, which is not as white as snow.

1:21.headline: "Full of justice": 481 synagogues, the number of מלאתי
1:21.body: The word has an extra yod. Rashi cites the Pesikta: Jerusalem had 481 synagogues, the number value of מלאתי.

sources.quote: בָּתֵּי כְנֵסִיּוֹת הָיוּ בִּירוּשָׁלַיִם כְּמִנְיַן מְלֵאֲתִי בְּגִימַטְרִיָּא
sources.says: Rashi cites the Pesikta: Jerusalem had as many synagogues as the number value of מלאתי.

sources.quote: מלאתי משפט. היו"ד נוספת
sources.says: Radak notes the yod in מלאתי is extra.

1:21.headline: "Justice lodged in her": overnight, or always?
1:21.body: ילין means to spend the night. Rashi says the morning offering atoned for the night's sins, or that judges let a death case wait overnight to find merit; Radak says it just means justice was always there.

sources.quote: תָּמִיד שֶׁל שַׁחַר הָיָה מְכַפֵּר עַל עֲבֵירוֹת שֶׁל הַלַּיְלָה
sources.says: Rashi says the morning offering atoned for the sins of the night.

sources.quote: שֶׁהָיוּ מְלִינִים בָּהּ דִּינֵי נְפָשׁוֹת
sources.says: Rashi's second reading: they let capital cases wait overnight.

sources.quote: ילין אינו לשון לינה ממש אלא לשון שקידה וההתמדה בדבר
sources.says: Radak says ילין is not literal lodging but constancy.

1:23.headline: שלמנים: judges trading favors, "rule for me, I'll rule for you"
1:23.body: שלמנים comes from שלם, "repay". The Targum, cited by Rashi, pictures one judge telling another: rule for me in my case today, and I will repay you in yours.

sources.quote: עֲבִיד לִי טַב בְּדִינִי וַאֲשַׁלֵּם לָךְ בְּדִינָךְ
sources.says: Rashi cites the Targum: do me good in my case and I will repay you in yours.

sources.quote: הֲוֵי רוֹדֵף תַּשְׁלוּם גְּמוּלוֹת
sources.says: Rashi says this is chasing the repayment of favors.

1:24.headline: Here הוי is a summons, not a groan
1:24.body: Rashi says this הוי is one of the rare ones that announce: let everyone know God will settle accounts with His foes. Ibn Ezra reads it the usual way, "woe to them".

sources.quote: הוֹי. לְשׁוֹן הַזְמָנָה וְהַכְרָזָה
sources.says: Rashi says הוי here is a word of summons and announcement.

sources.quote: הוי. כמו אוי להם בעשותי כך
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means "woe to them" when I do this.

1:25.headline: "As with בר": lye soap, or plain purity?
1:25.body: Rashi says בר is lye soap, named for cleanness, as in "pure of heart". Ibn Ezra prefers plain purity, as in "the cleanness of my hands".

sources.quote: כַּבֹּר. לְשׁוֹן בּוֹרִית
sources.says: Rashi says בר means lye soap.

sources.quote: וּלְשׁוֹנוֹ לְשׁוֹן נִקָּיוֹן
sources.says: Rashi says the word means cleanness.

sources.quote: כבור. כאילו כבורית, והנכון שהוא כבור ידי
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says some read it as soap, but it is better read as the purity of my hands.

1:29.headline: אילים here are trees, not the rams of verse 11
1:29.body: In verse 11 אילים are rams for offerings. Here Rashi and Radak say the same letters mean terebinth trees, under which people worshipped idols.

sources.quote: מֵאֵילִים. לְשׁוֹן אֵלָה, מִין אִילָן
sources.says: Rashi says אילים here comes from אלה, a kind of tree.

sources.quote: לַעֲבוֹד תַּחְתֵּיהֶם עֲבוֹדַת כּוֹכָבִים
sources.says: Rashi says they desired the trees to worship idols under them.

sources.quote: ואילים כמו אילנים
sources.says: Radak says אילים means trees.

1:31.headline: ופעלו: "his work", or "the one who made it"?
1:31.body: The Targum reads it as "the work of their hands". Rashi says the vowel shows it means "its maker": the strong man's riches become tinder, and the one who made them the spark.

sources.quote: וְאֵין זֶה אַחַר לְשׁוֹן הָעִבְרִית
sources.says: Rashi says the Targum's "their handiwork" does not follow the Hebrew.

sources.quote: וְהָעוֹשֶׂה אוֹתוֹ תֹּקֶף יִהְיֶה לְנִיצוֹץ אֵשׁ
sources.says: Rashi says the one who made that strength will become a spark of fire.

sources.quote: וְעוֹבַד יֶדְהוֹן כְּנִיצוֹץ נוּרָא
sources.says: The Targum renders it: the work of their hands like a spark of fire.

10:1.headline: Written papers, or judges who order the writing?
10:1.body: Rashi reads ומכתבים as a noun, "writings", built the way Arabic builds words. Ibn Ezra and Radak read it as a verb: the judges make their scribes write down the wrong.

sources.quote: לְשׁוֹן עֲרָבִי הוּא, כְּמוֹ ״מִכְתָּבִים״
sources.says: Rashi says the word is an Arabic-style form that means the same as the Hebrew word for writings.

sources.quote: פועל יוצא לשני' פעולים, מהבנין הכבד הדגוש
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it is a verb that acts on two objects: one person makes another write.

sources.quote: ואמר ומכתבים על הדיינים, כי הם מכתבים
sources.says: Radak says the word is about the judges, who have the scribes do the writing.

10:3.headline: "Your glory" here means the money you stole
10:3.body: כבודכם usually means "your honor", but Rashi and Metzudat Zion say it means the wealth the judges piled up by robbery. Ibn Ezra says it means their crowds of people.

sources.quote: כבודכם. כן יקרא העושר
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says wealth is called כבוד, as in Genesis 31:1.

sources.quote: אֶת כָּל הַכָּבוֹד אֲשֶׁר אַתֶּם קוֹבְצִים מִן הַגָּזֵל
sources.says: Rashi says it is all the wealth they gathered by robbery, which they will leave behind in exile.

sources.quote: כבודכם. הוא ההמון
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says כבודכם means the multitude.

10:4.headline: "Without me" or "except": one small word, two readings
10:4.body: Radak says the י at the end of בלתי can mean "me": this people is without God, so they will crouch among prisoners. Others read it as plain "except": only someone who hides among the captives and the dead will escape.

sources.quote: לפי שהעם הזה בלתי אינם עמי ולא שומעים אלי
sources.says: Radak reads בלתי as "without me": the people are not God's people and do not listen to Him.

sources.quote: יש מפרשים כן לא ימלט אלא מי שיכרע ויחביא עצמו בין האסורים
sources.says: Radak reports others who say only one who crouches and hides among the prisoners will escape.

sources.quote: לא ימלט רק מי שיכרע תחת אסיר
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says no one will escape except one who crouches under the prisoners.

10:5.headline: "Woe, Assyria" or "Come here, Assyria"?
10:5.body: הוי often means "woe", and Metzudat David reads it as a cry of grief. Ibn Ezra and Radak say it is a call: God summons Assyria to come and punish Israel.

sources.quote: לשון קריאה, קורא לו שיבא על ארץ ישראל
sources.says: Radak says הוי is a word of calling: God calls Assyria to come against the land of Israel.

sources.quote: הוי אשור. הוא דרך קריאה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it is a way of calling out.

sources.quote: יש להתאונן על כי אשור יהיה השבט
sources.says: Metzudat David says it is a lament that Assyria will be the rod.

10:13.headline: Erased borders: the Talmud rules the old nations are mixed
10:13.body: Sennacherib boasts that he removed the borders between peoples. In the Talmud, Rabbi Yehoshua uses this verse to let a convert from Ammon marry into Israel, because Sennacherib mixed up all the nations.

sources.quote: כְּבָר עָלָה סַנְחֵרִיב מֶלֶךְ אַשּׁוּר וּבִלְבֵּל אֶת כׇּל הָאוּמּוֹת
sources.says: Rabbi Yehoshua says Sennacherib already came and mixed up all the nations, citing this verse.

sources.quote: לפי שכבש כל הארצות כאלו הסיר כל הגבולות
sources.says: Radak says that by conquering every land he was like one who took away all the borders.

10:16.headline: Inside "his fat ones" the Talmud hears "eight"
10:16.body: The Talmud hears שמונה, "eight", in במשמניו: Hezekiah, who has eight names, will punish Sennacherib, who also has eight. Radak gives the plain sense, his strongest and healthiest men.

sources.quote: יָבֹא חִזְקִיָּהוּ שֶׁיֵּשׁ לוֹ שְׁמוֹנָה שֵׁמוֹת, וְיִפָּרַע מִסַּנְחֵרִיב שֶׁיֵּשׁ לוֹ שְׁמוֹנָה שֵׁמוֹת
sources.says: The Talmud explains the phrase: Hezekiah with eight names will come and punish Sennacherib with eight names.

sources.quote: ופירוש במשמניו גדולים שבהם גבורים ובריאים
sources.says: Radak says his "fat ones" are the great men among them, strong and healthy.

10:16.headline: "Under his glory": under his clothes, or his very body?
10:16.body: Rabbi Yochanan says כבודו, "his glory", means his clothes, which he called "the things that honor me". Rabbi Elazar says it means the body itself: the souls burned and the bodies stayed whole, like Aaron's sons.

sources.quote: תַּחַת כְּבוֹדוֹ, וְלֹא כְּבוֹדוֹ מַמָּשׁ. כִּי הָא דְּרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן קָרֵי לֵיהּ לְמָאנֵיהּ ״מְכַבְּדוֹתַי״
sources.says: Rabbi Yochanan says it means under his honor, not his actual self, since he called his clothes "my honorers".

sources.quote: תַּחַת כְּבוֹדוֹ מַמָּשׁ, כִּשְׂרֵיפַת בְּנֵי אַהֲרֹן
sources.says: Rabbi Elazar says it means his actual self, burned like the sons of Aaron.

sources.quote: תַּחַת בִּגְדֵיהֶם יִהְיוּ נִשְׂרָפִין, הַבְּגָדִים הֵם מְכַבְּדִים אֶת הָאָדָם
sources.says: Rashi says they will burn under their clothes, because clothes give a person honor.

10:19.headline: So few that a child could write them: exactly ten
10:19.body: The verse says a boy could write down the survivors, and the Talmud says that means ten. Rashi explains that every child can write a small י, the letter worth ten.

sources.quote: כַּמָּה נַעַר יָכוֹל לִכְתּוֹב? עֲשָׂרָה
sources.says: Rav says ten survived, since ten is what a child can write.

sources.quote: עֲשָׂרָה נִשְׁאַר מֵהֶם, שֶׁאֵין לְךָ קָטָן שֶׁאֵינוֹ כּוֹתֵב יוּ״ד קְטַנָּה
sources.says: Rashi cites the sages: ten were left, because every child can write a small yod.

10:21.headline: Isaiah's son's name, explained: "a remnant will return"
10:21.body: שאר ישוב, "a remnant will return", is the name of Isaiah's son (Isaiah 7:3). Ibn Ezra says this verse spells out the name: what is left of Jacob will come back to God.

sources.quote: שאר ישוב. הוא שם בן הנביא, והנה פירש כי טעם שאר ישוב על שאר יעקב
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says שאר ישוב is the prophet's son's name, and here the verse explains it as the remnant of Jacob.

sources.quote: שְׁאָר דְלָא חֲטוּ וּדְתָבוּ מֵחֲטָאָה
sources.says: The Targum says the remnant are those who did not sin and those who turned back from sin.

10:27.headline: The yoke breaks because of oil: Hezekiah's lamps of Torah
10:27.body: שמן means oil or fat, and Radak notes the reversal: a yoke usually wears away an ox's fat, but here the fat breaks the yoke. The Talmud reads it as the oil Hezekiah kept burning in the houses of study, and the Targum as "the anointed one".

sources.quote: חוּבַּל עוֹל שֶׁל סַנְחֵרִיב מִפְּנֵי שַׁמְנוֹ שֶׁל חִזְקִיָּהוּ, שֶׁהָיָה דּוֹלֵק בְּבָתֵּי כְנֵסִיּוֹת וּבְבָתֵּי מִדְרָשׁוֹת
sources.says: Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha says Sennacherib's yoke was broken because of Hezekiah's oil, which burned in synagogues and study halls.

sources.quote: והנה הוא בהפך כי שמן צואר השור ישחת מהעול אשר עליו תמיד
sources.says: Radak says the image is reversed: normally the yoke wears away the fat of the ox's neck.

sources.quote: וְיִתְּבְרוּן עַמְמַיָא מִן קֳדָם מְשִׁיחָא
sources.says: The Targum says the nations will be broken before the anointed one.

10:30.headline: Laish, the town, heard as ליש, a lion: Nebuchadnezzar
10:30.body: ליש is one of the Bible's words for a lion. The Talmud reads "listen, Laish" as a warning: do not fear Sennacherib, fear Nebuchadnezzar, who is likened to a lion.

sources.quote: אִיסְתַּפִי מִנְּבוּכַדְנֶאצַּר הָרָשָׁע, דִּמְתִיל כְּאַרְיֵה
sources.says: The Talmud says to fear Nebuchadnezzar, who is compared to a lion.

sources.quote: שִׁשָּׁה שֵׁמוֹת יֵשׁ לָאֲרִי
sources.says: Rabbi Yochanan says the lion has six names, and ליש is one of them.

10:31.headline: Not "grew bold" but "ran for shelter"
10:31.body: העיזו looks like it comes from עז, "strong". Rashi and Radak say it means they gathered in to flee, like "bring your cattle in to shelter" in Exodus 9:19.

sources.quote: הֵעִיזוּ. נֶאֶסְפוּ לִבְרוֹחַ
sources.says: Rashi says it means they gathered together to flee.

sources.quote: והעיזו, לשון אסיפה, כמו שלח העז את מקנך
sources.says: Radak says it is a word for gathering in, as in Exodus 9:19.

sources.quote: הבריחו נפשם או אחרים מישראל
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says they made themselves, or others, run away.

10:32.headline: "Still today at Nob": one day left of an old guilt
10:32.body: The Talmud reads עוד היום, "still today", as one day left of Israel's guilt for Nob, the priests' town that Saul destroyed. Sennacherib's stargazers told him he could take Jerusalem only on that day, so he rushed.

sources.quote: אוֹתוֹ הַיּוֹם נִשְׁתַּיֵּיר מֵעֲוֹנָהּ שֶׁל נוֹב
sources.says: Rav Huna says that one day was all that remained of the sin of Nob.

sources.quote: לְפִי שֶׁאָמְרוּ לוֹ אִיצְטַגְנִינָיו
sources.says: Rashi says he hurried because his astrologers told him he would win if he fought that day.

10:33.headline: A verb made from "branch" that means cutting branches off
10:33.body: מסעף appears only here and comes from סעיף, a branch, but it means cutting branches off. Metzudat Zion compares ויסקלהו in Isaiah 5:2, which means clearing away stones.

sources.quote: מסעף, יכרית הסעיפים, כמו לא תפאר אחריך
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means cutting off the branches, like "do not go over the boughs" in Deuteronomy 24:20.

sources.quote: יסיר הסעיפים וכן ויסקלהו
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means removing the branches, just as ויסקלהו means removing stones.

10:34.headline: "The mighty one": an angel, Hezekiah, or a king of Rome
10:34.body: Rashi says the forest falls by an angel, or by the merit of Hezekiah, Israel's mighty ruler. In the Talmud, Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai tells Vespasian that אדיר means a king and the Lebanon means the Temple.

sources.quote: עַל יְדֵי מַלְאָךְ יִפּוֹלוּ
sources.says: Rashi says they will fall by an angel.

sources.quote: בִּזְכוּת חִזְקִיָּהוּ שֶׁהוּא אַדִּירָם וּמוֹשְׁלָם שֶׁל יִשְׂרָאֵל
sources.says: Rashi also says it means by the merit of Hezekiah, Israel's mighty one and ruler.

sources.quote: וְאֵין ״אַדִּיר״ אֶלָּא מֶלֶךְ
sources.says: The Talmud says אדיר means a king.

sources.quote: וְאֵין ״לְבָנוֹן״ אֶלָּא בֵּית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ
sources.says: The Talmud says the Lebanon here means the Temple.

11:1.headline: A shoot from a stump, or a king's scepter
11:1.body: Rashi and Metzudat Zion read חטר as a rod: a king's scepter. The Targum drops the tree picture and says plainly that a king will come from Jesse's sons, and the Messiah from his grandsons.

sources.quote: חֹטֶר. שֵׁבֶט מְלוּכָה
sources.says: Rashi says חטר is a royal scepter.

sources.quote: ענינו כמו מטה וכן חוטר גאוה (משלי יד) ורצה לומר שבט מלוכה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means a rod, as in Proverbs 14:3, and here a royal scepter.

sources.quote: וְיִפּוֹק מַלְכָּא מִבְּנוֹהִי דְיִשַׁי וּמְשִׁיחָא מִבְּנֵי בְנוֹהִי יִתְרַבֵּי
sources.says: The Targum renders it: a king will come from Jesse's sons, and the Messiah will grow up from his grandsons.

11:1.headline: The stump of a felled tree can still sprout
11:1.body: Radak says גזע is what is left of a cut-down tree above the ground, and new shoots grow from its sides. Israel's kingdom was cut down like a tree, but the stump and roots remain, so it can grow again.

sources.quote: ופירוש גזע מה שנשאר מן העץ על הארץ ומצדי הגזע יעלו הנצרים
sources.says: Radak says the גזע is what remains of the tree on the ground, and shoots come up from its sides.

sources.quote: ולפי שישראל גלו מארצם זה כמה שנים ונפסקה מלכותם כאלו נכרת העץ אבל הגזע והשרשים נשארו
sources.says: Radak says Israel's exile and lost kingdom are like a felled tree, but the stump and roots remain.

11:4.headline: A rod made of words
11:4.body: The king strikes the land with “the rod of his mouth.” Ibn Ezra says his mouth works like a rod against the wicked, and Radak says he will curse them and they will die.

sources.quote: בפיו כאילו הוא שבט לרשעים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says he strikes with his mouth as though it were a rod for the wicked.

sources.quote: ופירוש בשבט פיו וברוח שפתיו, כי יקללם וימותו
sources.says: Radak says the rod of his mouth and breath of his lips mean he will curse them and they will die.

11:8.headline: The פתן, an old snake too deaf for any charm
11:8.body: Rashi says a snake that grows old goes deaf and is called a פתן. No snake charmer's whisper works on it, as Psalms 58:6 says.

sources.quote: נָחָשׁ מִשֶּׁהִזְקִין נַעֲשָׂה חֵרֵשׁ, וְנִקְרָא פֶּתֶן, שׁוּב אֵין לוֹ לַחַשׁ
sources.says: Rashi says a snake that has grown old becomes deaf and is called a פתן, and no charm works on it anymore.

11:8.headline: A snake's hole, or the glint of a snake's eye
11:8.body: Metzudat Zion reads מאורת as a hole or crack. Ibn Ezra and the Targum read it from אור, light: the snake's eye shines in the dark, and the child reaches for it thinking it is a bright stone.

sources.quote: ענינו בקוע וחריץ כמו באורים כבדו ה׳
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the word means a split or crack.

sources.quote: מאורת. העין שהיא בעלת האור
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it is the eye, which holds light.

sources.quote: כי הנחש כשהוא בחורו והוא מקום חשך וגלגל עינו מאיר והיונק רואה את האורה מבחוץ וסבור אבן מאירה היא
sources.says: Radak explains the Targum: the snake sits in its dark hole with its eye shining, and the baby sees the light and thinks it is a glowing stone.

11:11.headline: God “acquires” his people without paying anyone
11:11.body: קנה usually means to buy. Metzudat Zion says it can mean taking ownership with no price and no seller, as when God is called owner of heaven and earth (Genesis 14:19).

sources.quote: מצינו לשון קנין בלא מחיר ואף אם אין מוכר וכן קונה שמים וארץ
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the word for acquiring is used with no price and even with no seller, as in “owner of heaven and earth.”

11:13.headline: Ephraim: the northern tribes, or a Messiah descended from Joseph
11:13.body: Radak says Ephraim means all the tribes except Judah, and their old rivalry with Judah will end. Rashi reads it as two messiahs, one from Joseph and one from David, who will not envy each other.

sources.quote: ואפרים. ר"ל כל ישראל לבד מיהודה, ומפני שהיו ישראל מקנאים במלכות בית דוד
sources.says: Radak says Ephraim means all Israel apart from Judah, who were jealous of the house of David's kingship.

sources.quote: מָשִׁיחַ בֶּן יוֹסֵף וּמָשִׁיחַ בֶּן דָּוִד לֹא יְקַנְּאוּ זֶה בָּזֶה
sources.says: Rashi says the Messiah son of Joseph and the Messiah son of David will not envy each other.

11:14.headline: Fly at the Philistines, or grow tired from fighting them
11:14.body: Rashi and Radak read ועפו as flying: Israel will rush together at the Philistines. Others, reported by Radak, read it from עיף, tired: they will wear themselves out striking them.

sources.quote: יָעוּפוּ וְיָרוּצוּ יִשְׂרָאֵל שְׁכֶם אֶחָד עַל הַפְּלִשְׁתִּים
sources.says: Rashi says Israel will fly and run together, as one shoulder, against the Philistines.

sources.quote: ויש מפרשים ועפו ענין עיף ויגע, כלומר יהיו עיפים מהכות בכתף פלשתים
sources.says: Radak reports others who read ועפו as tired and weary: they will be worn out from striking the Philistines.

11:15.headline: A word found nowhere else: God's strong wind, or the waves
11:15.body: Rashi and Ibn Ezra say בעים has no match in Scripture and read it from context: “with the strength of his wind.” Radak's brother read it from עי, a heap, so it means “in the waves.”

sources.quote: אֵין לוֹ דִמְיוֹן בַּמִּקְרָא, וּלְפִי הָעִנְיָן יִפָּתֵר: בְּחֹזֶק רוּחוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says the word has no parallel in Scripture, and by context means the strength of his wind.

sources.quote: אין לו אח, והמ"ם שורש, וטעמו כמו בכח
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the word has no brother, its mem is part of the root, and it means “with strength.”

sources.quote: ורבי אחי רבי משה פירש עים מן לעי השדה שפירושו גל, ופירש בעים כמו בגלים
sources.says: Radak says his brother Rabbi Moshe read עים from עי, a heap, so בעים means “in the waves.”

12:2.headline: Half of God's name, next to the whole name
12:2.body: יה is a short form of God's name, and here it stands beside the full name. Rashi says the name has been split until now and becomes whole when Amalek falls.

sources.quote: עַד הֵנָּה הָיָה שְׁמוֹ חָלוּק, וּבְמַפַּלְתּוֹ שֶׁל עֲמָלֵק נַעֲשָׂה שָׁלֵם
sources.says: Rashi says that until now God's name was divided, and at Amalek's downfall it becomes complete.

sources.quote: פרוש חצי השם בספר תהלו'
sources.says: Ibn Ezra calls יה half of the Name and says he explains it in his Psalms commentary.

12:3.headline: Drawing water: new teaching, or the Temple's water festival?
12:3.body: The Targum reads 'you will draw water' as 'you will receive new teaching'. The Talmud uses the verse for the water-drawing on Sukkot, and the Jerusalem Talmud says they drew holy spirit there.

sources.quote: וּתְקַבְּלוּן אוּלְפַן חֲדַת בְּחֶדְוָא
sources.says: The Targum translates: you will receive new teaching with joy.

sources.quote: דְּאָמַר קְרָא: ״וּשְׁאַבְתֶּם מַיִם בְּשָׂשׂוֹן
sources.says: The Talmud gives this verse as the source for the water ceremony of Sukkot.

sources.quote: לָמָּה נִקְרָא שְׁמָהּ בֵּית שׁוֹאֵבָה. שֶׁמִּשָּׁם שׁוֹאֲבִים רוּחַ הַקּוֹדֶשׁ
sources.says: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says the water-drawing is so named because from there they drew holy spirit.

13:1.headline: A burden, a prophecy, or a cup of curses?
13:1.body: Rashi says משא is a burden of punishment laid on Babylon. Metzudat Zion says a prophecy is called משא because it is carried in the mouth, and the Targum calls it a cup of cursing for Babylon to drink.

sources.quote: מַשָּׂא פֻּרְעָנוּת שֶׁעַל בָּבֶל
sources.says: Rashi says it is the burden of punishment on Babylon.

sources.quote: כן נקראת הנבואה ע״ש שהיא נשאת בפי האדם
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says prophecy is called משא because it is carried in a person's mouth.

sources.quote: מַטֵל כָּס דִי לְוָט לְאַשְׁקָאָה יַת בָּבֶל
sources.says: The Targum renders it as the cup of cursing to give Babylon to drink.

13:2.headline: Through the nobles' gates, or with drawn swords?
13:2.body: Rashi and Radak say פתחי means 'into the gates' of Babylon's nobles, with the word 'in' left unsaid. Rashi cites Menachem ben Saruq, who reads it as drawn swords, as in Psalms 55:22.

sources.quote: פִּתְחֵי. כְּמוֹ ׳בְּפִתְחֵי׳
sources.says: Rashi says פתחי means 'in the gates'.

sources.quote: ויבאו פתחי נדיבים. כמו בפתחי חסר בי"ת השמוש
sources.says: Radak says it means 'in the gates', with the letter ב missing.

sources.quote: וּמְנַחֵם בֶּן סָרוּק פָּתַר: ׳חֲרָבוֹת׳
sources.says: Rashi says Menachem ben Saruq explained it as swords.

13:3.headline: 'My holy ones': the Persians, set apart for war
13:3.body: Ibn Ezra and Metzudat Zion say מקדשי here means 'those I have set aside', as in 'make yourselves ready' (Numbers 11:18). Rashi says they are the Persians and Medes, and the Talmud says they are set aside for Gehinnom.

sources.quote: למקדשי. ענין הזמנה כמו התקדשו למחר
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means designating, as in 'prepare yourselves for tomorrow'.

sources.quote: למקודשי. הם המזומנים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says they are the ones designated.

sources.quote: וְהֵם פָּרַס וּמָדַי, אַנְשֵׁי כּוֹרֶשׁ וְדָרְיָוֶשׁ, שֶׁזִּמַּנְתִּים לְכָךְ
sources.says: Rashi says they are Persia and Media, the men of Cyrus and Darius, whom God designated for this.

sources.quote: אֵלּוּ הַפַּרְסִיִּים הַמְקוּדָּשִׁין וּמְזוּמָּנִין לְגֵיהִנָּם
sources.says: The Talmud says these are the Persians, set aside and designated for Gehinnom.

13:3.headline: God 'commanded' an army that chose to march
13:3.body: Radak says God stirred up the attackers, as if He had commanded them. Maimonides gives this verse as an example of the prophets saying 'God commanded' about things people did by their own choice.

sources.quote: שהעיר את רוחם לבא אל בבל והרי הם כאלו צוה וקדש וזמן אותם לבא
sources.says: Radak says God stirred their spirit to come to Babylon, and so it is as if He commanded them.

sources.quote: צויתי. הערתי לבם
sources.says: Metzudat David says 'I commanded' means 'I stirred their hearts'.

sources.quote: וכן נאמר על מה שסיבתו היא בחירוֹת אנושיות
sources.says: Maimonides says things caused by human choice are also described as God's doing, and cites this verse.

13:6.headline: Ruin (שד) from the Almighty (שדי)
13:6.body: The verse sets שד, 'ruin', next to שדי, a name of God. Ibn Ezra says the ruin comes from God, so no one can stop it, and he cites others who read שדי as 'a mighty robber'.

sources.quote: כי זה השוד בא מהשם ומי יוכל לבטלו, ויש אומרים כי שדי כגבור שודד
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says this ruin comes from God and no one can cancel it, and cites others who say שדי means a mighty robber.

sources.quote: כדרך השוד הבא משדי בעל היכולת
sources.says: Metzudat David says it is like ruin that comes from Shaddai, the One with all power.

sources.quote: כשוד שיבא מחזק שאין דרך להנצל ממנו
sources.says: Radak says it is like ruin from a mighty one, with no way to escape it.

13:8.headline: Birth pains named after door hinges
13:8.body: Rashi and Metzudat Zion say צירים are the pains of a woman giving birth. The word is ציר, a hinge, because the 'doors' of the womb swing open.

sources.quote: שֶׁצִּירֵי דַּלְתֵי בִּטְנָהּ מִתְפָּרְקִים לְהִפָּתֵחַ
sources.says: Rashi says the hinges of the doors of her womb come loose so they can open.

sources.quote: הם יסורי אשה הכורעת לילד שצירי דלתי בטנה מתפרקין להפתח
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says these are the pains of a woman in labor, when the hinges of her womb's doors loosen to open.

13:8.headline: Faces like flames, or the faces of the Lehabim?
13:8.body: Radak says their faces burn red with shame, and Rashi says the attackers' faces are yellow and frightening. Ibn Ezra cites others who say להבים is the name of a people, like the Cushites.

sources.quote: כאדם שיש לו בשת שישובו פניו אדומים
sources.says: Radak says it is like a person ashamed, whose face turns red.

sources.quote: שֶׁפְּנֵיהֶם צְהוּבִים וּמְאוּיָּמִין מְאֹד
sources.says: Rashi says their faces are yellow and very frightening.

sources.quote: ויש אומרים כי להבים גוי ככושים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra cites others who say להבים is a nation, like the Cushites.

13:10.headline: The sun goes dark only for the defeated
13:10.body: Rashi says that in their distress the sun only seems dark to them. Maimonides says no one should think the stars really changed when Babylon fell: this is how a beaten man sees the world, when every light looks black.

sources.quote: מִתּוֹךְ צָרָתָם נִדְמֶה לָהֶם כְּאִלּוּ חָשַׁךְ הַשֶּׁמֶשׁ
sources.says: Rashi says from their distress it seems to them as if the sun has gone dark.

sources.quote: הנביאים מדברים דרך משל
sources.says: Radak says the prophets are speaking in images.

sources.quote: אלא זה תיאור מצבו של המובס, שהוא רואה בלי ספק כל אור
sources.says: Maimonides says this describes the state of the defeated, who sees every light as black.

13:12.headline: Who becomes dearer than gold?
13:12.body: Radak says human life will be worth more than gold, because the Medes will take no ransom to spare anyone. Rashi says it is Daniel, honored that night when he read the writing on the wall, and the Targum says it is those who fear God.

sources.quote: לא יקחו מדי ופרס בהם משקלם זהב שלא יהרגו אותם
sources.says: Radak says the Medes and Persians will not take their weight in gold to spare them.

sources.quote: בּוֹ בַּלַּיְלָה אֲכַבֵּד אֶת דָּנִיֵּאל מִפָּז
sources.says: Rashi says that very night God will honor Daniel above fine gold.

sources.quote: אֲחַבֵּב דַחֲלַי מִדַהֲבָא
sources.says: The Targum renders it 'I will love those who fear Me more than gold'.

13:15.headline: One who joined the city, or one swept away?
13:15.body: Rashi and Radak read הנספה from 'add': anyone who joined the city to shelter there during the siege will die by the sword. Radak cites others who read it as 'swept away': whoever's time to die has come will die by the sword, not in bed.

sources.quote: עַל בְּנֵי הָעִיר לִהְיוֹת נִקְלָט עִמָּהֶם בַּמָּצוֹר
sources.says: Rashi says it is one who joined the city's people to take shelter with them in the siege.

sources.quote: ופירוש הנספה כמו נוסף שהוא מעם אחר ונוסף אל אנשי העיר
sources.says: Radak says it means one added, from another people, who joined the city's people.

sources.quote: ויש מפרשים כל הנספה כמו ויש נספה בלא משפט
sources.says: Radak cites others who read it as 'swept away', as in Proverbs 13:23.

13:16.headline: Written with a blunt word, read aloud with a polite one
13:16.body: The verse is written תשגלנה but read aloud as תשכבנה. Ibn Ezra says the written word is a term for lying with a woman, and it is read aloud as תשכבנה out of respect.

sources.quote: תשגלנה. כנוי לשכיבה ויקרא תשכבנה דרך כבוד
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says תשגלנה is a term for lying with a woman, and it is read תשכבנה out of respect.

sources.quote: תשגלנה. מלשון משגל ומשכב
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the written word comes from the words for intercourse and lying down.

13:19.headline: Five verses ago צבי was a gazelle; here it is glory
13:19.body: In verse 14 צבי is a gazelle. Here Metzudat Zion says it means beauty and splendor, and Radak says it means the city every kingdom longed for.

sources.quote: צבי. ענין הדר ופאר
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says צבי means beauty and splendor.

sources.quote: ופירוש צבי חפץ שכל הממלכות היו חפצים בה
sources.says: Radak says צבי means desire, since all the kingdoms desired Babylon.

13:21.headline: Hairy goats, or demons dancing in the ruins?
13:21.body: Rashi and Radak say שעירים are demons, and Radak says they are named for the goat-like shape believers see in them. Ibn Ezra says they are hairy wild creatures that look like demons.

sources.quote: וּשְׂעִירִים. שֵׁדִים
sources.says: Rashi says שעירים are demons.

sources.quote: ונקראו כן לפי שהם נראים כדמות שעירים למאמין בהם
sources.says: Radak says demons are called this because they appear like goats to those who believe in them.

sources.quote: כדמות שדים, והם שעירים ברים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says they look like demons and are hairy wild creatures.

13:22.headline: Wild animals will howl there, or make their dens there?
13:22.body: Rashi first reads וענה as 'dwell', as in מעון, a den, and then as raising the voice. Radak and Metzudat Zion take the voice: the animals will cry out like mourners.

sources.quote: ״וּמְעוֹנוֹתָיו טָרֶף״
sources.says: Rashi compares 'his dens with prey', reading it as dwelling.

sources.quote: וְיֵשׁ לְפָרֵשׁ עוֹד וְעָנָה: לְשׁוֹן עֲנִיַּת קוֹל
sources.says: Rashi gives a second reading: raising the voice.

sources.quote: והוא כקול אבל
sources.says: Radak says their cry is like the voice of mourning.

sources.quote: וענה. ענין הרמת קול
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means raising the voice.

13:22.headline: Not islands here, but wild creatures
13:22.body: איים usually means islands. Ibn Ezra says here it is the plural of איה, a bird of prey, and the Targum says wild cats will live in Babylon's palaces.

sources.quote: וענה איים. לשון רבים מן האיה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says איים is the plural of איה, a bird.

sources.quote: איים. שם חיה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it is the name of an animal.

sources.quote: וִינַפְצוּן חֲתוּלִין
sources.says: The Targum renders it as cats.

13:22.headline: In its palaces, or with its widows?
13:22.body: Radak and the Targum read באלמנותיו as בארמנותיו, 'in its palaces', with ל in place of ר. Ibn Ezra rejects that swap and reads 'widows': each animal crying out there with its widows.

sources.quote: באלמנותיו. כמו בארמנותיו, כתרגומו
sources.says: Radak says it means 'in its palaces', as the Targum renders it.

sources.quote: ״וְיָגוּרוּ חֲתוּלִים בְּאַרְמְנוֹתָיו״
sources.says: Rashi quotes the Targum: cats will live in its palaces.

sources.quote: ולא יתכן שיתחלף אות באות לבד מאותיות אה"וי
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says letters do not swap except the weak letters, so it cannot mean palaces.

sources.quote: וכן פירושו וענה שם כל אחד מהאיים עם אלמנותיו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra explains: each animal will cry out there with its widows.

14:1.headline: "Attached" to Jacob: the Talmud hears a skin rash in it
14:1.body: Plainly ונספחו means the converts will join the house of Jacob, as Rashi says. Rabbi Chelbo hears ספחת, a skin rash named in Leviticus, and says converts are as hard on Israel as a rash.

sources.quote: וְנִסְפְּחוּ. וְנוֹסְפוּ
sources.says: Rashi says ונספחו means they will be added.

sources.quote: קָשִׁים גֵּרִים לְיִשְׂרָאֵל כְּסַפַּחַת
sources.says: Rabbi Chelbo says converts are as hard for Israel as a skin rash.

sources.quote: כְּתִיב הָכָא ״וְנִסְפְּחוּ״, וּכְתִיב הָתָם ״לַשְּׂאֵת וְלַסַּפַּחַת״
sources.says: The Talmud links ונספחו here to ספחת, the rash in Leviticus.

14:4.headline: מדהבה: the city of gold, or "measure and bring"?
14:4.body: Radak and Metzudat Zion read it from the Aramaic דהב, "gold": Babylon, rich on the tribute of every land. The sages, cited by Rashi, split it into מדוד והבא, "measure and bring": the nation that demanded payment.

sources.quote: מדהבה. תרגום של זהב הוא דהבא
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the Aramaic for gold is דהבא.

sources.quote: והוא תאר לבבל שהיתה בעלת הזהב שהיתה לוקחת מס מכל הארצות
sources.says: Radak says it describes Babylon, owner of the gold, which took tribute from every land.

sources.quote: וְרַבּוֹתֵינוּ דָּרְשׁוּ (שבת קמט:-קנ.): הָאוֹמְרִים ״מְדוֹד וְהָבֵא״
sources.says: Rashi says the sages read it as those who say "measure and bring".

14:8.headline: Even the cypresses rejoice: real trees, or the rulers?
14:8.body: Ibn Ezra reads it plainly: the king used to cut the cypresses and cedars to build siege works. The Targum, cited by Rashi, reads the trees as rulers, and Radak says even kings were glad he fell.

sources.quote: הטעם שהיה מצוה לכרות הברושים והארזים לבנות מצור וסוללה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the king used to order cypresses and cedars cut for siege works.

sources.quote: ״אַף שַׁלְטוֹנִין חֲדִיאוּ״
sources.says: Rashi cites the Targum: even the rulers rejoiced.

sources.quote: והוא משל על המלכים
sources.says: Radak says the cypresses are a figure for the kings.

14:9.headline: רפאים: giants, or the dead, named for their weakness
14:9.body: Elsewhere the Refaim are a race of giants, and Rashi says those giants lie here. Metzudat Zion says the dead are called רפאים because death left them weak, from רפה, "slack".

sources.quote: רְפָאִים. עֲנָקִים הַשּׁוֹכְבִים שָׁם
sources.says: Rashi says the רפאים are the giants lying there.

sources.quote: כן נקראים המתים כי נרפו ונחלשו על ידי המיתה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the dead are called this because death made them slack and weak.

sources.quote: רפאים. הם המתים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the רפאים are the dead.

14:9.headline: "He-goats of the earth": kings who walk before the flock
14:9.body: עתודים are he-goats. Radak says kings are called this because, like the goats that walk in front of the flock, they lead the people.

sources.quote: כמו שהעתודים מנהיגים הצאן והולכים לפניהם
sources.says: Radak says kings are like he-goats, which lead the flock and walk before it.

sources.quote: הַכָּתוּב מוֹשְׁלָם לְפָרִים וְלִפְרוֹת וְלַעֲתוּדִים
sources.says: Rashi says Scripture compares rulers to bulls, cows, and he-goats.

14:11.headline: נבליך: your harps, or your scoundrels?
14:11.body: Rashi first reads נבל as a harp: the music of your court has gone down to the grave. He adds a second reading from נבל, "scoundrel": the uproar of the base men in your army.

sources.quote: נְבָלִים וְכִנּוֹרוֹת שֶׁהָיוּ מְזַמְּרִים לְפָנֶיךָ
sources.says: Rashi says these are the harps and lyres that played before you.

sources.quote: הֶמְיַת בְּנֵי נָבָל, עוֹשֵׂי נְבָלָה שֶׁבַּחֲיָלוֹתֶיךָ
sources.says: Rashi's second reading: the noise of the base men in your armies.

14:12.headline: הילל, "son of dawn": the morning star, named for shining
14:12.body: Ibn Ezra says הילל is the planet Venus, seen near daybreak and brighter than any star, named from הלל, "to shine". The king of Babylon was like the morning star, and has fallen from the sky.

sources.quote: הקרוב אל הדעת שהוא כוכב נוגה, והעד בן שחר
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it is most likely the planet Venus, as "son of dawn" shows.

sources.quote: על כן נקרא הילל, מגזרת לא יהלו אורם
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it is called הילל from the word for shining light.

sources.quote: כּוֹכַב הַנֹּגַהּ הַמֵּאִיר אוֹר כְּכוֹכַב הַבֹּקֶר
sources.says: Rashi says it is the bright star that shines like the morning star.

14:12.headline: חולש: overpowering the nations, or casting lots over them?
14:12.body: Radak and Ibn Ezra read it as "overpowering", as Joshua overpowered Amalek. The Talmud reads it as casting lots, and Rashi says the king drew lots to decide which king would serve him on which day.

sources.quote: חולש. כמו ויחלש יהושע
sources.says: Radak says it means overpowering, as Joshua overpowered Amalek.

sources.quote: מַאי מַשְׁמַע דְּהַאי ״חֲלָשִׁים״ לִישָּׁנָא דְפוּרָא הוּא
sources.says: The Talmud uses this verse to show that חלשים means lots.

sources.quote: מֵטִיל גּוֹרָל עֲלֵיהֶם, עַל הַמְּלָכִים, מִי מֵהֶם יְשָׁרֶתְךָ בְּיוֹם פְּלוֹנִי
sources.says: Rashi says he cast lots over the kings to see which would serve him on which day.

14:13.headline: "The mount of meeting": Zion, or Babylon itself?
14:13.body: Rashi says it is Mount Zion, where all Israel gathered. Radak's father read it as Babylon, where the whole world came to meet its king.

sources.quote: הַר שֶׁהַכֹּל מִתְוַעֲדִים שָׁם, הוּא הַר צִיּוֹן
sources.says: Rashi says it is the mountain where all gather, Mount Zion.

sources.quote: וקורא בבל הר מועד לפי שכל העולם היו נועדים שם אל מלך בבל
sources.says: Radak reports his father's reading: Babylon is the mount of meeting, where the world gathered to its king.

14:13.headline: "The far north": the north side of the Temple altar
14:13.body: ירכה means a side, literally a thigh. Rashi reads it as the Temple court, on the north side where offerings were slaughtered, as Leviticus says "on the side of the altar, northward".

sources.quote: בַּעֲזָרָה, מָקוֹם שֶׁנִּבְחַר בּוֹ יֶרֶךְ הַצְּפוֹנִי
sources.says: Rashi says it is the Temple court, the place chosen on the north side.

sources.quote: בירכתי. ענינו צד ועבר וכן ירך המזבח
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means side, as in the side of the altar.

14:19.headline: Thrown from his grave: his son had to see him dead
14:19.body: The sages tell that Nebuchadnezzar jailed his son for ruling in his place, and when he died the son would not take the throne until they dug up the body. Radak notes a version of the Targum that reads it more plainly: thrown from your place.

sources.quote: כְּשֶׁנַּעֲשָׂה בְּהֵמָה וְחַיָּה שֶׁבַע שָׁנִים, הִמְלִיכוּ עַם הָאָרֶץ אֶת אֱוִיל מְרוֹדַךְ
sources.says: Rashi says that when Nebuchadnezzar lived as a beast for seven years, the people crowned his son Evil-Merodach.

sources.quote: וְלֹא הֶאֱמִין, עַד שֶׁהוֹצִיאוּהוּ מִקִּבְרוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says the son did not believe his father was dead until they took him out of his grave.

sources.quote: וזה נוטה לדרך הפשט יותר
sources.says: Radak says the Targum version, "thrown from your place", is closer to the plain meaning.

14:19.headline: מטעני חרב: stabbed by the sword, a word read from Arabic
14:19.body: Rashi and Ibn Ezra say מטען means "stabbed" in Arabic. Ibn Ezra notes others read it from טען, "to load", and calls that far-fetched.

sources.quote: מְדֻקְּרֵי רְמָחִים, ׳מְדֻקָּר׳ בִּלְשׁוֹן עֲרָבִי: מֻטְעָן
sources.says: Rashi says it means pierced by spears, and "pierced" in Arabic is מטען.

sources.quote: בלשון קדר כמו מדוקרים, ויש אומר מגזרת טענו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says in Arabic it means stabbed, and some derive it from "load".

sources.quote: מטעני חרב. מדוקרי חרב והוא לשון ערבי
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means pierced by the sword, an Arabic word.

14:21.headline: ערים: cities, or enemies?
14:21.body: The Targum, Rashi, and Radak read ערים as "enemies", from a word also found in Samuel and in Aramaic: his sons must not rise and fill the world with foes. Rashi and Radak also read it plainly as cities: once his line is gone, towns will be rebuilt.

sources.quote: וְכֵן תִּרְגֵּם יוֹנָתָן: ״בַּעֲלֵי דְבָבִין״, כְּמוֹ ״וַיְהִי עָרֶךָ״
sources.says: Rashi says the Targum renders it "enemies", like "and He became your enemy".

sources.quote: וּמָלְאוּ פְנֵי תֵבֵל עֲיָרוֹת
sources.says: Rashi's second reading: the world will be filled with towns.

sources.quote: ערים. שונאים, כמו ויהי ערך
sources.says: Radak says ערים means enemies.

14:22.headline: "Offspring and descendant": the Talmud finds Queen Vashti here
14:22.body: נכד means a grandchild. The Talmud opens the book of Esther with this verse and says the נכד cut off from Babylon is Vashti; Rashi adds that the נין is Belshazzar.

sources.quote: ״נִין״ — זֶה מַלְכוּת, ״וָנֶכֶד״ — זוֹ וַשְׁתִּי
sources.says: The Talmud says נין is the kingdom and נכד is Vashti.

sources.quote: נִין – זֶה בֵּלְשַׁצַּר, וָנֶכֶד – זוֹ וַשְׁתִּי
sources.says: Rashi says נין is Belshazzar and נכד is Vashti.

sources.quote: ונכד. הוא בן הבן
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says נכד is a grandson.

14:23.headline: "Sweep her with a broom": the sages learned it from a maid
14:23.body: Ibn Ezra says every commentator agrees this word has no match. The Talmud says the rabbis did not know it until they heard a maid in Rabbi's house say, "take the broom and sweep the house".

sources.quote: לָא הֲווֹ יָדְעִי רַבָּנַן מַאי ״וְטֵאטֵאתִיהָ בְּמַטְאֲטֵא הַשְׁמֵד״
sources.says: The Talmud says the rabbis did not know what this phrase meant.

sources.quote: שְׁקוּלִי טָאטִיתָא וְטַאטִי בֵּיתָא
sources.says: They heard a maid say: take the broom and sweep the house.

sources.quote: כל המפרשים אמרו כי אין למלה הזאת אחות
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says all the commentators say this word has no sister.

14:23.headline: The קפוד: a creature named for curling itself up?
14:23.body: Radak gives its Arabic name and says it is always found near water. Ibn Ezra reports that some read it from קפד, "to roll up", because it rolls itself up.

sources.quote: וקפוד הוא הנקרא בערבי קנאפד
sources.says: Radak says the קפוד is called קנאפד in Arabic.

sources.quote: והיא נמצאת תמיד במקום המים
sources.says: Radak says it is always found near water.

sources.quote: יש אומרים שהוא מגזרת קפדתי כאורג חיי
sources.says: Ibn Ezra reports some derive it from "I rolled up my life like a weaver".

14:29.headline: "From the snake's root": a king, or Jesse, David's father?
14:29.body: Rashi says the snake is a king who struck the Philistines, and the viper from its root is Hezekiah, worse for them still. The Targum reads נחש as Jesse, and Radak notes Jesse was called Nahash: from his line comes the Messiah.

sources.quote: מִשּׁוֹרֶשׁ אוֹתוֹ נָחָשׁ יֵצֵא צֶפַע, שֶׁהוּא קָשֶׁה מִנָּחָשׁ
sources.says: Rashi says from that snake's root will come a viper, worse than a snake.

sources.quote: אֲרֵי מִבְּנֵי בְנוֹהִי דְיִשָׁי יִפּוֹק מְשִׁיחָא
sources.says: The Targum renders it: from the descendants of Jesse the Messiah will come.

sources.quote: אמר נחש על ישי כי כן נקרא כמו שכתוב אשר בא אל אביגיל בת נחש
sources.says: Radak says the Targum takes נחש as Jesse, who was called Nahash.

14:30.headline: "Firstborn of the poor": their leaders, or the poorest of all?
14:30.body: בכור means firstborn. Rashi and Metzudat Zion read it as "great ones", as God calls David His firstborn; Radak reads it as those who had the first and largest share of poverty.

sources.quote: בְּכוֹרֵי לְשׁוֹן ׳שָׂרִים׳
sources.says: Rashi says בכורי means princes.

sources.quote: בכורי. ענין גדולים וחשובים
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means great and important ones.

sources.quote: ישראל שהיה להם עד עתה בכורה וחלק גדול בדלות
sources.says: Radak says it is Israel, who until now had the firstborn's large share of poverty.

14:31.headline: "None alone in his ranks": no straggler, or no refuge?
14:31.body: Rashi, with the Targum, says no soldier lags behind alone: they all come together. Ibn Ezra reads מועדיו as palaces: smoke fills them, and no one can stay even alone in his house.

sources.quote: תִּרְגֵּם יוֹנָתָן: ״וְלֵית דְּמְאַחֵר בְּזִמְנוֹהִי״
sources.says: Rashi cites the Targum: no one lags behind at his appointed time.

sources.quote: במועדיו. בארמוניו בא העשן ולא יכול אדם לשבת אפילו לבדו בביתו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the smoke enters the palaces and no one can stay even alone in his house.

15:1.headline: Moab is struck silent, or cut off
15:1.body: נדמה can come from silence or from destruction. Rashi says Moab lay still like a sleeper who cannot fight. Ibn Ezra says it means cut off, and Metzudat Zion joins the two: a ruined place falls silent.

sources.quote: נִדְמָה מוֹאָב כְּאִלּוּ יָשֵׁן דּוֹמֶה וְאֵין יָכוֹל לְהִלָּחֵם
sources.says: Rashi says Moab was still, as if asleep, and could not fight.

sources.quote: נכרת כמו ודמיתי אמך
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means cut off, as in Hosea 4:5.

sources.quote: ענין שתיקה כמו וידם אהרן
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means silence, used for ruin because the place is now silenced.

15:3.headline: "Going down in tears" means moaning
15:3.body: ירד usually means to go down. Rashi and Metzudat Zion say it means to moan, as in Judges 11:37. Radak says the whole body seems to melt down in tears.

sources.quote: גּוֹנֵחַ וְנוֹהֵם בִּבְכִי
sources.says: Rashi says it means groaning and moaning in tears.

sources.quote: ענין נהימה וגניחה כמו אריד בשיחי
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means moaning, as in Psalms 55:3.

sources.quote: כאילו כל גופו יורד ונתך בבכי
sources.says: Radak says it is as if the whole body goes down and melts in weeping.

15:5.headline: An Israelite prophet weeps for the enemy Moab
15:5.body: "My heart cries out for Moab." Rashi says this shows Israel's prophets grieve even over punishment of other nations, unlike Balaam. Radak instead says the prophet speaks in the voice of the people of Moab.

sources.quote: וּנְבִיאֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל מִתְאוֹנְנִים עַל פֻּרְעָנוּת הַבָּאָה עַל הָאֻמּוֹת
sources.says: Rashi says Israel's prophets mourn over disasters that come on the nations.

sources.quote: מדבר הנביא על לשון העם שיאמר כל אחד מהם כך
sources.says: Radak says the prophet speaks as each of the people would speak.

15:5.headline: Moab's bolts and strongholds, or its runaways?
15:5.body: בריח is a bar that bolts a gate, so Rashi reads it as Moab's strongholds. The Targum, as Rashi reports, and Metzudat Zion read it as those fleeing.

sources.quote: עַל כָּל חָזְקָה שֶׁל מוֹאָב יִזְעַק לִבִּי
sources.says: Rashi says it means all of Moab's strong places.

sources.quote: וְיוֹנָתָן תִּרְגֵּם בְּרִיחֶהָ כְּמוֹ בּוֹרְחֶיהָ
sources.says: Rashi reports that the Targum reads it as "her runaways".

sources.quote: מלשון הברחה וניסה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it comes from fleeing.

15:5.headline: A "third" heifer: a calf in its prime
15:5.body: Moab is called עגלת שלשיה, a "third" heifer. Rashi says a third-born calf is the strongest. Radak says it is a three-year-old cow, the best age.

sources.quote: כְּעֶגְלָה שֶׁהִיא שְׁלִישִׁית לַבֶּטֶן
sources.says: Rashi says it is like the third calf born, and gives another reading: a strong one.

sources.quote: עגלה גדולה בת שלשה שנים כי היא הטובה
sources.says: Radak says it is a grown heifer three years old, which is the best.

15:5.headline: A strange word for a cry of breaking
15:5.body: Ibn Ezra calls יעערו a strange word. Rashi says it means to cry out, from Aramaic. Radak links it to breaking: they beat themselves as they wail.

sources.quote: והטעם כמו עוררו, והיא מלה זרה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means "they stir up", and that it is an odd word.

sources.quote: יִצְעָקוּ, וְלָשׁוֹן אֲרָמִי הוּא
sources.says: Rashi says it means they cry out, and that it is Aramaic.

sources.quote: ולפי דעתי שהוא מענין שבר
sources.says: Radak says in his view it comes from the idea of breaking.

15:7.headline: Moab's extra: its wealth, or its arrogance?
15:7.body: יתרה means something extra. Ibn Ezra says it is their wealth. Rashi elsewhere reads it as pride, and in Isaiah he says Moab overstepped by being ungrateful to Abraham's children.

sources.quote: יתרה. שם, ממון
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says יתרה is a noun meaning money.

sources.quote: יֶתֶר הוּא לְשׁוֹן גַּאֲוָה, כְּמוֹ ״יִתְרָה עָשָׂה״
sources.says: Rashi says יתר can mean pride, as in this verse.

sources.quote: שֶׁהָיוּ כְּפוּיֵי טוֹבָה
sources.says: Rashi says the punishment came because Moab was ungrateful.

15:7.headline: The brook of willows may be Babylon
15:7.body: ערבים are willows. Radak says this is a willow brook near a Moabite city. Rashi's second reading says it is Babylon, where exiles hung their harps on the willows.

sources.quote: נחל סמוך לעיר מואב שהיו בו ערבים כמו ערבי נחל
sources.says: Radak says it is a brook near a city of Moab where willows grew.

sources.quote: הָאוֹיְבִים יַגְלוּ אוֹתָם אֶל אֶרֶץ בָּבֶל שֶׁהוּא נַחַל עֲרָבִים
sources.says: Rashi says the enemy will exile them to Babylon, the land of willows in Psalms 137:2.

15:9.headline: The river Dimon will fill with dam, blood
15:9.body: The river's name דימון sounds like דם, blood. Rashi and Metzudat David say God adds real blood to a river already named for it.

sources.quote: שמו דימון מלשון דם ואוסיף עליו דם חללים והוא ענין מליצה לשון נופל על לשון
sources.says: Metzudat David says the name comes from דם and calls this a play of word on word.

sources.quote: דָּם שְׁמוֹ, וְדָם חֲלָלִים אוֹסִיף עָלָיו לְמַלְּאוֹתוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says blood is in its name, and God will add the blood of the slain to fill it.

16:1.headline: Send the lamb: the old tribute Moab stopped paying
16:1.body: Rashi and Radak read כר as a lamb, the tribute Moab's king Mesha once paid Israel, 100,000 lambs (2 Kings 3:4). Ibn Ezra reads it as a kind of camel that runs fast.

sources.quote: ״הָיָה נוֹקֵד וְהֵשִׁיב לְמֶלֶךְ יִשְׂרָאֵל מֵאָה אֶלֶף כָּרִים״, שִׁלְחוּ אוֹתוֹ כַּר
sources.says: Rashi recalls that Mesha king of Moab paid Israel's king 100,000 lambs, and says: send that lamb.

sources.quote: כלומר אותן כרים ואלים שהייתם שולחים למלך ישראל למס ומרדתם בו
sources.says: Radak says it means the lambs and rams Moab used to send Israel's king as tribute before it rebelled.

sources.quote: מין ממיני הגמל שירוץ מגזרת הכרי והרצים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says כר is a kind of camel that runs, from the same root as the royal runners.

16:9.headline: I will soak you with my tears like rain
16:9.body: Ibn Ezra calls אריוך a strange word form. Radak says it means “I will water you with my tears,” an overstatement, as if tears fell like rain on the land.

sources.quote: אריוך. מלה זרה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra calls אריוך a strange word.

sources.quote: ארוה אותך דמעתי, והוא דרך הפלגה כאלו הדמעה כמטר שמרוה הארץ
sources.says: Radak says it means “I will water you with my tears,” an overstatement, as if the tears were rain watering the land.

16:10.headline: You tread grapes, not wine
16:10.body: No one treads wine. Radak says the grapes are called by what they will become, just as people speak of grinding flour.

sources.quote: אמר על היין לא ידרך על שם סופו, כמו וטחני קמח
sources.says: Radak says the verse speaks of treading wine by naming what the grapes end up as, like “grind flour.”

16:13.headline: Spoken long ago: by Isaiah, or back in Balaam's day
16:13.body: Rashi says “long ago” means Isaiah foretold this many years before it happened. He also gives a second reading: the decree began when Moab's king Balak hired Balaam.

sources.quote: מִיָּמִים רַבִּים לִפְנֵי בֹּא הָרָעָה עָלָיו נִבָּא לוֹ יְשַׁעְיָה אֶת זֹאת. דָּבָר אַחֵר: מֵאָז – מֵעֵת אֲשֶׁר שָׂכַר בָּלָק אֶת בִּלְעָם
sources.says: Rashi says Isaiah prophesied this many days before the disaster came, or else that “long ago” means since Balak hired Balaam.

17:1.headline: Not 'discipline' here, but 'removed'
17:1.body: מוסר usually means discipline or teaching. Rashi and Ibn Ezra say here it comes from הסיר, 'remove': Damascus will be removed from being a city.

sources.quote: מוּסָר מֵעִיר. לְשׁוֹן הֲסָרָה
sources.says: Rashi says מוסר here is a word for removing.

sources.quote: מוסר. מגזרת הסיר
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it comes from the verb 'to remove'.

sources.quote: מוסר מעיר. מוסר מהיות עיר
sources.says: Radak says it means removed from being a city.

17:1.headline: A heap of ruins, not 'my insides'
17:1.body: מעי usually means 'my insides'. Ibn Ezra and Metzudat Zion say here it is a heap of rubble, like עי in Micah 1:6, while Rashi says it means lowness.

sources.quote: מעי. כמו לעיים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says מעי is like עיים, heaps of ruins, with an added מ.

sources.quote: מעי. תל ודגור כמו לעי השדה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it is a mound and heap, as in Micah 1:6.

sources.quote: מְעִי. לְשׁוֹן שִׁפְלוּת וְעֹמֶק
sources.says: Rashi says it is a word for lowness and depth.

17:3.headline: Like Israel's glory, which is about to fade
17:3.body: Ibn Ezra says Aram's remnant will have the same 'glory' as Israel, and the next verse says Israel's glory will shrink. Others he cites say Aram will be so shamed that Israel's lot will look like glory beside it.

sources.quote: יהי' להם כבוד ככבוד בני ישראל, שכתב אחריו ידל כבוד יעקב
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says Aram will have glory like Israel's, which the next verse says will grow thin.

sources.quote: ויש אומרים ושאר ארם כל כך יהיו בחרפה עד שיהיה ככבוד לישראל
sources.says: Ibn Ezra cites others who say Aram will be so disgraced that Israel's state will look like glory.

sources.quote: העושר נקרא כבוד
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says wealth is called כבוד.

17:5.headline: Here קציר is the reaper, not the harvest
17:5.body: קציר usually means the harvest. Radak says here it is the reaper himself, a word built like שריד, 'survivor', and פליט, 'refugee'.

sources.quote: קציר. שם תאר בפלס שריד ופליט
sources.says: Radak says קציר here describes a person, in the pattern of שריד and פליט.

sources.quote: כמו שהקוצר יאסוף הקמה ויקצרנה
sources.says: Radak explains the image as the reaper who gathers the standing grain and cuts it.

17:6.headline: Leftover grapes, named after small children
17:6.body: Metzudat Zion says עוללות are the small grapes left on the vine that no one bothers with. He says the word comes from עולל, a small child.

sources.quote: הם הענבים הקטנים הנשארים באילן ואין מי חושש עליהם והוא מלשון עולל ויונק
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says these are small grapes left on the vine that no one cares about, from the word for a small child.

17:6.headline: The treetop, from the word for 'raised high'
17:6.body: Ibn Ezra links אמיר to האמירך, 'He raised you high', in Deuteronomy 26:18, and says Arabic has the same word. Radak says Jerusalem is the treetop: high up, where the enemy's hand cannot reach.

sources.quote: הוא המעולה בזית מגזרת ויי האמירך
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it is the finest part of the olive tree, from 'the Lord has raised you high'.

sources.quote: וכן בלשון קדר
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the word is the same in Arabic.

sources.quote: כן היא ירושלם שהיא גבוהה ומעולה שבארץ ישראל ואשר יהיו בתוכה לא תשיגם יד מלך אשור
sources.says: Radak says Jerusalem is the highest and best place in the land, and the king of Assyria cannot reach those inside it.

17:10.headline: Pleasant plants, or a fast-growing plant known in Arabic?
17:10.body: Rashi and Metzudat Zion read נעמנים from נעים, 'pleasant': Rashi says Israel was first planted as pleasant plants, the twelve sons of Jacob. Ibn Ezra says the word keeps its Arabic meaning, a plant that sprouts quickly.

sources.quote: נעמנים. מל׳ נעים ויופי
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it comes from the word for pleasant and beautiful.

sources.quote: נָטַעְתִּי נֶטַע נַעֲמָנִים, שְׁנֵים עָשָׂר בְּנֵי יַעֲקֹב
sources.says: Rashi says God planted pleasant plants, the twelve sons of Jacob.

sources.quote: נעמנים. כמשמעו בלשון קדר, והוא צמח שיצמח מהרה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the word has its Arabic meaning, a plant that grows quickly.

17:11.headline: Here קציר is a branch, not a harvest
17:11.body: Metzudat Zion says קציר here means a branch, as in Psalms 80:12, 'it sent out its branches'. Radak links it to Job 14:9, where a tree 'makes branches like a sapling'.

sources.quote: קציר. ענינו ענף כמו תשלח קציריה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says קציר means a branch, as in 'it sent out its branches'.

sources.quote: קציר. כמו ועשה קציר כמו נטע
sources.says: Radak compares Job 14:9, 'and it makes branches like a sapling'.

17:11.headline: Not 'inheritance' here, but a day of sickness
17:11.body: נחלה usually means inheritance. Ibn Ezra and Metzudat Zion read it from חלה, 'be sick': a day of a painful blow, which fits the 'deadly pain' that follows.

sources.quote: נחלה. מל׳ חולי
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the word comes from sickness.

sources.quote: ביום נחלה. תחסר מכה, והנה נחלה תאר למכה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the word 'blow' is understood, and נחלה describes it as a sickening blow.

17:13.headline: He fled 'from far off', still running when already far
17:13.body: The verse says 'flee from far off' where we expect 'flee far off'. Radak says the king kept running even when already far away, and Metzudat David says they fled from a voice coming from far off, from heaven.

sources.quote: ובאמרו ממרחק והיה לו לומר למרחק
sources.says: Radak notes the verse says 'from far' where one would expect 'to far'.

sources.quote: ואפילו כשהיה רחוק מירושלים נס עדין מאותו מקום רחוק כי לא היה בוטח בעצמו
sources.says: Radak says even when far from Jerusalem he kept fleeing, because he did not feel safe.

sources.quote: וינוס מפני הקול הבא ממרחק מן השמים
sources.says: Metzudat David says he fled from the voice that came from afar, from heaven.

17:14.headline: בלהה is בהלה, 'terror', with its letters swapped
17:14.body: Ibn Ezra and Metzudat Zion say בלהה is the word בהלה, 'sudden terror', with two letters swapped, like כשב and כבש for a lamb. Rashi says demons came and terrified the enemy at night.

sources.quote: וטעם בלהות בהלות, הפוך כמו כשב וכבש
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says בלהות means בהלות, with letters reversed, like כשב and כבש.

sources.quote: בלהה. הוא הפוך מן בהלה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it is בהלה reversed.

sources.quote: שֵׁדִים בָּאִים עַל הָאוֹיֵב וּמְבַהֲלִין אוֹתוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says demons come upon the enemy and terrify him.

18:1.headline: "Shade of wings": the sails of many ships, or flocks of birds?
18:1.body: צלצל is a doubled form of צל, "shade". Radak and the Targum say the wings are ship sails spread out like a bird's wings, while Rashi says birds gather in that hot eastern land.

sources.quote: צלצל כנפים. כפול מצל
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says צלצל is the word צל, shade, doubled.

sources.quote: צלצל. מל׳ צל
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says צלצל comes from צל, shade.

sources.quote: וקראה צלצל כנפים לרוב הספינות אשר בה, כי בפרש הקלעים בהם ידמו לכנפים
sources.says: Radak says the land is called this for its many ships, whose spread sails look like wings.

sources.quote: וְקִלְעֵיהוֹן פְּרִיסָן כְּנִשְׁרָא דְטָאִיס בְּכַנְפוֹהִי
sources.says: The Targum says their sails are spread like an eagle flying on its wings.

sources.quote: לְפִי שֶׁהֵן שְׁרוּיִין בַּמִּזְרָח וְהָאָרֶץ חַמָּה, הָעוֹפוֹת נֶאֱסָפִים שָׁם
sources.says: Rashi gives his own view: the land is in the hot east, so birds gather there and fill it with their wings.

18:2.headline: קו קו: a builder's line, measure for measure, hope, or filth
18:2.body: Each commentator hears this doubled word differently. Radak sees a builder's line laid row by row, Rashi sees measure for measure or else the word for vomit, and Metzudat Zion hears "hope".

sources.quote: כמו שהבנאי נוטה הקו ועושה נדבך אחד
sources.says: Radak says it is like a builder who stretches his line and lays one row after another, so little by little.

sources.quote: שֶׁנִּפְרַע בּוֹ בַּעֲוֹנוֹ מִדָּה בְּמִדָּה וְנִתַּן לִמְבוּסָה. דָּבָר אַחֵר: קַו קָו – לְשׁוֹן קִיא
sources.says: Rashi says the nation was paid back measure for measure for its sin, or else that קו קו comes from the word for vomit.

sources.quote: קו. מלשון תקוה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says קו comes from תקוה, hope.

sources.quote: בכל זמן גלותם היה מקוה לה׳ וחוזר ומקוה
sources.says: Metzudat David says all through their exile they hoped in God, and hoped again.

18:2.headline: An odd spelling: בזאו means "they plundered"
18:2.body: The word looks strange. Radak, Ibn Ezra and Metzudat Zion say it is בזזו, "they plundered", with an alef standing in for the doubled letter.

sources.quote: בזאו כמו בזזו האלף תמורת הכפל
sources.says: Radak says בזאו is like בזזו, with the alef in place of the doubled letter.

sources.quote: בזאו. בזזו ובא האל״ף במקום אות הכפל
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says בזאו means בזזו, with an alef in place of the doubled letter.

sources.quote: בזאו לחסרון אות הכפל
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the alef of בזאו makes up for the missing doubled letter.

18:4.headline: Here אור, "light", may mean rain, or green plants
18:4.body: Radak and Metzudat Zion read אור here as rain, as in Job 37:11. Rashi reads it as green plants, like the אורות gathered in 2 Kings 4:39, so the sun shines warm on the greens.

sources.quote: אור. ענינו מטר כמו יפיץ ענן אורו
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says אור here means rain, as in "the cloud scatters its אור".

sources.quote: חם צח ובהיר עלי אור, והוא המטר
sources.says: Radak says the clear heat comes after the אור, which is the rain.

sources.quote: כְּחֹם הַשֶּׁמֶשׁ צַח עַל יָרָק, כְּמוֹ ״לְלַקֵּט אֹרֹת״
sources.says: Rashi says it is like the sun's heat on green plants, as in "to gather אורות" (herbs).

18:5.headline: התז, "cut off", is explained from the language of the sages
18:5.body: The word is rare in the Bible. Ibn Ezra, Radak and Metzudat Zion explain it from later rabbinic Hebrew, where התיז את הראש means to cut off the head.

sources.quote: התז. כמו כרת ובלשון קדמונינו ז"ל ימצא
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says התז means cut off, and the word is found in the language of the early sages.

sources.quote: התז. ענין כריתה וחתוך ובדרז״ל התיז את הראש
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means cutting, as in the sages' phrase "he cut off the head".

sources.quote: והוא מפעלי הכפל שרשו תזז, מדברי רבותינו ז"ל רוח תזזית
sources.says: Radak says its root is תזז, known from the sages' phrase רוח תזזית.

18:6.headline: "Winter on them": a verb made from the word for winter
18:6.body: תחרף comes from חורף, winter, just as וקץ earlier in the verse comes from summer. Rashi says the bodies lie there all winter, and from this the sages said Gog's judgment will last twelve months.

sources.quote: תֶּחֱרָף. כָּל יְמוֹת הַחֹרֶף. מִכָּאן אָמְרוּ: מִשְׁפַּט גּוֹג לֶעָתִיד לָבוֹא שְׁנֵים עָשָׂר חֹדֶשׁ
sources.says: Rashi says it means all the days of winter, and from here the sages said Gog's judgment will last twelve months.

sources.quote: תחרף. מלשון חורף
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says תחרף comes from חורף, winter.

sources.quote: תחרף. מגזרת חורף
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says תחרף comes from חורף, winter.

19:1.headline: God riding a cloud: a picture of how fast the blow comes
19:1.body: Maimonides says flying is never said of God in a plain sense. Riding a swift cloud is a picture of speed, and Radak agrees: the decree against Egypt will arrive very fast.

sources.quote: והכוונה למהירות פגיעת האסון הזה בהם
sources.says: Maimonides says the point of the image is how quickly this disaster will strike them.

sources.quote: רוכב על עב קל דרך משל לרוב מהירות הגזירה עליהם
sources.says: Radak says riding a swift cloud is a figure for how fast the decree comes upon them.

19:3.headline: Egypt's "spirit" drains away: its plans and its will
19:3.body: רוח means wind or spirit, but Maimonides says here it means intention and will: Egypt's plans will scatter. Rashi says its wisdom will be emptied out.

sources.quote: דהיינו: יתפזרו כוונותיו והנהגתו תסתתר
sources.says: Maimonides says it means Egypt's intentions will scatter and its way of governing will be hidden from it.

sources.quote: תִּתְרוֹקֵן חָכְמָתוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says Egypt's wisdom will be emptied.

19:4.headline: Hand Egypt over, or shut it up like a dammed spring?
19:4.body: Radak and Metzudat Zion read וסכרתי as וסגרתי, "I will hand over", with כ standing for ג. Ibn Ezra says those letters do not swap and links it to the springs of the deep that were "shut" (Genesis 8:2).

sources.quote: כמו וסגרתי, מן יסגרך ה' בידי
sources.says: Radak says it is like וסגרתי, "I will deliver", as in 1 Samuel 24:19.

sources.quote: יש מחליפין הכ"ף בגימ"ל, ולא יתחלפו באמת
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says some swap כ for ג, but those letters do not really interchange.

sources.quote: אֶסְתְּמֶנּוּ וְאֶחְבְּשֶׁנּוּ
sources.says: Rashi offers that it means "I will block it up and lock it away", like the springs of the deep.

19:4.headline: "A hard masters": one master named in the plural of honor
19:4.body: אדנים is plural but קשה, "hard", is singular. Rashi and Radak say Hebrew speaks of a single lord in the plural as a mark of rank, as with Joseph's master.

sources.quote: כָּל לְשׁוֹן אַדְנוּת קָרוּי בִּלְשׁוֹן רַבִּים, וַאֲפִלּוּ יָחִיד
sources.says: Rashi says every word of lordship is said in the plural, even of one person.

sources.quote: ואדונים לשון תפארת ליחיד
sources.says: Radak says אדונים is a plural of honor for a single master.

19:6.headline: A word that starts with both a Hebrew and an Aramaic prefix
19:6.body: והאזניחו appears only here, and Radak reports a view that it was written with both the Hebrew ה and the Aramaic א. Rashi says it means the shrinking rivers turn to mud and are abandoned.

sources.quote: וכתבו הה"א על לשון עברית והאל"ף על לשון ארמית
sources.says: Radak reports that some say the ה was written in the Hebrew way and the א in the Aramaic way.

sources.quote: הַטִּיט נִכָּר בָּהֶם, וְנַעֲשִׂין רֶפֶשׁ וְנִזְנָחִין
sources.says: Rashi says the mud shows, they become mire, and they are abandoned.

sources.quote: האל״ף נוספת כי הוא ענין עזיבה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the א is extra and the word means being abandoned.

19:6.headline: Rivers of the fortress, or simply the rivers of Egypt?
19:6.body: מצור usually means siege or fortress, and Metzudat Zion reads it as the moats that guard a city. Radak says מצור is simply a name for Egypt.

sources.quote: מל׳ צור וחוזק כי חריצי המים הסביב לעיר הם לה לחוזק
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means strength, since the water trenches around a city protect it.

sources.quote: ופירוש מצור מצרים
sources.says: Radak says מצור means Egypt.

19:7.headline: Rooted green plants, or banks stripped bare?
19:7.body: ערות appears only here. Rashi and Radak say it means lush, well-rooted plants by the Nile, while others cited by Ibn Ezra read it from ערה, "bare": the banks will be stripped of their cover.

sources.quote: לְשׁוֹן דָּבָר הַמְעוֹרֶה וְנִשְׁרָשׁ יָפֶה יָפֶה
sources.says: Rashi says it means something deeply rooted, as in Psalms 37:35.

sources.quote: ערות תאר לירקות ולדשאים הלחים
sources.says: Radak says ערות describes moist greens and grasses.

sources.quote: ויש אומרים נחשף כל מה שהיה על היאור ועל פיו, כי הצמח הוא כמכסה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra reports some who say everything along the Nile will be laid bare, since plants are like a covering.

19:9.headline: Combed flax, or flax of a reddish color?
19:9.body: שריקות appears only here. Metzudat Zion and Radak say it is flax combed with a מסרק, while Ibn Ezra says it names a color, like the שרקים horses of Zechariah 1:8.

sources.quote: מלשון מסרק והוא שם כלי עשוי לסרוק הפשתן
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it comes from מסרק, a tool for combing flax.

sources.quote: והנכון שהוא עין השורק, וכן השרוקים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it is better read as a color, as in the שרקים of Zechariah.

sources.quote: ויש מפרשים שריקות הטוב שבפשתן, וכן נקרא בערבי שרק
sources.says: Radak reports some who say it is the finest flax, called שרק in Arabic.

19:9.headline: Weavers of white linen, or of nets full of holes?
19:9.body: חורי appears only here, and Ibn Ezra reads "white cloth". Radak and Metzudat Zion read "holes": the weavers of fishing nets lose their work when the Nile dries.

sources.quote: חורי. הלבנים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says חורי means the white ones.

sources.quote: חורי. נקבים וכן סלי חורי
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means holes, as in the baskets of Genesis 40:16.

sources.quote: כי הרשתות הן עשויות נקבים נקבים
sources.says: Radak says the nets are made full of holes.

19:10.headline: Not wage earners: dam builders who pooled water for fish
19:10.body: עשי שכר looks like "workers for hire". Ibn Ezra, Radak and Metzudat Zion read שכר as סכר, a dam: people who blocked the water to make fish pools.

sources.quote: שכר. ענין סתימה כמו ויסכרו מעיינות תהום
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says שכר means blocking, as in the springs that were shut in Genesis 8:2.

sources.quote: רוצה לומר שסוגרים בפני המים כדי שיקוו המים ויצודו בהם דגים
sources.says: Radak says they shut off the water so it would pool and they could catch fish in it.

sources.quote: דַהֲווֹ עָבְדִין סִכְרָא וְכָנְשִׁין מַיָא
sources.says: The Targum says they used to build dams and gather water.

19:10.headline: Still pools, pools of fish, or people sick at heart?
19:10.body: Rashi reads אגמי נפש as pools of resting water, and Ibn Ezra as pools full of living fish. Radak hears עגמי נפש, "grieved in spirit": the dam builders mourn their loss.

sources.quote: אַגְמֵי שֶׁבֶת לָשׁוֹן ״שָׁבַת וַיִּנָּפַשׁ״
sources.says: Rashi says these are pools of rest, from "He rested" in Exodus 31:17.

sources.quote: האגמים ששם נפשות הדגים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says they are the pools where the fish live.

sources.quote: אגמי נפש. והיא כמו עגמי, מן עגמה נפשי
sources.says: Radak says it is like עגמי, from "my soul was grieved".

19:13.headline: Egypt's foolish princes, used to warn scholars who study alone
