19:13.body: נואלו means "became fools". The Talmud cites this verse to prove that meaning when it warns that scholars who study alone grow foolish.

sources.quote: שֶׁיּוֹשְׁבִין וְעוֹסְקִין בַּתּוֹרָה בַּד בְּבַד, וְלֹא עוֹד אֶלָּא שֶׁמִּטַּפְּשִׁין
sources.says: The Talmud says scholars who sit and study Torah alone become foolish.

sources.quote: וְאִיבָּעֵית אֵימָא מֵהָכָא: ״נוֹאֲלוּ שָׂרֵי צֹעַן״
sources.says: It brings this verse as a proof that the word means foolishness.

sources.quote: ענין אוילות ושטות
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says נואלו means foolishness and folly.

19:15.headline: Head and tail, palm branch and reed: who are they?
19:15.body: Metzudat Zion says כפה is a palm branch, and Radak reads the pair as Egypt's strong and weak wise men. Rashi says they are the astrologers, named for the stars they read.

sources.quote: כפה. ענינו ענף כמו כפות תמרים
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says כפה means a branch, as in palm fronds.

sources.quote: כי כפה הם החזקים בחכמה, ואגמון הם החלושים
sources.says: Radak says כפה are those strong in wisdom and אגמון the weak ones.

sources.quote: הֵם הַחַרְטוּמִים וְאִצְטַגְנִינִים הַחוֹזִים בַּכּוֹכָבִים
sources.says: Rashi says they are the magicians and astrologers who read the stars.

19:17.headline: Judah becomes Egypt's terror: they reel like drunkards
19:17.body: חגא appears only here. Rashi and Radak link it to יחוגו, "they reel like a drunkard" (Psalms 107:27): the mere name of Judah will make Egypt shake.

sources.quote: לְשׁוֹן שֶׁבֶר, וְאֵימָה וָפַחַד
sources.says: Rashi says it is a word of breaking, terror and fear.

sources.quote: פירוש תנועות הפחד ורעדה וכן יחוגו וינועו כשכור
sources.says: Radak says it means the shaking of fear and trembling, as in "they reel and stagger like a drunkard".

19:18.headline: City of destruction, or city of the sun?
19:18.body: The Targum and the Talmud read ההרס as if it were החרס, "the sun" (Job 9:7), so the city is Beit Shemesh, and Rashi says the Targum kept both meanings. Ibn Ezra rejects the swap of ה for ח, and Radak says any town that left God would be called "the city to destroy".

sources.quote: וּמִמַּאי דְּ״עִיר הַהֶרֶס״ לִישָּׁנָא דְּשִׁימְשָׁא הִיא? דִּכְתִיב: ״הָאוֹמֵר לַחֶרֶס וְלֹא יִזְרָח״
sources.says: The Talmud asks how we know עיר ההרס refers to the sun, and answers from "who commands the sun (חרס) and it does not rise".

sources.quote: הַהֶרֶס תִּרְגְּמוֹ יוֹנָתָן לִשְׁנֵי פָנִים
sources.says: Rashi says the Targum translated ההרס both ways, as sun and as destruction.

sources.quote: עיר ההרס. שם עיר, והתמה מהמחליף ה"א בחי"ת
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it is the name of a city and wonders at anyone who swaps ה for ח.

sources.quote: שאם תשוב מעבודת האל אחת מחמש ערים יאמר לה עיר ההרס
sources.says: Radak says that if one of the five cities turned from God, it would be called the city to be destroyed.

19:18.headline: "The language of Canaan" is Hebrew
19:18.body: Ibn Ezra learns from this phrase that the Canaanites spoke Hebrew, the holy tongue. Radak says it means the language of the Land of Israel, which these Egyptians learned on their visits there.

sources.quote: מזה נלמוד כי הכנענים בלשון הקדש היו מדברים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says we learn from this that the Canaanites spoke the holy tongue.

sources.quote: רוצה לומר שפת ארץ ישראל שהיא לשון עברי
sources.says: Radak says it means the language of the Land of Israel, which is Hebrew.

19:19.headline: An altar to God in Egypt: freed captives, or a runaway priest?
19:19.body: Rashi cites Seder Olam: captives that Hezekiah freed went home to Egypt and built an altar to God. The Talmud also reads it as the altar of Onias, a high priest's son who fled to Alexandria and built one there.

sources.quote: וְהָלְכוּ וּבָנוּ מִזְבֵּחַ לַה׳ בְּאֶרֶץ מִצְרַיִם
sources.says: Rashi says the freed captives went and built an altar to God in Egypt.

sources.quote: הָלַךְ לַאֲלֶכְּסַנְדְּרִיָּא שֶׁל מִצְרַיִם, וּבָנָה שָׁם מִזְבֵּחַ
sources.says: The Talmud says Onias went to Alexandria in Egypt and built an altar there, citing this verse.

sources.quote: עַל מִזְבַּח בֵּית חוֹנְיוֹ, בְּנוֹ שֶׁל שִׁמְעוֹן הַצַּדִּיק
sources.says: Rashi notes that some sages read it as the altar of Onias, son of Shimon the Righteous.

19:22.headline: Strike first, then heal: how God treats Egypt
19:22.body: Resh Lakish says God prepares Israel's cure before the blow. With other nations, as this verse shows of Egypt, He strikes first and heals afterwards.

sources.quote: מַכֶּה אוֹתָן וְאַחַר כָּךְ בּוֹרֵא לָהֶם רְפוּאָה
sources.says: Resh Lakish says God strikes the nations and only afterwards creates their cure, citing this verse.

sources.quote: וְאַחַר הַמַּכָּה יָבִיא לָהֶם רְפוּאָה
sources.says: Rashi says that after the blow He will bring them healing.

19:24.headline: Israel "the third", or Israel the ruling officer?
19:24.body: Ibn Ezra says most readers link שלישיה to שלישים, the officers of Exodus 14:7. He holds the plain sense is "third": Israel will stand beside Egypt and Assyria as a third nation that knows God.

sources.quote: רובי המפרשים אמרו כי שלישיה מגזרת ושלישים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says most commentators derive שלישיה from שלישים, officers.

sources.quote: ועל הפשט מגזרת שלשה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the plain sense is from שלשה, three.

sources.quote: מל׳ שלש או יתכן שהוא מענין ממשלת ונסיכות
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means three, or perhaps rule and rank.

19:25.headline: "Blessed be My people Egypt": Egypt itself, or Israel?
19:25.body: Ibn Ezra and Radak say God calls Egypt itself "My people", because they turned to Him and built Him an altar. Rashi and the Targum read it as Israel, the people God chose in Egypt and took out of it.

sources.quote: ויאמר ברוך עמי מצרים ששבו להיות עמי
sources.says: Radak says God calls Egypt blessed because they returned to be His people.

sources.quote: בעבור שיעשו מזבח לשם בפרהסיא קראם עמי
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says God calls them "My people" because they will openly build an altar to Him.

sources.quote: בְּרִיךְ עַמִי דְאַפְקֵית מִמִצְרַיִם
sources.says: The Targum reads: blessed is My people whom I brought out of Egypt.

sources.quote: יִשְׂרָאֵל, אֲשֶׁר בָּחַרְתִּי לִי לְעָם בִּהְיוֹתָם בְּמִצְרָיִם
sources.says: Rashi says "My people" is Israel, whom God chose while they were in Egypt.

2:2.headline: A taller mountain, or a mountain that matters more
2:2.body: Ibn Ezra says the Temple mount will not grow taller: people will run to it from every side as if it stood above all hills. Rashi says the miracles done there will be greater than those of Sinai, Carmel and Tabor.

sources.quote: ידענו כי הר הבית לא יהיה נשא, רק פירושו, נכון יהיה הר הבית, שירוצו אליו מארבע הפאות כאלו הוא נשא מכל הגבעות
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the Temple mount will not be physically raised; people will run to it from all four sides as though it were higher than every hill.

sources.quote: יִגְדַּל נֵס שֶׁנַּעֲשָׂה בּוֹ, מִנִּסֵּי סִינַי וְכַרְמֶל וְתָבוֹר
sources.says: Rashi says the miracle done on it will be greater than the miracles of Sinai, Carmel and Tabor.

2:2.headline: The nations will stream to it like rivers
2:2.body: ונהרו comes from נהר, a river. Rashi says the nations will be drawn to the mountain like rivers, and Radak says a river is named for running, so here the nations run.

sources.quote: יִתְקַבְּצוּ, יִמָּשְׁכוּ אֵלָיו כַּנְּהָרוֹת
sources.says: Rashi says they will gather and be drawn to it like rivers.

sources.quote: ונהרו. וירוצו, ומזה נקרא מקום מרוצת מים הרבים נהר
sources.says: Radak says ונהרו means they will run, and that a river is named for the running of much water.

2:3.headline: Why “the house of Jacob's God,” not Abraham's or Isaac's
2:3.body: Rashi says Jacob was the one who called this place a house, בית אל, so the house is named for him. Abraham had called it a mountain and Isaac a field.

sources.quote: לְפִי שֶׁהוּא קְרָאוֹ ״בֵּית אֵל״
sources.says: Rashi says it is because Jacob called it Beth El, the house of God.

sources.quote: אֲבָל אַבְרָהָם קְרָאוֹ ״בְּהַר ה׳ יֵרָאֶה״
sources.says: Rashi says Abraham called it a mountain, and Isaac called it a field.

2:6.headline: Did God leave his people, or did they leave him?
2:6.body: Radak reads נטשתה as the prophet speaking to God: you have left your people. The Targum reads it as speaking to Israel: you have left the Mighty One who used to save you.

sources.quote: כנוי ונטשתה כנגד האל, אמר אתה האל שנטשתה עמך בית יעקב
sources.says: Radak says the word speaks to God: you, God, have left your people, the house of Jacob.

sources.quote: אֲרֵי שְׁבַקְתּוּן דַחֲלָא תַקִיפָא דַהֲוָה פָּרֵיק לְכוֹן דְבֵית יַעֲקֹב
sources.says: The Targum renders it: you of the house of Jacob have left the Mighty One who used to save you.

2:6.headline: Filled with ways from the East, or full as in old times
2:6.body: Rashi reads מקדם as “from the East”: the people filled up with the magic of the Arameans who lived there. The Targum reads it as “as before,” and Radak explains that it means as in the days of the Canaanites.

sources.quote: נִתְמַלְּאוּ צִבְאוֹתָם מִמַּעֲשֵׂי אֲרַמִּיִּים שֶׁהָיוּ יוֹשְׁבִים בַּמִּזְרָח
sources.says: Rashi says their hosts filled up with the deeds of the Arameans who lived in the East.

sources.quote: ויונתן תרגם כי מלאו מקדם ארי אתמליאת וגו', ר"ל כמו שהיתה בימי הכנענים
sources.says: Radak says the Targum takes it to mean the land is full as it was in the days of the Canaanites.

2:6.headline: Foreign children, or foreign ideas?
2:6.body: Rashi reads ילדי נכרים plainly: children born to foreign wives. Maimonides says ילד, “give birth,” is also used for ideas a mind produces, so the verse means they are content with the nations' ideas.

sources.quote: בּוֹעֲלִים בְּנוֹת עַכּוּ״ם וּמִתְעָרְבִים בָּהֶם, וְיוֹלְדוֹת לָהֶם יְלָדִים
sources.says: Rashi says they took foreign women, mixed with them, and had children by them.

sources.quote: כן הושאל המונח לחידושי המחשבות, ולדעות ולשיטות
sources.says: Maimonides says ילד is borrowed for new thoughts, opinions and teachings, and reads this verse as Israel being content with the nations' opinions.

2:9.headline: Two words for “person”: the small and the great
2:9.body: Rashi says אדם here means ordinary, lowly people and איש means the great men and warriors. Radak thinks the verse just says the same thing twice, but reports that reading too.

sources.quote: וַיִּשַּׁח אָדָם. הַקְּטַנִּים
sources.says: Rashi says אדם here means the small, ordinary people.

sources.quote: וַיִּשְׁפַּל אִישׁ. הַגְּדוֹלִים וְהַגִּבּוֹרִים אַנְשֵׁי הַחַיִל
sources.says: Rashi says איש here means the great ones, the warriors and men of valor.

sources.quote: כפל הענין במלות שונות, ויש מפרשים אדם הקטנים, איש הגדולים
sources.says: Radak says the verse repeats one idea in different words, and reports others who read אדם as the small and איש as the great.

2:16.headline: Fine stone floors, or painted pictures
2:16.body: שכיות is a rare word. Rashi says it means palaces with laid marble floors, like the אבן משכית of Leviticus 26:1, and Radak says it means pictures.

sources.quote: פַּלְטֵרִין רְצוּפִין בְּמַשְׂכִּית, רִצְפַת שַׁיִשׁ
sources.says: Rashi says it means palaces paved with a stone floor of marble.

sources.quote: פירוש שכיות ציורים, כמו איש בחדרי משכיתו
sources.says: Radak says שכיות means pictures, as in “each man in his room of images.”

2:20.headline: Moles, a night bird, or deep pits?
2:20.body: The verse writes לחפר פרות as two words, and many read them as one, חפרפרות. Rashi says idols shaped like moles, Ibn Ezra says a bird that flies at night, and Metzudat Zion says deep pits.

sources.quote: גִּלּוּלִים בִּדְמוּת חֲפַרְפָּרוֹת, מִינֵי שְׁרָצִים שֶׁחוֹפְרִין הָאָרֶץ
sources.says: Rashi says these are idols shaped like moles, small creatures that dig the ground.

sources.quote: והוא שם עוף יעוף בלילה כעטלף, ומביא עצמו ביום במקום סתר, ויש אומרי' שהוא עוף שיאכל הפירו' בלילות, והם שתי מלות
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it is a bird that flies at night like a bat and hides by day, and reports others who read two words: a bird that eats fruit at night.

sources.quote: פתרונו כמו מלה אחת והוא מל׳ חפירה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it is read as one word, from digging, meaning deep pits.

2:21.headline: Hiding in the rocks' “branches”
2:21.body: סעיף is a tree branch. Radak and Metzudat Zion say the verse borrows it for a ledge of rock that juts out like a branch.

sources.quote: ודמה שן הסלע לסעיף האילן הגבוה
sources.says: Radak says the verse compares a jutting rock to the branch of a tall tree.

sources.quote: והוא ל׳ מושאל מהנוף הבולט מן האילן הנקרא סעיף
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the word is borrowed from the branch that sticks out of a tree.

20:2.headline: Untie the sackcloth, or bind it on? The Targum reverses it
20:2.body: ופתחת plainly means 'untie'. The Targum translates the opposite, 'bind sackcloth on your loins', and Rashi defends it: פתח can mean to engrave, so the sackcloth is tied so tight it presses into the skin.

sources.quote: תרגם יונתן: ״ותיסר סקא בחרצך״
sources.says: Rashi reports that Jonathan translated 'bind sackcloth on your loins'.

sources.quote: ופירוש ופתחת כמו ״מפתחות פתוחי חותם״
sources.says: Rashi explains ופתחת like engraving a seal: the sackcloth is bound tightly enough to mark the flesh.

sources.quote: ויונתן תרגם ופתחת השק בהפך העניין
sources.says: Radak notes that Jonathan translated the phrase in the opposite sense.

20:2.headline: Barefoot, or only in patched shoes?
20:2.body: יחף plainly means without shoes. The Talmud reads it here as wearing patched shoes, to match its reading of 'naked' as wearing rags.

sources.quote: ויחף. ענין חוסר מנעלים
sources.says: Metzudat Zion gives the plain sense: without shoes.

sources.quote: ״ויחף״ — במנעלים המטולאים
sources.says: The Talmud says 'barefoot' here means in patched shoes.

sources.quote: הכא נמי במנעלים המטולאים
sources.says: The Talmud says that just as 'naked' means in rags, here too 'barefoot' means in patched shoes.

20:4.headline: Egypt led away with buttocks bared, payback for Ham
20:4.body: שת is a rare word for the buttocks, which Metzudat Zion ties to the word for a foundation. Rashi and the midrash say this shame repays Ham, Egypt's ancestor, who saw his father's nakedness and did not cover it.

sources.quote: וגמול זה היה להם תחת חם אביהם, אשר ראה ערות אביו ולא כסה אותה
sources.says: Rashi says this was their payment for their ancestor Ham, who saw his father's nakedness and did not cover it.

sources.quote: שת. ענין יסוד כמו שתותיה מדוכאים
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the word means foundation, since this part is to a person what a foundation is to a building.

sources.quote: אמר הקדוש ברוך הוא לחם, אתה בזית ערות אביך, חייך שאני פורע לך
sources.says: The midrash has God tell Ham that because he scorned his father's nakedness, He will repay him, and cites this verse.

20:5.headline: Cush was their 'gaze', where their eyes hung for help
20:5.body: מבט comes from the word for looking. Ibn Ezra says Cush was where their eyes hung, and the Targum translates it as 'the house of their trust'.

sources.quote: מכוש מבטם. שעיניהם תלויות אליהם
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says their eyes were hanging on Cush.

sources.quote: כל המביטים ומצפים על עזרת כוש
sources.says: Rashi says it means all who looked and waited for help from Cush.

sources.quote: מכוש בית רוחצניהון
sources.says: The Targum translates it as Cush, the house of their trust.

22:1.headline: Jerusalem, a city on a mountain, called a "valley" of vision
22:1.body: Rashi says the "valley of vision" is Jerusalem, the subject of most prophecies. Radak asks why a city on a mountain is called a valley, and answers that its sins brought it down from a mountain to a valley.

sources.quote: הִיא יְרוּשָׁלַיִם, גֵּיא שֶׁנִּתְנַבְּאוּ עָלֶיהָ רֹב נְבוּאוֹת
sources.says: Rashi says it is Jerusalem, the valley about which most prophecies were spoken.

sources.quote: ומה שקראם גיא והיא הר לכנותה לרעה
sources.says: Radak says it is called a valley though it is a mountain, as a name of disgrace.

22:1.headline: Why the whole city went up to the roofs
22:1.body: Ibn Ezra says people climbed to the roofs to watch the enemy armies, though some say it was to burn incense to the stars. Rashi cites the sages: it was the priests, who climbed onto the Temple roof holding its keys.

sources.quote: יש אומרים כי טעם עלית לגגות לקטר למלאכת השמים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra reports some who say they went up to the roofs to burn incense to the host of heaven.

sources.quote: וְרַבּוֹתֵינוּ פֵּרְשׁוּ עַל כֹּהֲנִים, שֶׁעָלוּ עַל גַּגּוֹ שֶׁל הֵיכָל וּמַפְתְּחוֹת הָעֲזָרָה בְּיָדָם
sources.says: Rashi says the sages explain it as the priests who went up on the Temple roof with the keys of the courtyard in their hands.

sources.quote: וַעֲלֵיהֶן קוֹנֵן יְשַׁעְיָהוּ הַנָּבִיא
sources.says: The Talmud says it was over them that Isaiah the prophet lamented with this verse.

22:5.headline: A verb built from "wall" that means tearing the wall down
22:5.body: מקרקר is made from קיר, a wall, but it means knocking one down. Radak compares משרש, which is made from שרש, a root, and means uprooting.

sources.quote: הורס הקיר כמו משרש עוקר השורש
sources.says: Radak says it means destroying the wall, as משרש means pulling out the root.

sources.quote: מל׳ קיר וכותל ר״ל הורס את הקיר
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it comes from קיר, wall, and means tearing the wall down.

sources.quote: יוֹם קִרְקוּר קִיר הַחוֹמָה
sources.says: Rashi says it is the day the city wall is knocked down.

22:5.headline: A cry toward the mountain: the Talmud hears God crying too
22:5.body: Rashi says the cry is of people fleeing to the hills. The Talmud says that of God too it is written, "crying out toward the mountain".

sources.quote: וְקוֹל שַׁוְעָה לָנוּס אֶל הֶהָרִים
sources.says: Rashi says it is a cry to flee to the mountains.

sources.quote: אַף בְּהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא נֶאֱמַר: ״מְקַרְקַר קִר וְשׁוֹעַ אֶל הָהָר״
sources.says: The Talmud says that even of God it is said, "tearing down walls and crying to the mountain".

22:6.headline: Kir bared its shields, or shields pressed to the wall?
22:6.body: קיר can be the land of Kir or a wall, and ערה can mean "bared" or "attached". So either the men of Kir uncovered their shields, or, as the Targum reads, the attackers pressed their shields against Jerusalem's wall.

sources.quote: ערה. ענין גלוי, כמו את מקורה הערה
sources.says: Radak says ערה means uncovering, as in Leviticus 20:18.

sources.quote: ויש לפרש קיר כמשמעו כותל וערה ענין דבוק
sources.says: Radak says one may also read קיר as a wall and ערה as attached.

sources.quote: ׳קִיר׳ שֵׁם הָעִיר
sources.says: Rashi offers that Kir is the name of a city whose people bared their shields.

sources.quote: וְעַל שׁוּר דְבַקוּ תְרֵיסִין
sources.says: The Targum says they stuck shields against the wall.

22:8.headline: Judah's "covering" stripped away: its Temple, or its hidden treasure?
22:8.body: Rashi says Judah's covering is the Temple, which sheltered them, and Radak says they wrongly trusted it to shield them. The Targum reads it as Judah's hidden treasures, laid bare.

sources.quote: הוּא בֵּית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ, שֶׁהָיָה מֵגִין וּמֵיסַךְ וּמְסַכֵּךְ עֲלֵיהֶם
sources.says: Rashi says it is the Temple, which protected and covered them.

sources.quote: שהיו סבורים שהיו מסוככין שלא תבא עליהם רעת האויב מפני בית המקדש
sources.says: Radak says they thought they were covered and safe from the enemy because of the Temple.

sources.quote: וְגַלֵי יַת מַטְמוֹרִית בֵּית יְהוּדָה
sources.says: The Targum says He uncovered the hidden treasures of the house of Judah.

22:11.headline: Planned "from afar": Jerusalem was in God's plan before the world
22:11.body: Rashi reads "from afar" as from the time God created the world, when Jerusalem and the Temple were already in His thought. Radak explains the sages' saying that such things came before creation: they were the purpose the world was made for.

sources.quote: מֵאָז שֶׁבָּרָא אֶת הָעוֹלָם, עָלְתָה יְרוּשָׁלַיִם וּבֵית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ בַּמַּחֲשָׁבָה
sources.says: Rashi says that from when God created the world, Jerusalem and the Temple were in His thought.

sources.quote: לפי שהדברים האלה הם תכלית בריאת העולם
sources.says: Radak says these things are said to precede the world because they are the goal of its creation.

22:13.headline: "For tomorrow we die": a taunt about the world to come
22:13.body: Rashi says the feasters mean the next world: the prophets say we have no share there, so let us enjoy this one. The Talmud warns anyone who feasts at home while the community suffers that this verse is about him.

sources.quote: בָּעוֹלָם הַבָּא, הַנְּבִיאִים אוֹמְרִים לָנוּ מֵאֵת הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא שֶׁלֹּא יִהְיֶה לָנוּ חֵלֶק לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא
sources.says: Rashi says they mean the world to come, since the prophets tell them they have no share in it.

sources.quote: בִּזְמַן שֶׁהַצִּבּוּר שָׁרוּי בְּצַעַר, אַל יֹאמַר אָדָם: אֵלֵךְ לְבֵיתִי, וְאוֹכַל וְאֶשְׁתֶּה
sources.says: The Talmud says that when the community is suffering, a person must not say "I will go home and eat and drink", and applies this verse to one who does.

22:14.headline: "Until you die": which death, and what it wipes away
22:14.body: Ibn Ezra says it means death at the enemy's hand, while the Targum says it is the "second death" in the world to come. The Talmud learns from it that for disgracing God's name, only death completes the atonement.

sources.quote: עד תמותון. ביד האויב הצר עליכם
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means until you die at the hand of the enemy besieging you.

sources.quote: ״מוֹתָא תִּנְיָינָא לְעוֹלָם הַבָּא״
sources.says: Rashi cites the Targum: the second death, in the world to come.

sources.quote: אֶלָּא כּוּלָּן תּוֹלִין, וּמִיתָה מְמָרֶקֶת
sources.says: The Talmud says that for desecrating God's name, repentance, Yom Kippur and suffering only hold it off, and death scours it away.

22:15.headline: Shevna "the sokhen": a treasurer, or a man of pleasures?
22:15.body: Ibn Ezra says סכן means a treasurer, from the storehouses of Exodus 1:11. The Talmud reads it as a man who indulged himself, comparing the word used of Abishag, and a midrash in Rashi says he came from a town called Sichni.

sources.quote: הסכן. כמו ערי מסכנות
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says סכן is like the store cities of Exodus 1:11, meaning a keeper of treasures.

sources.quote: שֶׁבְנָא בַּעַל הֲנָאָה הָיָה
sources.says: Rabbi Elazar says Shevna was a man of pleasures, comparing "she was his סכנת" in 1 Kings 1:2.

sources.quote: וּמִדְרַשׁ אַגָּדָה אוֹמֵר: מִן סִכְנִי הָיָה וּבָא לוֹ לִירוּשָׁלַיִם
sources.says: Rashi cites a midrash that he came from Sichni to Jerusalem.

22:17.headline: Hurled like a man, or like a rooster?
22:17.body: The sages read טלטלה גבר as "a man's exile", harder than a woman's, and a midrash in Rashi reads גבר as a rooster chased from place to place. Radak says גבר addresses Shevna himself: "you, mighty man".

sources.quote: טִלְטוּלָא דְּגַבְרָא קָשֶׁה מְדְאִיתְּתָא
sources.says: Rashi cites the sages: a man's exile is harder than a woman's.

sources.quote: כְּהָדֵין תַּרְנְגוֹלָא דְּמִטַּלְטֵל מֵאֲתַר לַאֲתַר
sources.says: Rashi cites the midrash: like a rooster tossed from place to place.

sources.quote: ולפי דעתי כי מלת גבר הוא לשון קריאה, כלומר אתה הגבר הנה ה' מטלטלך טלטלה
sources.says: Radak says גבר is a way of addressing him: you, the mighty man, God will hurl you.

22:17.headline: Wrapped up, flown off like a bird, or struck with leprosy?
22:17.body: Radak reads ועטך as wrapping, like a cloth rolled into a ball, and Rashi as עיט, a bird of prey: God will fly him off into exile. The Talmud links it to the leper who "covers" his lip (Leviticus 13:45) and says leprosy broke out on him.

sources.quote: כמו שאדם עוטה הבגד, וצונפו וכורכו כמו כדור
sources.says: Radak says it is like a person who wraps a garment and rolls it up like a ball.

sources.quote: לְשׁוֹן ׳עַיִט׳ – יַפְרִיחֲךָ כְּעוֹף בַּגָּלוּת
sources.says: Rashi says it is from עיט, a bird of prey: He will make you fly like a bird into exile.

sources.quote: מְלַמֵּד שֶׁפָּרְחָה בּוֹ צָרַעַת
sources.says: Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Chanina says this teaches that leprosy broke out on him.

22:18.headline: Chariots of honor turn to disgrace: dragged behind horses
22:18.body: The Talmud says Shevna sought to disgrace his master Hezekiah, so his own honor was turned to disgrace. Radak tells the sages' story: the Assyrians tied him to their horses' tails and dragged him.

sources.quote: הוּא בִּיקֵּשׁ קְלוֹן בֵּית אֲדֹנָיו, לְפִיכָךְ נֶהְפַּךְ כְּבוֹדוֹ לְקָלוֹן
sources.says: The Talmud says he sought the disgrace of his master's house, so his honor was turned to disgrace.

sources.quote: נקבוהו בעקביו וקשרוהו בזנבות סוסיהם
sources.says: Radak cites the sages: they pierced his heels and tied him to their horses' tails.

22:22.headline: Who carries a key on his shoulder? Two pictures in one
22:22.body: Radak notes that no one carries a key on his shoulder. He says two pictures are joined: the key is the power to open and close, and the shoulder is the weight of running the kingdom.

sources.quote: ואמר על שכמו והמפתח לא ישא אדם אותו על שכמו אמר הענין בשני משלים
sources.says: Radak says no one carries a key on his shoulder, so the verse puts the idea in two images.

sources.quote: מַפְתֵּחַ בֵּית מִקְדְשָׁא וְשׁוּלְטַן בֵּית דָוִד
sources.says: The Targum says the key of the Temple and the rule of the house of David.

23:2.headline: Be silent, or be broken?
23:2.body: דמו can mean 'be still'. Rashi and Metzudat Zion read that the islanders sit silent in mourning. The Targum reads 'they were broken', as Radak points out.

sources.quote: הִתְאַבְּלוּ וְשְׁבוּ דוֹמִים
sources.says: Rashi says they mourn and sit silent.

sources.quote: דומו. ענין שתיקה כמו וידום אהרן
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the word means silence, as when Aaron was silent.

sources.quote: ויונתן תרגם דמו אתברו
sources.says: Radak notes that the Targum renders the word as 'they were broken'.

23:8.headline: Her "Canaanites" are her traders
23:8.body: כנען usually names the people of Canaan. Here it means merchants, as in Hosea, 'a Canaan with false scales in his hand'. The Talmud uses this very verse to prove that כנעני can mean a trader.

sources.quote: כִּנְעָנֶיהָ. תַּגָּרֶיהָ, כְּמוֹ ״כְּנַעַן בְּיָדוֹ מֹאזְנֵי מִרְמָה״
sources.says: Rashi says the word means her traders, as in Hosea's 'Canaan with false scales'.

sources.quote: וּכְנַעֲנִי מְנָלַן דְּאִיקְּרִי תַּגָּר
sources.says: The Talmud asks how we know a Canaanite can mean a trader.

sources.quote: אֲשֶׁר סוֹחֲרֶיהָ שָׂרִים כִּנְעָנֶיהָ נִכְבַּדֵּי אָרֶץ
sources.says: The Talmud answers with this verse from Isaiah.

23:11.headline: Canaan the land, or Canaan the trading city?
23:11.body: Rashi reads כנען as the land: Tyre and Sidon were Canaanite cities. Metzudat Zion and Radak read it as 'trade', so it names Tyre as a merchant city.

sources.quote: צוֹר וְצִידוֹן מִשֶּׁל כְּנַעַן הָיוּ
sources.says: Rashi says Tyre and Sidon belonged to Canaan.

sources.quote: כנען. ענין תגר ומסחר
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says כנען here means a trader and trade.

sources.quote: אל צור שהיא כנען, כלומר שהיא עיר סחורה
sources.says: Radak says Tyre is called Canaan because it is a city of trade.

23:15.headline: "The days of one king": David, the Messiah, or any king?
23:15.body: Tyre is forgotten seventy years, 'as the days of one king'. Rashi says David lived seventy years but admits he does not know why. Radak says seventy is a normal lifetime. The Talmud reads 'one king' as a unique king, the Messiah.

sources.quote: יְמֵי דָוִד שִׁבְעִים שָׁנָה הָיוּ; וְאֵינִי יוֹדֵעַ מַהוּ הַסִּימָן הַזֶּה
sources.says: Rashi says David's days were seventy years, and he does not know what the sign means.

sources.quote: לפי שימי האדם הם שבעים שנה ברוב
sources.says: Radak says a person's life is usually seventy years.

sources.quote: אֵיזֶהוּ מֶלֶךְ מְיוּחָד? הֱוֵי אוֹמֵר: זֶה מָשִׁיחַ
sources.says: The Talmud asks which king is unique and answers: the Messiah.

23:17.headline: "She will play the harlot" means she will trade
23:17.body: The verse says Tyre will go whoring with all the kingdoms. Rashi, Radak and the Targum say it means she will trade with them again. The prophet chose an insulting word for it.

sources.quote: וּתְסַפֵּק סְחוֹרָה, אַךְ בְּלָשׁוֹן גְּנַאי כִּנָּה אוֹתָהּ
sources.says: Rashi says it means she will supply goods, but the prophet used an insulting word.

sources.quote: וזנתה. תסחר
sources.says: Radak says the word means she will trade.

sources.quote: וּתְהֵי מְסַפְּקָא סְחוֹרָא
sources.says: The Targum renders it 'she will supply goods'.

23:18.headline: How can a harlot's wage be holy?
23:18.body: The Torah forbids bringing a harlot's wage to God, yet here Tyre's wage is 'holy to the LORD'. Ibn Ezra raises this and answers that the word is only a figure of speech: Tyre is not a real harlot.

sources.quote: ויש שואלים והלא התורה אסרה אתנן זונה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra notes the question that the Torah forbids a harlot's wage.

sources.quote: וזה שאמר הנביא הוא על דרך משל ואיננה זונה כלל
sources.says: Ibn Ezra answers that the prophet speaks in a figure and Tyre is no harlot at all.

24:1.headline: Cutting the land off, or opening it like a gate
24:1.body: Metzudat Zion and Radak read ובולקה as cutting the land off from all settlement. Radak’s father read it from Arabic as “opening”: God opens the land like a gate so its people pour out.

sources.quote: ובולקה. ענין כריתה וכן בוקה ומבוקה ומבולקה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says ובולקה means cutting off, as in Nahum 2:11.

sources.quote: ואדוני אבי ז"ל פירש ענין פתיחה מן הערבי בלקת אלכאב, ר"ל פתיחת השער, ופירוש בולקה פותח אותה שיצאו אנשיה ממנה
sources.says: Radak cites his father, who read it from an Arabic word for opening a gate: God opens the land so its people leave.

24:2.headline: Two kinds of lender: one of money, one of goods
24:2.body: The verse lists a מלוה, a lender, and then a נושה. Rashi and Metzudat Zion explain the difference: one lends money, the other lends goods such as wine, oil and grain.

sources.quote: לוֶֹה נוֹפֵל בְּכֶסֶף, וְנוֹשֶׁה נוֹפֵל בְּכָל שְׁאָר דְּבָרִים, כְּגוֹן: יַיִן וְשֶׁמֶן וּתְבוּאָה וּדְבַשׁ
sources.says: Rashi says לוה is used for money, and נושה for other things such as wine, oil, grain and honey.

sources.quote: כנשה. ענין הלואת דברים זולת הכסף כיין ושמן ותבואה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says נושה is lending things other than money, like wine, oil and grain.

24:4.headline: The land “seasoned” with commandments
24:4.body: Metzudat Zion says תבל is the inhabited world. Rashi reads it as the Land of Israel, which is “seasoned” (מתובלת) with many commandments.

sources.quote: תבל. כן נקראה הארץ המיושבת
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says תבל is the name for the inhabited earth.

sources.quote: תֵּבֵל. הִיא אֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל, שֶׁהִיא מְתֻבֶּלֶת בְּמִצְוֹת הַרְבֵּה
sources.says: Rashi says תבל is the Land of Israel, which is seasoned with many commandments.

24:5.headline: A land that flatters: stalks with no wheat inside
24:5.body: חנף usually means polluted or corrupt. Rashi and Metzudat David read it as flattery: the land puts on a show of grain stalks, but there is no wheat in them.

sources.quote: כְּמִין חֲנִיפוּת: עוֹשָׂה עֵשֶׂב וְאֵינוֹ עוֹשֶׂה קָמָה, מַרְאָה קָמָה וְאֵין חִטִּין בְּקַשֶּׁיהָ
sources.says: Rashi says the land acts like a flatterer: it grows grass and shows stalks, but there is no wheat in them.

sources.quote: כמו המחניף בשפתיו ולבו בל עמו כן הארץ עושה עשב ואינה עושה קמה מראה קמה ואין חטים בקשיה
sources.says: Metzudat David compares the land to a flatterer whose lips and heart do not match.

24:6.headline: Not found guilty, but laid waste
24:6.body: ויאשמו looks like “they were found guilty” (אשם). Metzudat Zion and Radak read it as “they were laid waste,” from שממה, as with the flocks in Joel that were desolate (נאשמו).

sources.quote: ויאשמו. מלשון שממה וכן גם עדרי הצאן נאשמו
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says ויאשמו comes from desolation, as in Joel 1:18.

sources.quote: ויאשמו. בשו"א האל"ף והשי"ן והוא לשון שממה
sources.says: Radak says ויאשמו means desolation.

24:11.headline: All joy has turned to evening
24:11.body: ערבה comes from ערב, “evening”: all joy has grown dark. Radak and Metzudat David explain that joy is called light, so its loss is told as nightfall.

sources.quote: ערבה כל שמחה. חשכה כל שמחה כי השמחה ביין, כמו שאמר ויין ישמח לבב אנוש, וערבה מן ערב שהוא חשך, והשמחה אורה והפכה חשך
sources.says: Radak says ערבה means grew dark, from ערב, because joy is light and its opposite is darkness.

sources.quote: ולפי שהשמחה קרויה אור לזה אמר בהעדרה ענין חושך
sources.says: Metzudat David says joy is called light, so its absence is described as darkness.

24:15.headline: Honor God in the light, or in the valleys
24:15.body: The Targum, cited by Rashi, reads אורים as light: when light comes to the righteous. Menachem reads it as clefts where people fled, as in אור כשדים, and Radak as valleys.

sources.quote: תִּרְגֵּם יוֹנָתָן: ״בְּמֵיתֵי נְהוֹרָא לְצַדִּיקַיָּא״, עַל שְׁתֵּי בְּשׂוֹרוֹת (ספרים אחרים: מְאוֹרוֹת) שֶׁל גָּאוּלַת בָּבֶל וְשֶׁל אֱדוֹם. וּמְנַחֵם אָמַר (מחברת: אר) ׳אוּרִים׳ לְשׁוֹן ׳נְקִיעִים וּסְעִיפִים׳ שֶׁהָיוּ בּוֹרְחִים שָׁם, וְכֵן ״אוּר כַּשְׂדִּים״ (בראשית יא:כח) בִּקְעַת כַּשְׂדִּים
sources.says: Rashi gives the Targum’s “when light comes to the righteous,” and Menachem’s reading of אורים as clefts, as in אור כשדים.

sources.quote: בעמקים כמו מאור כשדים
sources.says: Radak reads באורים as “in the valleys,” as in אור כשדים.

24:16.headline: From the wing of the earth: its far edge, or the Temple
24:16.body: Maimonides says כנף, a wing, is borrowed for the far edges of the inhabited world, and he cites this verse. The Targum, cited by Rashi, reads it as the Temple, near the eastern end of the land.

sources.quote: אחר כך הושאל לחלקים הנידחים ביותר של הארץ הנושבת ולקצותיה המרוחקים ממקומותינו: "לֶאֱחֹז בְּכַנְפוֹת הָאָרֶץ" (איוב לח,יג), "מִכְּנַף הָאָרֶץ זְמִרֹת שָׁמַעְנוּ
sources.says: Maimonides says כנף was borrowed for the most remote parts of the inhabited earth, citing this verse.

sources.quote: מִכְּנַף הָאָרֶץ. תִּרְגֵּם יוֹנָתָן: ״מִבֵּית מַקְדְּשָׁא״, שֶׁהוּא בְּסוֹף אֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל בְּמִזְרָחָהּ
sources.says: Rashi says the Targum renders it “from the Temple,” which is at the eastern end of the Land of Israel.

24:16.headline: “My secret,” or “I am wasting away”
24:16.body: רזי can mean “my secret” or “my leanness.” Metzudat Zion reads the first רזי as a secret and the second as wasting away, while Rashi hears two secrets, one of punishment and one of rescue.

sources.quote: רזי. קדמאה ענין סוד כמו וכל רז לא אנס לך (דניאל ד׳:ו׳) ותניינא ענין רזון וכחישות
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the first רזי means a secret and the second means leanness.

sources.quote: אוֹי לִי שֶׁנִּגְלוּ לִי שְׁנֵי רָזִים: רָז פֻּרְעָנוּת וְרָז יְשׁוּעָה
sources.says: Rashi says the prophet was shown two secrets: one of punishment and one of salvation.

24:23.headline: The moon blushes, or its worshippers do
24:23.body: Plainly, the moon blushes and the sun is ashamed. The Targum reads it as those who worship the moon and sun being shamed, and Maimonides praises this reading, though Ibn Ezra says it does not fit the passage.

sources.quote: יונתן בן עֻזיאל עליו השלום פִּרשֵן את הדברים האלה בפרשנות נאה ביותר, ואמר שכשיקרה לסנחריב מה שעתיד לקרות לירושלם, אז ידעו עובדי הכוכבים שזהו מעשה אלוהי, ויוכו בתדהמה וייבושו
sources.says: Maimonides praises Targum Jonathan’s reading: when Sennacherib falls, the star worshippers will know it is God’s act and be ashamed.

sources.quote: וְיִבְהֲתוּן דְפָלְחִין לְסִיהֲרָא וְיִתְכַּנְעוּן דְסָגְדִין לְשִׁמְשָׁא
sources.says: The Targum renders it: those who serve the moon will be ashamed, and those who bow to the sun will be humbled.

sources.quote: ויש אומרים כי הטעם על עובדי המאורות ואיננו דבק בטעמי הפרשה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra reports that some read it as the worshippers of the lights, and says this does not fit the passage.

25:5.headline: The tyrants' song, or the tyrants cut down?
25:5.body: זמיר can come from זמר 'to sing' or from זמר 'to prune'. Ibn Ezra reads it as the tyrants' songs. Rashi and Radak read it as cutting, as in 'do not prune your vineyard'.

sources.quote: והנה זמיר עריצים. כמו שאון זרים מגזרת זמירות
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says זמיר is from the word for songs, like the noise of strangers.

sources.quote: זְמִיר. לשון ״לא תִזְמֹר״
sources.says: Rashi links זמיר to 'do not prune'.

sources.quote: זמיר. ענין כריתה, כמו וכרמך לא תזמור
sources.says: Radak says זמיר means cutting down, as in 'do not prune your vineyard'.

25:7.headline: Swallow up the veil, or uncover it?
25:7.body: בלע usually means swallow or destroy, and Radak reads it that way. Ibn Ezra reads it as 'uncover', as in Numbers 4, where the holy things are 'swallowed' meaning exposed to view.

sources.quote: ובלע. כמו כבלע את הקודש
sources.says: Ibn Ezra compares it to 'when the holy things are covered/uncovered' in Numbers.

sources.quote: כטעם גלוי
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the sense is uncovering.

sources.quote: ובלע. ענין השחתה
sources.says: Radak says ובלע means destroying.

25:7.headline: A veil over the nations, or their rulers?
25:7.body: Metzudat Zion and Ibn Ezra read המסכה as a covering, like the veil in the same verse. Rashi reads it from נסיך 'prince', meaning rule and power. The Targum also reads it as the face of the king who rules all kingdoms.

sources.quote: וְהַמַּסֵּכָה. לְשׁוֹן נְסִיכוּת וְשָׂרָרָה
sources.says: Rashi says המסכה means princely rule and authority.

sources.quote: והמסכה. גם הוא ענין מכסה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says המסכה also means a covering.

sources.quote: וְאַפֵּי מַלְכָּא דְשַׁלִיט עַל כָּל מַלְכְּוָתָא
sources.says: The Targum renders it the face of the king who rules over all kingdoms.

25:8.headline: Death swallowed forever: all death, or only killing?
25:8.body: The Talmud asks how death can end when another verse says a man will die at a hundred. It answers that death ends for Israel. Radak says only violent death in exile ends, not natural death.

sources.quote: יְכַסֶּנּוּ וְיַעֲלִימֶנּוּ עוֹלָמִית מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל
sources.says: Rashi says God will hide death away from Israel forever.

sources.quote: לָא קַשְׁיָא: כָּאן בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל, כָּאן בַּגּוֹיִם
sources.says: The Talmud resolves the clash: one verse is about Israel, the other about the nations.

sources.quote: ר"ל מיתה מקרית לא מיתה טבעית
sources.says: Radak says this means death by violence, not natural death.

25:9.headline: "This is our God": the righteous point with a finger
25:9.body: זה means 'this', a word you say while pointing. The Talmud reads it that way: in the time to come each righteous person will point with a finger at God.

sources.quote: וְכׇל אֶחָד וְאֶחָד מַרְאֶה בְּאֶצְבָּעוֹ
sources.says: The Talmud says each one will point with his finger, citing this verse.

25:10.headline: A dung heap, or the Moabite town of Madmen?
25:10.body: Rashi reads מדמנה as mud and Radak as a dung heap: Moab is trampled like straw in dung. Radak's father read it as Madmen, a Moabite town named in Jeremiah.

sources.quote: מַדְמֵנָה. טִיט
sources.says: Rashi says מדמנה means mud.

sources.quote: מדמנה. הוא האשפה, כי הזבל שבאשפה יקרא דמן
sources.says: Radak says מדמנה is a dung heap, since dung is called דמן.

sources.quote: ואדוני אבי ז"ל פירש מדמנה שם עיר מערי מואב
sources.says: Radak says his father read מדמנה as the name of a Moabite town.

25:11.headline: Who spreads out his hands like a swimmer?
25:11.body: Ibn Ezra and Radak say it is God, who spreads His hands through Moab like a swimmer pushing the water aside. Rashi says it is Moab, beating his arms in grief.

sources.quote: האל יפרש ידיו בקרב מואב כאשר יפרוש השוחה לשחות
sources.says: Radak says God spreads His hands through Moab the way a swimmer spreads his to swim.

sources.quote: וְשָׁבַר יָדָיו וּזְרוֹעוֹתָיו בְּסִפּוּק כַּפַּיִם בִּבְכִי
sources.says: Rashi says Moab strikes his hands and arms together in weeping.

26:2.headline: Not “keeping” faith, but waiting for God's promise
26:2.body: שמר usually means to guard or keep. Rashi says here it means to wait, as Jacob “kept the matter” in mind. The righteous nation waited through exile for God to keep his word.

sources.quote: שֹׁמֵר. מַמְתִּין, וְכֵן (בראשית לז:יא) ״וְאָבִיו שָׁמַר אֶת הַדָּבָר״
sources.says: Rashi says שומר means waiting, as when Jacob kept the matter in mind.

sources.quote: ענין המתנה ותקוה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means waiting and hope.

26:4.headline: God the “Rock”: the source of everything, not a stone
26:4.body: צור means a rock. Maimonides says God is called צור because he is the origin and cause of all else, and he lists this verse among his examples.

sources.quote: נקרא ה' יתעלה "צור", כי הוא הראשית והסיבה הפועלת לכל מה שזולתו
sources.says: Maimonides says God is called צור because he is the beginning and the cause of everything besides him.

sources.quote: כי הוא צור עולמים, פירוש חוזק הזמנים כולם
sources.says: Radak says צור עולמים means the strength of all the ages.

26:11.headline: Where the accent falls changes the time: “Your hand was raised”
26:11.body: Rashi notes the stress in רמה falls on the first syllable, which marks a past tense. So it means God's hand had withdrawn from his enemies, not that it is raised now. He sets aside a midrash on this ground.

sources.quote: כָּל ׳יָד רָמָה׳ שֶׁבַּמִּקְרָא טַעֲמוֹ לְמַטָּה וְזֶה טַעֲמוֹ לְמַעְלָה
sources.says: Rashi says every other יד רמה in Scripture is stressed on the last syllable, but this one on the first.

sources.quote: נִסְתַּלְּקָה יַד גְּבוּרָתְךָ מֵעַל צָרֶיךָ
sources.says: Rashi reads it as: your mighty hand has withdrawn from your enemies.

26:14.headline: The dead are called “the slack ones”
26:14.body: רפאים is a name for the dead. Metzudat Zion says it comes from רפה, to go limp, since death weakens them. Rashi says these are people who let their hands go slack from God's commands.

sources.quote: הם המתים שנרפו ונחלשו ע״י המיתה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says they are the dead, gone limp and weak through death.

sources.quote: וְהָרְפָאִים הָאֵלֶּה שֶׁרִפּוּ יְדֵיהֶם מִמִּצְווֹתֶיךָ
sources.says: Rashi says they are those who let their hands go slack from God's commands.

26:16.headline: An odd word for pouring out a prayer
26:16.body: Ibn Ezra calls צקון a strange word. He and Radak say it comes from יצק, to pour, with a letter dropped and a נ added. In their pain they poured out prayer.

sources.quote: והיא מלה זרה, והיתה ראויה להיותה יצקו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it is a strange word that should have been יצקו, they poured.

sources.quote: הנו"ן נוספת כנו"ן אשר לא ידעון אבותיך, והוא חסר פ"א הפעל ושרשו יצק
sources.says: Radak says the נ is extra, the first root letter is missing, and the root is יצק.

26:16.headline: A whispered prayer, or Torah studied in secret
26:16.body: לחש is a whisper. Radak says prayer is called this because it is said quietly. He reports that the Targum reads it as Israel studying Torah and keeping the commands in secret when it was forbidden.

sources.quote: ולחש פירוש תפלה, נקראת כן לפי שהיא נאמרת בלחש
sources.says: Radak says לחש means prayer, called this because it is said in a whisper.

sources.quote: שהיו גוזרים עליהם שלא ללמוד תורה ושלא לעשות מצות והם היו לומדים ועושים בחשאי
sources.says: Radak explains the Targum: when they were forbidden to study Torah and keep the commands, they did so in secret.

26:18.headline: The nations did not fall, or could do no wonders
26:18.body: יפלו usually means fall. Rashi says the nations who rule the world have not fallen. He adds that the Targum hears פלא, wonder, in the word: the nations cannot work wonders.

sources.quote: וְאֵין נוֹפְלִין הָעַמִּים, שֶׁהֵם יוֹשְׁבֵי תֵבֵל
sources.says: Rashi says the nations, who fill the world, are not falling.

sources.quote: אֵין יוֹשְׁבֵי תֵבֵל יְכוֹלִין לַעֲשׂוֹת פֶּלֶא
sources.says: Rashi gives the Targum's reading: the people of the world cannot work a wonder.

26:19.headline: Dew of light, or dew for green plants
26:19.body: אורות can mean lights or green herbs. Rashi reads it as a dew of light. Radak reads it as herbs, as in 2 Kings 4:39: as dew revives plants, God's dew will revive the dead.

sources.quote: שֶׁיְּהֵא טַל תּוֹרָתְךָ וּמִצְווֹתֶיךָ לָהֶם טַל שֶׁל אוֹר
sources.says: Rashi says the dew of God's Torah and commands will be a dew of light for them.

sources.quote: אורות הם ירקות, כמו ללקוט אורות
sources.says: Radak says אורות are green plants, as in going out to gather אורות.

sources.quote: כמו שהטל מחיה הירקות ומצמיחם כן טלך
sources.says: Radak says as dew revives and grows plants, so God's dew will revive the dead.

26:20.headline: Go into your rooms: houses of study, or your own heart
26:20.body: The verse tells the people to hide in their rooms until the anger passes. Rashi brings Rabbi Tanchuma: the rooms are synagogues and study halls, or the inner rooms of the heart where one weighs one's deeds.

sources.quote: בְּבָתֵּי כְנֵסִיּוֹת וּבְבָתֵּי מִדְרָשׁוֹת. דָּבָר אַחֵר: הִתְבּוֹנֵן עַל מַעֲשֶׂיךָ בְּחַדְרֵי לִבְּךָ
sources.says: Rashi says the rooms are synagogues and study halls, or else: look at your deeds in the rooms of your heart.

28:5.headline: A crown named for going around the head
28:5.body: צפירה is an unusual word for a crown or headband. Radak and Metzudat Zion say it comes from going around, like the rim woven around a basket in the Mishnah.

sources.quote: וצפירה הוא ענין סבוב לפיכך נקראה העטרה או מצנפת הראש צפירה לפי שהיא סביב הראש, ובמשנה הקופה משיעשה בה שתי צפירות והם מה שעושין מן הגומא סביב הקופה
sources.says: Radak says צפירה means going around, so a crown or turban is called this, and compares the rim around a basket in the Mishnah.

sources.quote: ולצפירת. כן יקרא העטרה או המצנפת המסבב את הראש כי צפירה היא ענין סבוב
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the crown or turban that circles the head is called צפירה, because the word means going around.

28:10.headline: A short word for “command” found nowhere else
28:10.body: Radak says צו is a noun meaning a commandment, used this way nowhere else, and here a small one, taught bit by bit as to children. Rashi hears the people answering the prophet: we have a command of our own, worth more than yours.

sources.quote: צו הוא שם כמו מצוה ולא נאמרה המצוה בזה הלשון במקום אחר, ורוצה בו באמרו צו מצוה קטנה
sources.says: Radak says צו is a noun like מצוה, used this way nowhere else, meaning a small command.

sources.quote: וְהֵם יֵשׁ לָהֶם צַו שֶׁל עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה כְּנֶגֶד צַו זֶה; וְחוֹזֵר הַנָּבִיא וּמוֹכִיחָם, וְהֵם תָּמִיד אוֹמְרִים: ״יֵשׁ לָנוּ צַו לְצַו שֶׁלָּנוּ חָשׁוּב מִשֶּׁלְּךָ
sources.says: Rashi says the people answer each command of the prophet with a command of their idol worship, which they call more important.

28:13.headline: A measuring line that also sounds like hope
28:13.body: קו is a builder’s measuring line, and Rashi reads it as a measured line of punishment for their sins. He also hears תקוה, “hope”: they will hope for light and find darkness.

sources.quote: קַו שֶׁל פֻּרְעָנוּת כְּנֶגֶד קַו שֶׁל עֲבֵירוֹת שֶׁבְּיָדָם, קַו לָקָו תִּקְוָה חִלּוּף תִּקְוָה, יְקַוּוּ לְאוֹר וְהִנֵּה חֹשֶׁךְ
sources.says: Rashi reads קו as a line of punishment matching their line of sins, and also as hope that turns into its opposite.

28:14.headline: Rulers of the people, or men who mock in proverbs
28:14.body: משלי can mean “rulers” or “those who speak in sayings.” Ibn Ezra reports the first reading but prefers the second, and Rashi says they mock in the language of parables.

sources.quote: יש אומרים מגזרת ממשלה, והטעם השרים, והנכון שהוא כמו על כן יאמרו המושלים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra reports that some read “rulers,” but says the right reading is “those who speak in sayings,” as in Numbers 21:27.

sources.quote: הָאוֹמְרִים לָצוֹן בְּלָשׁוֹן מָשָׁל
sources.says: Rashi says these are people who mock in the language of parables.

28:15.headline: A pact with the grave: a border, or a face-to-face meeting
28:15.body: Rashi reads חזה as a border that the grave agreed not to cross. Radak keeps the sense of seeing: a face-to-face meeting, the way a man meets his opponent to make peace.

sources.quote: גְּבוּל שֶׁלֹּא יַעַבְרֶנְהוּ, וְכֵן ״מְחוֹז חֶפְצָם
sources.says: Rashi says חזה means a border that will not be crossed, as in מחוז חפצם.

sources.quote: חוזה. שם כמו רואה שפירשנו, כלומר מחזה עשינו עמו כאדם המתראה פנים עם בעל דינו לעשות שלום עמו
sources.says: Radak says חזה comes from seeing: a meeting face to face, like a man who meets his opponent to make peace.

28:16.headline: Not a tested stone but a fortress stone
28:16.body: Elsewhere בחן is about testing. Rashi and Metzudat Zion read אבן בחן here as a stone of strength, a fortress.

sources.quote: לְאֶבֶן בֹּחַן, לְשׁוֹן מִבְצָר וְחֹזֶק, כְּמוֹ (ישעיהו לב:יד) ״עֹפֶל וָבַחַן
sources.says: Rashi reads בחן as a fortress and strength, as in עפל ובחן.

sources.quote: בוחן. ענין מבצר חזק כמו הקימו בחוניו
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says בחן means a strong fortress, as in הקימו בחוניו.

28:17.headline: Hail will sweep away the false shelter like ash
28:17.body: Rashi reads ויעה from the יעים, the shovels that scraped ash out of the stoves. The hail will sweep away the lie they hid behind.

sources.quote: וְיָעָה לְשׁוֹן ׳טִאוּט׳, כְּמוֹ ״אֶת הַיָּעִים״ (מלכים א ז:מ) שֶׁגּוֹרְפִין בָּהֶן אֵפֶר הַכִּירוֹת
sources.says: Rashi says ויעה means sweeping, like the יעים used to scrape out the ash.

sources.quote: ויעה מגזרת יעים שהם המנקות שמנקה אדם בהם הבית
sources.says: Radak says ויעה comes from יעים, tools used to clean.

28:18.headline: The word for atonement here means wiping away
28:18.body: כפר usually goes with atonement. Rashi says every כפרה is really wiping clean and removing something, so their pact with death will be wiped out.

sources.quote: וְיִתְבַּטֵּל הַבְּרִית אֲשֶׁר אֲמַרְתֶּם כָּרַתְנוּ בְרִית אֶת מָוֶת. כָּל ׳כַּפָּרָה׳ לְשׁוֹן ׳קִנּוּחַ׳ וְ׳סִלּוּק דָּבָר׳, וְכֵן ״אֲכַפְּרָה פָנָיו
sources.says: Rashi says the pact will be cancelled, and that every כפרה means wiping clean and removing, as in אכפרה פניו.

28:20.headline: The sages hear “two companions” inside the word for stretching out
28:20.body: The plain sense is a bed too short to stretch out on. Rashi cites the sages, who hear in מהשתרע “two companions (רעים) ruling (השתרר)” over one bed: God and the idol Manasseh put in the Temple cannot share it.

sources.quote: וְרַבּוֹתֵינוּ דְּרָשׁוּהוּ (יומא טב) עַל עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה שֶׁהִכְנִיס מְנַשֶּׁה לַהֵיכָל (דברי הימים ב לג:ז): קָצַר הַמַּצָּע הַזֶּה מֵהִשְׂתָּרֵעַ, מֵהִשְׂתָּרֵר עָלָיו שְׁנֵי רֵעִים
sources.says: Rashi cites the sages, who apply the verse to the idol Manasseh brought into the Temple and read the bed as too short for two companions to rule over.

28:25.headline: Wheat planted by measure, or wheat that rules the field
28:25.body: Radak reads שורה as “by measure,” as in במשורה. Rashi links it to שררה, “rule”: wheat goes in the middle of the field and rules over the barley and spelt around it.

sources.quote: שורה. מדה, כמו במשקל ובמשורה שפירושו מדה
sources.says: Radak says שורה means measure, as in במשקל ובמשורה.

sources.quote: שׂוֹרָה לְשׁוֹן ׳שְׂרָרָה׳, זוֹרֵעַ בָּאֶמְצַע, וְנִמְצָאָה שׂוֹרָה עַל הַשְּׂעוֹרִין וְהַכּוּסְמִין
sources.says: Rashi says שורה is from שררה: wheat sown in the middle ends up ruling over the barley and spelt.

28:26.headline: God teaches the farmer, or God sends him rain
28:26.body: Metzudat Zion reads יורנו as “teaches him”: God gave the farmer his know-how. Radak’s father reads it from יורה, the early rain: the farmer sows properly and then hopes God sends rain.

sources.quote: יורנו. ענין למוד כמו יורנו בדרך יבחר
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says יורנו means teaching.

sources.quote: פירוש ימטירנו מענין יורה ומלקוש, כלומר הזורע יזרע כמשפט ואח"כ יקוה לאל שיתן מטר
sources.says: Radak cites his father, who read יורנו as “gives him rain,” from יורה ומלקוש.

28:29.headline: Wisdom called by the word for “what exists”
28:29.body: Metzudat Zion reads תושיה, “wisdom,” from יש, “there is.” Torah wisdom has this name because it lasts forever and never returns to nothing.

sources.quote: תושיה. מל׳ יש וחכמת התורה נקראת כן על כי ישנה לעולם ולא תשוב לאין כשאר הדברים שבעולם
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says תושיה comes from יש, because Torah wisdom exists forever and does not fade like other things.

sources.quote: תושיה. חכמה, ויאמר רבי משה הכהן שהוא מגזרת יש
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says תושיה means wisdom and cites Rabbi Moshe ha-Kohen, who derived it from יש.

29:1.headline: אריאל, "lion of God": the altar where fire crouched like a lion
29:1.body: The Targum reads אריאל as God's altar, as Ezekiel also calls it. Rashi says it is named for the fire from heaven that crouched on the altar like a lion (ארי); the sages said the Temple itself was shaped like a lion, narrow behind and wide in front.

sources.quote: וַי מַדְבְּחָא מַדְבְּחָא
sources.says: The Targum renders it: woe, altar, altar.

sources.quote: עַל שֵׁם אֵשׁ שֶׁל מַעְלָה שֶׁהָיְתָה רוֹבֶצֶת כַּאֲרִי עַל גַּבֵּי הַמִּזְבֵּחַ
sources.says: Rashi says it is named for the heavenly fire that crouched like a lion on the altar.

sources.quote: וְרַבּוֹתֵינוּ פֵּרְשׁוּ עַל הַהֵיכָל, שֶׁהָיָה צַר מֵאַחֲרָיו וְרָחָב מִלְּפָנָיו
sources.says: Rashi says the sages read it as the Temple, narrow behind and wide in front.

sources.quote: ויש אומרים שנקראת כן בעבור שמזלה אריה, וזה רחוק
sources.says: Ibn Ezra reports that some tie it to the sign of the lion, and calls that far-fetched.

29:1.headline: חגים: your festivals, or the lambs offered on them?
29:1.body: חג usually means a festival, and Rashi reads that your festivals will be cut off. Radak and Metzudat Zion read it as the festival offerings themselves, as in Psalms, "bind the festival offering with cords".

sources.quote: עַד שֶׁחַגִּים שֶׁלָּכֶם יִנְקֹפוּ וְיִכָּרְתוּ
sources.says: Rashi says your festivals will be cut off.

sources.quote: חגים. כמו כבשים, וכן אסרו חג בעבותים
sources.says: Radak says חגים means lambs, as in "bind the festival offering with cords".

sources.quote: חגים. כן יקראו הקרבנות על כי רובם באים בחג
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says offerings are called חגים because most come on festivals.

29:2.headline: תאניה ואניה: mourning and moaning, two words that echo
29:2.body: Metzudat Zion says the pair means grief and sorrow, as in Lamentations. Ibn Ezra reports a reading from אנה, "where?": nothing of the city will be left but its place.

sources.quote: תאניה ואניה. ענין אבל וצער
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the words mean mourning and sorrow.

sources.quote: ויש אומרים מגזרת אנה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra reports some derive it from אנה, where.

sources.quote: שלא ישאר רק מקומה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra explains that reading: only her place will remain.

29:2.headline: Jerusalem will be "like an altar": ringed with the slain
29:2.body: Rashi says the city will be surrounded by the fallen as the altar is surrounded by offerings. Ibn Ezra adds a second reading: like an altar left empty of offerings.

sources.quote: תְּהֵא מֻקֶּפֶת חַלְלֵי חֶרֶב, כְּמִזְבֵּחַ הַמֻּקָּף זִבְחֵי בְּהֵמָה
sources.says: Rashi says she will be ringed by the slain, as the altar is ringed by animal offerings.

sources.quote: שהמזבח שמם מהעולות, או כאריאל שיזבחו כלם
sources.says: Ibn Ezra reads it as an altar empty of offerings, or as an altar where all are slaughtered.

29:3.headline: Camped "like a כדור": a ring of troops, or a thrown ball
29:3.body: Rashi and Radak read כדור as a circle: troops will ring the city. Ibn Ezra reads it as a ball: the army will land suddenly, like a ball thrown into open country.

sources.quote: כְּשׁוּרָה שֶׁל גְּיָסוֹת מַקִּיפוֹת
sources.says: Rashi says it is like a line of troops surrounding the city.

sources.quote: כדור. סבוב, וכן במשנה הכדור והאמום, ונקרא כן לפי שהוא עגול
sources.says: Radak says כדור means a circle, like the ball in the Mishnah, named for being round.

sources.quote: וחניתי כדור. פתאם כמו כדור אל ארץ רחבת ידים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means suddenly, like a ball thrown into a wide land.

29:4.headline: Your words will chirp from the dust like small birds
29:4.body: Rashi says צפצוף is the faint chirp of small birds. Radak ties it to the day Hezekiah's officials begged the Assyrian envoy to speak Aramaic, quietly, so the people would not understand.

sources.quote: צִפְצוּף. הוּא לְשׁוֹן קוֹל לַחַשׁ כְּקוֹל עוֹפוֹת דַּקִּים
sources.says: Rashi says צפצוף is a whispering sound, like the voice of small birds.

sources.quote: והענין הזה אמר על אליקים ושבנא ויואם שאמר אל רבשקה דבר נא אל עבדיך ארמית
sources.says: Radak says this refers to Hezekiah's officials asking Rabshakeh to speak to them in Aramaic.

29:8.headline: "His soul is empty": here נפש means the body
29:8.body: The hungry man dreams he eats and wakes with an empty נפש. Metzudat Zion says נפש here means the body, as in Psalms, "iron entered his soul".

sources.quote: נפשו. כמו גופו וכן ברזל באה נפשו
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says נפשו means his body, as in "iron entered his soul".

29:9.headline: השתעשעו: it sounds like delight, but means blind yourselves
29:9.body: The word looks like שעשוע, "delight". Rashi reads it from "smear his eyes" in Isaiah 6: be blind; Metzudat Zion reads it as crying out.

sources.quote: הִשְׁתַּעַשְׁעוּ. לְשׁוֹן ״עֵינָיו הָשַׁע״
sources.says: Rashi says it comes from "smear his eyes".

sources.quote: הָיוּ עִוְּרִים מֵרְאוֹת
sources.says: Rashi says it means: be blind and unable to see.

sources.quote: השתעשעו ושעו. ענין צעקה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means crying out.

29:10.headline: God "poured" a spirit of sleep: mixed it, or covered you?
29:10.body: Rashi reads נסך as mixing a drink, or from נסיך, "prince": God set sleep over you. Radak reads it as "covered", and Ibn Ezra says the verse's last word, כסה, "covered", proves it.

sources.quote: לְשׁוֹן ״מֶזֶג״, כְּמוֹ ״מָסְכָה יֵינָהּ״
sources.says: Rashi says it means mixing, as in "she mixed her wine".

sources.quote: אוֹ לְשׁוֹן ׳נְסִיכוּת׳
sources.says: Rashi's second reading: from rule, as a prince rules.

sources.quote: כי נסך. כסה, כמו והמסכה הנסוכה
sources.says: Radak says נסך means covered.

sources.quote: והנה כסה לעד על מלת נסך
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the word כסה is the witness for the meaning of נסך.

29:10.headline: ויעצם: God shut your eyes, as if laying a bone on them
29:10.body: Metzudat Zion says the verb means to shut. Ibn Ezra hears עצם, "bone", in it: as if God laid a bone over your eyes.

sources.quote: ויעצם. ענין סתימה וסגירה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means closing and shutting.

sources.quote: ויעצם. מגזרת עצם כאילו שם עצם על עיניכם
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it comes from עצם, as if He put a bone over your eyes.

29:17.headline: Farmland "counted as forest": a forest of people
29:17.body: Lebanon's forest becomes farmland, and the farmland becomes a "forest". The Targum and the midrash, cited by Rashi, read that forest as towns so packed with people they look like woods.

sources.quote: תִּרְגֵּם יוֹנָתָן: ״קִירְוִין סַגִּיאִין יֵיתִיב״
sources.says: Rashi cites the Targum: it will hold many towns.

sources.quote: חוּרְשִׁין דְּבַר אִינָשׁ, יִשּׁוּב עָרִים וּבְנֵי אָדָם רָצוּף וּמָלֵא כַּיַּעַר הַזֶּה
sources.says: Rashi cites the midrash: forests of people, towns as crowded and full as a forest.

29:21.headline: יקשון: they set a snare, or gather his faults like straw?
29:21.body: Rashi reads it from מוקש, "snare": they trap the one who rebukes them. Radak offers קשש, "gather straw": they collect his faults from here and there and throw them back at him.

sources.quote: לְשׁוֹן ׳מוֹקֵשׁ׳
sources.says: Rashi says it comes from מוקש, a snare.

sources.quote: כי כמו שמקושש עצים או קשים לוקט מכאן ומכאן ואוספן יחד כן מחרף האדם מלקט מומיו מזה ומזה
sources.says: Radak says as one gathers sticks or straw from here and there, so they gather a man's faults to taunt him.

sources.quote: ור' משה הכהן אמר כי הם יוכיחו המוכיח, מגזרת התקוששו וקושו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra reports Rabbi Moshe HaKohen's reading from "gather yourselves": they rebuke the rebuker.

29:22.headline: "Who redeemed Abraham": God from Ur, or Jacob from heartache?
29:22.body: Rashi reads it plainly: God, who saved Abraham from Ur of the Chaldees. The Talmud reads it as Jacob redeeming Abraham, by taking on the pain of raising the children.

sources.quote: אֲשֶׁר פָּדָה אֶת אַבְרָהָם. מֵאוּר כַּשְׂדִּים
sources.says: Rashi says God redeemed Abraham from Ur of the Chaldees.

sources.quote: וְכִי הֵיכָן מָצִינוּ בְּיַעֲקֹב שֶׁפְּדָאוֹ לְאַבְרָהָם
sources.says: The Talmud asks: where do we find that Jacob redeemed Abraham?

sources.quote: שֶׁפְּדָאוֹ מִצַּעַר גִּידּוּל בָּנִים
sources.says: Rav Yehuda answers: he redeemed him from the pain of raising children.

29:22.headline: יחורו: a face turns white with shame
29:22.body: חיור is Aramaic for "white". Metzudat Zion says a shamed face goes pale, and Radak links it to the sages' phrase for shaming someone in public: "whitening his face".

sources.quote: יחורו. תרגום של לבן הוא חיור והוא ענין בושה כי המתבייש יתלבנו פניו
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the Aramaic for white is חיור, and it means shame, for a shamed face turns white.

sources.quote: וכן בדברי רז"ל המלבין פני חברו ברבים
sources.says: Radak compares the sages' phrase: one who whitens his fellow's face in public.

3:2.headline: A diviner among the leaders, or the king himself
3:2.body: A קוסם is usually a diviner, and Metzudat Zion reads it so: one who reads the future in the stars. Rashi says it means the king, citing “a קסם is on the lips of a king.”

sources.quote: וקוסם. הוא כחוזה בכוכבים ויודע מהעתידות
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says a קוסם is like a stargazer who knows the future.

sources.quote: וְקֹסֵם. זֶה מֶלֶךְ, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר ״קֶסֶם עַל שִׂפְתֵי מֶלֶךְ
sources.says: Rashi says the קוסם here is the king, citing Proverbs 16:10.

3:3.headline: A craftsman, a deep thinker, or a teacher who silences the room
3:3.body: Ibn Ezra reads חכם חרשים as a skilled craftsman, and Radak as a deep thinker, from “do not plot (תחרש) evil.” Rashi hears חרשים, “the deaf”: when he teaches Torah, everyone falls silent like the deaf.

sources.quote: וחכם חרשים. הוא האומן
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says חכם חרשים is the craftsman.

sources.quote: ופירוש חרשים מענין מחשבה, כמו אל תחרוש על רעך רעה, כי עיקר החכמה במחשבת הלב
sources.says: Radak says חרשים comes from thinking, as in Proverbs 3:29, because wisdom lives in the mind.

sources.quote: שֶׁכְּשֶׁפּוֹתֵחַ בְּדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה נַעֲשׂוּ הַכֹּל כְּחֵרְשִׁים
sources.says: Rashi says that when he opens with words of Torah, everyone becomes like the deaf.

3:4.headline: Little children, foxes, or mockers will rule them
3:4.body: Radak reads תעלולים as small children, like עוללים, matching the youths earlier in the verse. Rashi gives a midrash, “foxes,” meaning weak men, and then his own plain reading: mockers who abuse the people.

sources.quote: ותעלולים. כמו נערים, וכן עוללים שאלו לחם
sources.says: Radak says תעלולים means youths, like עוללים, “infants.”

sources.quote: שׁוּעָלִים, בְּנֵי אָדָם חֲלָשִׁים. וַאֲנִי אוֹמֵר לְפִי פְּשׁוּטוֹ: תַּעֲלוּלִים לֵיצָנֵי בְּנֵי אָדָם הַמִּתְעוֹלְלִים בָּהֶן וּמְבַזִּין אוֹתָם
sources.says: Rashi gives “foxes,” weak men, and in the plain sense mockers who abuse and shame the people.

3:9.headline: Judges who play favorites, or faces that give them away
3:9.body: Rashi first reads הכרת פניהם as “recognizing faces” in court, judges who play favorites. He then reads it as brazen faces that give them away, and Radak’s father backs this with an Arabic word for a hard face.

sources.quote: עָוֹן שֶׁהֵם מַכִּירִים פָּנִים בַּדִּין, הִיא עָנְתָה בָּם לְפָנַי. לָשׁוֹן אַחֵר: הַכָּרַת פְּנֵיהֶם – נִכָּרִים הֵם בְּעַזּוּת פְּנֵיהֶם
sources.says: Rashi reads it as the sin of favoring faces in judgment, or as being recognizable by brazen faces.

sources.quote: ואדוני אבי ז"ל פי' הכרת הה"א שרש ופירש עזות פניהם, וכן פירש לא תבושו תהכרו לי, תעיזו פניכם לי, ודמהו ללשון ערב שאומרים הכר לעזות מצח
sources.says: Radak cites his father, who read הכרת as brazenness and compared an Arabic word for a hard forehead.

3:12.headline: Your guides, or those who keep telling you “happy are you”
3:12.body: Rashi reads מאשריך as “your guides,” those meant to lead you down a good road. Radak reads it as those who tell you “happy are you” (אשריך) when you do wrong, the false prophets.

sources.quote: מְאַשְּׁרֶיךָ. מַדְרִיכֶיךָ, שֶׁיֵּשׁ לָהֶם לְאַשְּׁרֶךָ בְּדֶרֶךְ טוֹב, הֵם מַתְעִים אוֹתָם
sources.says: Rashi says מאשריך are your guides, who should lead you on a good road but lead you astray.

sources.quote: מי שאומר לך אשריך כשתעשה מעשים רעים אותם הם מתעים אותך והם נביאי השקר
sources.says: Radak says they are those who tell you “happy are you” when you do evil, the false prophets.

3:16.headline: Jingling anklets, or venom like a snake’s
3:16.body: Radak reads תעכסנה as jingling the bells (עכסים) on their ankles. Rashi links it to עכס, a snake’s venom: they brushed a foot against young men to stir up desire, like poison.

sources.quote: תעכסנה.  מקשקשות הרגליהם בעכסים שתלוין בהם שהם הפעמונים ומשמיעין קול
sources.says: Radak says they jingled the bells hanging on their feet.

sources.quote: כְּשֶׁהָיוּ עוֹבְרוֹת בַּשּׁוּק אֵצֶל בַּחוּרֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל, דּוֹרַסְתּוֹ בְּרַגְלוֹ וְרוֹמֶזֶת לוֹ צַד חִבַּת נוֹאֲפוֹת, כְּדֵי לְהַבְעִיר בּוֹ יֵצֶר הָרָע כְּעֶכֶס זֶה שֶׁל נָחָשׁ. ״עֶכֶס״ (משלי ז:כב) הוּא אֶרֶס שֶׁל נָחָשׁ
sources.says: Rashi says they pressed a foot against young men to stir desire, like עכס, a snake’s venom.

3:17.headline: A scab on the head, and slave women in the spelling
3:17.body: ושפח means God will strike them with a scab, like מספחת in Leviticus. Because it is spelled with ש, the sages also hear שפחות, “slave women,” and משפחות, whole “families” of lice.

sources.quote: וְשִׂפַּח. לְשׁוֹן צָרַעַת, כְּמוֹ (ויקרא יג:) ״מִסְפַּחַת הִיא״. וְעַל שֶׁנִּכְתַּב בְּשִׁי״ן דָּרְשׁוּ בּוֹ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ (פסיקתא דרב כהנא יז:) שֶׁתֵּעָשֶׂינָה שְׁפָחוֹת מְכֻדָּנוֹת, וְיֵשׁ שֶׁדְּרָשׁוּהוּ (שם) שֶׁהִרְבָּה בָּהֶן מִשְׁפָּחוֹת מִשְׁפָּחוֹת שֶׁל כִּנִּים
sources.says: Rashi says it means a skin disease, and that because it is written with ש the sages read “slave women” and “families of lice.”

sources.quote: ושפח ה'. כתוב בשי"ן והוא ענין ספחת
sources.says: Radak says the word is written with ש but means a scab.

3:20.headline: Earrings named for the place where people whisper
3:20.body: The לחשים are earrings. Rashi and Radak say they are named for the ear, the place where people whisper (לחש).

sources.quote: וְהַלְּחָשִׁים. נִזְמֵי הָאֹזֶן, מָקוֹם שֶׁלּוֹחֲשִׁין לָהּ שָׁם
sources.says: Rashi says they are earrings, worn where people whisper.

sources.quote: והלחשים. הוא עדי שתולין אותו הנשים באזניהם נקראו כן לפי שהאזנים בעלות הלחש
sources.says: Radak says they are ear ornaments, named because ears are where whispering happens.

3:23.headline: Mirrors named for what they reveal
3:23.body: Rashi and Radak say גליונים are mirrors, named because they reveal (גלה) the face. Rashi also suggests the mirrors may have rolled up (נגלל).

sources.quote: הֵן הַמַּרְאוֹת, כְּתַרְגּוּמוֹ: ״מַחְזְיָתָא״ (ספייקיי״ו בלע״ז), עַל שֵׁם שֶׁמְּגַלּוֹת צוּרוֹת הַפָּנִים קְרוּיִין גִּלְיוֹנִים, אוֹ שֶׁמָּא מַרְאוֹת שֶׁלָּהֶם נִגְלָלוֹת הָיוּ
sources.says: Rashi says they are mirrors, named for showing the face, or perhaps because they rolled up.

sources.quote: והגליונים. המראות נקראו כן לפי שנגלים בו הפנים לרואה בהם
sources.says: Radak says they are mirrors, called so because the face is revealed in them.

3:24.headline: “For” instead of beauty, or a burn instead of beauty
3:24.body: כי usually means “for” or “because.” Some read it as כויה, a burn, and Radak cites the Talmud’s Rava: “in place of beauty, a burn mark.”

sources.quote: ויש מפרשים כי זה לשון כויה, וכן בדברי רבותינו ז"ל כי תחת יופי, אמר רבא היינו דאמרי אנשי חלופי שופרא כואה
sources.says: Radak says some read כי as a burn, and cites Rava’s saying “instead of beauty, a burn.”

sources.quote: ואחרים אמרו שמלת כי מגזרת כויה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra reports others who read כי as coming from כויה, a burn.

3:26.headline: Not cleansed but emptied out
3:26.body: נקה usually means clean or innocent. Maimonides says here it means emptied out, and uses this verse to explain “he will not wipe out completely” among God’s thirteen attributes.

sources.quote: כי דבריו "וְנַקֵּה לֹא יְנַקֶּה" (שם) פירושם 'וְשָׁרֵשׁ לא ישרש' (=לא ישמיד לגמרי), כדבריו "[מְתַיִךְ בַּחֶרֶב יִפֹּלוּ, וּגְבוּרָתֵךְ בַּמִּלְחָמָה. וְאָנוּ וְאָבְלוּ פְּתָחֶיהָ] וְנִקָּתָה, לָאָרֶץ תֵּשֵׁב
sources.says: Maimonides says ונקה לא ינקה means “he will not uproot completely,” as נקתה means in this verse.

sources.quote: ונקתה. תהיה נקיה וריקנית מכל טובה
sources.says: Metzudat David says Zion will be cleaned out and empty of all good.

30:6.headline: The camel’s hump is named for the honey rubbed on it
30:6.body: דבשת is the camel’s hump, where the load sits. Rashi and Metzudat Zion say it is always getting sore, and people rub honey (דבש) on it to heal it, so it is called דבשת.

sources.quote: וְעַל שֵׁם שֶׁמִּתְרַקֶּבֶת תָּמִיד וְסָכִין שָׁם דְּבַשׁ לִרְפוּאָה קְרוּיָה דַּבֶּשֶׁת
sources.says: Rashi says the hump keeps rotting and is smeared with honey as a cure, so it is called דבשת.

sources.quote: דבשת גמלים. הוא חטוטרות הגמל שמניחים המשא עליו וע״ש שמרקיב תדיר ורפואתו למשחו בדבש קרוי דבשת
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the hump carries the load and is named for the honey used to heal it.

30:6.headline: A “flying” snake that has no wings
30:6.body: The verse speaks of a שרף מעופף, a “flying” snake. Rashi and Metzudat Zion stop to say it has no wings: it leaps so far that it seems to fly.

sources.quote: וְאַף שָׂרָף מְעוֹפֵף מִין נָחָשׁ הוּא, וְלֹא שֶׁיִּהְיוּ לוֹ כְּנָפַיִם לָעוּף, אֶלָּא קוֹפֵץ וּמְדַלֵּג רָחוֹק מְאֹד
sources.says: Rashi says the “flying” serpent has no wings, but jumps and leaps very far.

sources.quote: ושרף מעופף. מין נחש הדולג ממקום למקום ונראה כאלו הוא עף ופורח
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it is a snake that leaps from place to place and only looks as if it flies.

30:14.headline: Scooping up water, or laying the hollow bare
30:14.body: Rashi reads ולחשף as drawing up water. Ibn Ezra hears its usual sense, laying bare, and Radak joins the two: scooping out the last water leaves the hollow bare.

sources.quote: וְלַחְשֹׂף מַיִם. לִדְלוֹת, וְכֵן (חגי ב:טז) ״לַחְשֹׂף חֲמִשִּׁים פּוּרָה
sources.says: Rashi says ולחשף means to draw water, as in Haggai 2:16.

sources.quote: וטעם לחשוף לגלות, כי המים הם בסתר
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says לחשוף means to uncover, because the water is hidden.

sources.quote: וכאשר יקח המים מן הגבא הנה נשאר הגבא חשוף ומגולה, לפיכך אמר ולחשוף
sources.says: Radak says that taking the water leaves the hollow bare, and that is why the verse says ולחשף.

30:16.headline: They say “we will rise on horses,” God answers “you will flee”
30:16.body: The people boast על סוס ננוס, “on horses we will rise high like a banner (נס).” God answers with the same sound, תנוסון, “you will flee,” and Metzudat David points out the play.

sources.quote: ננוס. מלשון נס והוא כלונס ארוך וענינו הרמה כנס
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says ננוס comes from נס, a tall pole, and means being raised up like one.

sources.quote: על כן תנוסון. בעבור זה תנוסון מפני האויב ויהיה לכם השפלה ולפי שהוא לשון נופל על לשון אמר כן
sources.says: Metzudat David says “you will flee” was said because it sounds like the word they used.

30:20.headline: Your teacher will no longer hide behind his garment’s corner
30:20.body: Rashi pictures God no longer hiding his face behind the corner (כנף) of his garment. Maimonides, citing Ibn Janah, says כנף itself can mean hiding, as in Arabic, and calls this a fine reading.

sources.quote: לֹא יִתְכַּסֶּה מִמְּךָ בִּכְנַף בְּגָדָיו, כְּלוֹמַר, לֹא יַסְתִּיר מִמְּךָ פָּנָיו
sources.says: Rashi says God will not cover himself from you with the corner of his garment, meaning he will not hide his face.

sources.quote: אבן ג'נאח (ספר השרשים, ערך כנף) אמר שהוא נאמר גם במשמעות של הסתר, בדומה לערבית שבה אומרים "כַּנַפְתֻּ אלשַּׁי (=הסתרתי את הדבר)" במשמעות של "הסתרתי אותו", ואמר בפירוש של "וְלֹא יִכָּנֵף עוֹד מוֹרֶיךָ [וְהָיוּ עֵינֶיךָ רֹאוֹת אֶת מוֹרֶיךָ]" (ישעיהו ל,כ) – ולא ייסתר ממך מאירך ולא ייעלם, וזה פירוש נאה
sources.says: Maimonides cites Ibn Janah, who says כנף can mean hiding, like an Arabic word, and reads the verse as “your teacher will not be hidden,” calling it a fine reading.

30:21.headline: Not “you will believe” but “you will turn right”
30:21.body: תאמינו looks like “you will believe.” Radak and Metzudat Zion read it from ימין, “right,” with an alef in place of the yod: whether you turn right or left, you will hear which way to go.

sources.quote: תאמינו, כמו כי תימינו האל"ף תמורת היו"ד
sources.says: Radak says תאמינו means “you turn right,” with alef in place of yod.

sources.quote: תאמינו. מל׳ ימין ובאה האל״ף במקום היו״ד
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says תאמינו comes from ימין, with alef in place of yod.

30:26.headline: Light like seven days: a way of saying “many,” or Solomon’s feast
30:26.body: Radak reads “seven” as a way of saying “a great many.” Maimonides thinks “the seven days” points to the seven days when Solomon dedicated the Temple, the happiest days the nation ever had.

sources.quote: ושבעתים ר"ל אורות גדולות רבות, כמו שבעתים יוקם קין, ר"ל נקמות רבות לא שני פעמים שבעה לבד, כי חשבון שבע ושבעה יבא להגדיל החשבון
sources.says: Radak says seven here means many great lights, because seven is used to make a number large.

sources.quote: אשר לדבריו "כְּאוֹר שִׁבְעַת הַיָּמִים", המפרשים אמרו שהוא מתכוון לריבוי, כי דוברי העברית משתמשים במספר "שבע" לציין ריבוי. ומה שנראה לי, שהוא רומז לשבעת הימים שלחנוכת הבית שהיו בימי שלמה (מלכים־א ח,סה), שמעולם לא היו לאומה שגשוג ואושר ושמחה כללית כמו בימים ההם, ועל כן אמר ששגשוגם ואושרם אז יהיו כמו שבעת הימים הללו
sources.says: Maimonides reports that commentators read seven as “many,” but thinks it points to the seven days of Solomon’s Temple dedication, the nation’s happiest time.

30:33.headline: The pit named for those who let themselves be seduced
30:33.body: Rashi says תפתה is Gehinnom, named so because whoever is seduced (מתפתה) by his urges falls there. Ibn Ezra describes a real filthy place near Jerusalem, where refuse was dumped and smoke rose.

sources.quote: תָּפְתֶּה. גֵּיהִנֹּם (בראשית רבה ד ו), שֶׁכָּל הַמִּתְפַּתֶּה בְּיִצְרוֹ נוֹפֵל שָׁם
sources.says: Rashi says תפתה is Gehinnom, because whoever is seduced by his urge falls there.

sources.quote: תפתה. שם מקום מטונף סביב ירושלים, ושם ישליכו כל דומן ויעלה ממנו עשן
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says תפתה was a filthy place around Jerusalem where refuse was thrown and smoke rose.

31:3.headline: Flesh and not spirit: here 'spirit' means an angel
31:3.body: רוח can mean wind, breath or spirit. Ibn Ezra, Radak and Metzudat Zion say here it means an angel: Egypt's horses are only flesh, not angels.

sources.quote: רוח. כן נקרא המלאך
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says an angel is called רוח.

sources.quote: ולא רוח. מלאך כמו יי אלהים שלחני ורוחו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says 'not spirit' means not an angel, as in Isaiah 48:16.

sources.quote: בשר ולא רוח, ופי' ולא מלאך
sources.says: Radak says 'flesh and not spirit' means not an angel.

31:4.headline: The lion 'murmurs' over its prey: a soft word for a roar
31:4.body: הגה is the low sound of moaning, as doves moan. Metzudat Zion says the word is borrowed here for the lion's roar, and Ibn Ezra reads it simply as 'roars'.

sources.quote: כאשר יהגה. המית קול, כמו ״וכיונים הגה נהגה״
sources.says: Rashi says it is a sound of moaning, as in 'we moan like doves'.

sources.quote: והושאל על שאגת האריה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the word is borrowed for the lion's roar.

sources.quote: יהגה, כטעם ישאג
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means 'roars'.

31:5.headline: God 'passes over' Jerusalem, the word of the first Passover
31:5.body: פסח is the word for God passing over Israel's houses in Egypt. Rashi gives two readings, skipping over or sparing, and the Mekhilta cites this verse to show that פסח means sparing.

sources.quote: פסח. דלוג, ויש עוד לפתרו לשון ׳חיס׳
sources.says: Rashi says it means skipping, and can also be read as sparing.

sources.quote: פסוח. מגזרת ופסח יי על הפתח
sources.says: Ibn Ezra ties it to 'the Lord will pass over the door' in Exodus 12:23.

sources.quote: ופסחתי עלכם". אין פסיחה אלא חיס
sources.says: The Mekhilta says the Passover word means sparing, and brings this verse as proof.

31:9.headline: A furnace in Jerusalem: the Talmud places Gehinnom's gate there
31:9.body: Plainly this is a fire to burn the enemy, as Radak says. The school of Rabbi Yishmael reads the fire in Zion as Gehinnom, and the furnace in Jerusalem as its entrance.

sources.quote: זה האור וזה התנור יש לו בירושלם שישרפם
sources.says: Radak says God has this fire and furnace in Jerusalem to burn them.

sources.quote: ותנור לו בירושלים״ — זו פתחה של גיהנם
sources.says: The Talmud says the furnace in Jerusalem is the entrance to Gehinnom.

32:2.headline: Not 'in Zion', but in a dry land
32:2.body: בציון looks like 'in Zion'. Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Metzudat Zion say it comes from ציה, dry desert: like streams of water in a parched place.

sources.quote: בְּצָיוֹן. לְשׁוֹן ׳יֹבֶשׁ׳, צִיָּה
sources.says: Rashi says it is a word for dryness, from ציה.

sources.quote: כציון, מגזרת ציה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it comes from ציה, a dry place.

sources.quote: בציון. מל׳ ציה ומדבר
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it comes from the words for dry land and desert.

32:3.headline: Eyes no longer smeared shut: Isaiah 6 reversed
32:3.body: Rashi says the word means 'smeared over', as in Isaiah 6:10, where the people's eyes are sealed. Metzudat Zion says it means turning away, and both read this verse as undoing that blindness.

sources.quote: וְעֵינָיו הָשַׁע״ (ישעיהו ו:י), לְשׁוֹן ׳טוּחַ׳
sources.says: Rashi says it is the word in 'smear its eyes' (6:10), meaning plastered over.

sources.quote: תשעינה. ענין הסרה והפנה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means turning aside.

sources.quote: מענין ועיניו השע, שני שרשים והענין אחד
sources.says: Radak says it has the same meaning as 'smear its eyes', from a different root.

32:5.headline: The miser who says 'it's mine': כילי as כי לי
32:5.body: Rashi and Metzudat Zion say כילי is a cheat, and Radak says he is a tight-fisted man who gives only what he must. Ibn Ezra cites a reading of it as two words, כי לי, 'for it is mine'.

sources.quote: ויש על דרך דרש שמלת כילי שתים מלות, כי יאמר שלי שלי
sources.says: Ibn Ezra cites a midrashic reading that splits כילי into two words, because he says 'mine is mine'.

sources.quote: רַמַּאי, נוֹכֵל, חוֹרֵשׁ רָעִים
sources.says: Rashi says he is a cheat, a swindler, a plotter of evil.

sources.quote: ולכילי. שנותן במדה לא יותר דבר בשום פנים ועינו צרה
sources.says: Radak says he gives by exact measure, never more, and is stingy.

32:5.headline: A lord people turn to, or a free giver?
32:5.body: Rashi says שוע means a lord, because everyone turns (שועין) to him. Radak and Metzudat Zion say it means a generous person, and Radak ranks him above the נדיב.

sources.quote: לְשׁוֹן ׳אָדוֹן׳, שֶׁהַכֹּל שׁוֹעִין וּפוֹנִין אֵלָיו
sources.says: Rashi says it means a lord, since all turn to him.

sources.quote: הוא ותרן בממונו מאד שמח במתנותיו והוא יותר במעלה מהנדיב
sources.says: Radak says he is very free with his money, glad to give, and higher than the נדיב.

sources.quote: שוע. ענינו כמו נדיב
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means the same as a generous man.

32:5.headline: 'No longer' implies flattery is allowed for now
