32:5.body: The verse says a villain will 'no longer' be called noble. The Talmud reasons that in this world flattering the wicked is still allowed, while Radak says 'no longer' means during Hezekiah's reign.

sources.quote: מוּתָּר לְהַחְנִיף לִרְשָׁעִים בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה
sources.says: The Talmud says it is permitted to flatter the wicked in this world, learning it from this verse.

sources.quote: אינו אומר עוד כל ימי עולם אלא עוד כל ימי חזקיהו
sources.says: Radak says 'no longer' means for all of Hezekiah's days, not forever.

32:6.headline: 'Speaking error about God': Maimonides on wrong praise
32:6.body: Metzudat Zion says תועה is the opposite of truth, borrowed from someone who loses his way. Maimonides applies this verse to people who describe God with praises that do not fit Him.

sources.quote: ענינו הפך האמת והוא שאול מהתועה בדרך
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means the opposite of truth, borrowed from one who strays on the road.

sources.quote: התרת הלשון כלפי ה' יתעלה ותיאורו בתארים שהוא נעלה מהם
sources.says: Maimonides warns against loose speech about God and describing Him with attributes He is above, and cites this verse.

32:6.headline: Water kept from the thirsty: food, or Torah?
32:6.body: Rashi says the plain sense is robbing the poor of food and drink. The Targum, which Rashi quotes, says the wicked try to cancel words of Torah, which are like water to the thirsty.

sources.quote: לְפִי פְּשׁוּטוֹ, שֶׁגּוֹזְלִין הָעֲנִיִּים
sources.says: Rashi says in its plain sense it means robbing the poor.

sources.quote: וּפִתְגָמֵי אוֹרַיְתָא דְאִינוּן כְּמַיָא לְצַחָיָא מְדַמָן לְבַטָלָא
sources.says: The Targum says they plan to cancel words of Torah, which are like water to the thirsty.

32:7.headline: The miser and his 'tools': כלי beside כליו
32:7.body: The verse sets כלי, the miser, beside כליו, his tools. Radak says the tools are his ways and his measures, which come up short when he sells, and Ibn Ezra says they are the tools of the courts he bends.

sources.quote: ופי' כליו רעים מדותיו
sources.says: Radak says 'his tools are bad' means his ways.

sources.quote: כן כליו רעים וחסרים וכשימכור ימכור במדה חסרה
sources.says: Radak says his vessels are short, and when he sells he sells by a short measure.

sources.quote: וכילי כליו. הטעם כלי המשפט
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the tools are the tools of judgment, since these officials twisted the law.

32:7.headline: One word with three meanings in court
32:7.body: Rashi says משפט can mean the opening of a case, the verdict, or the punishment, and here it is the poor man's opening plea. Metzudat Zion reads it as honest, fair words.

sources.quote: ׳מִשְׁפָּט׳ מְשַׁמֵּשׁ שְׁלֹשָׁה לְשׁוֹנוֹת
sources.says: Rashi says the word משפט has three meanings.

sources.quote: כְּשֶׁמְּדַבֵּר הָאֶבְיוֹן טַעֲנוֹתָיו, זֶה יוֹעֵץ מְזִמּוֹת לְהַכְשִׁילוֹ בְּנִכְלָיו
sources.says: Rashi says that when the poor man states his claims, this schemer plots to trip him up.

sources.quote: משפט. ענינו דברים ישרים ונכוחים
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means straight, honest words.

32:9.headline: Complacent women, or complacent towns?
32:9.body: The Targum, followed by Rashi and Radak, reads 'women' as provinces and 'daughters' as walled cities. Ibn Ezra prefers real women, and the Talmud learns from this verse that God promised women more than men.

sources.quote: נָשִׁים שַׁאֲנַנּוֹת. ״מְדִינָן דְּיָתְבָן שַׁלְיָן״
sources.says: Rashi quotes the Targum: provinces that sit at ease.

sources.quote: נשים. כתרגומו מדינן, וכן בנות כרכין
sources.says: Radak follows the Targum: women are provinces, daughters are cities.

sources.quote: והנכון בעיני כי הנשים הם כמשמעם
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the right reading is that the women are real women.

sources.quote: גְּדוֹלָה הַבְטָחָה שֶׁהִבְטִיחָן הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לְנָשִׁים יוֹתֵר מִן הָאֲנָשִׁים
sources.says: The Talmud says God gave women a greater promise than men, citing this verse.

32:12.headline: Beating their chests, or mourning the sages who nursed Israel
32:12.body: Rashi and the Talmud say mourners beat on their chests, and the Talmud learns from this that a eulogy goes with striking the heart. A midrash in Rashi reads the breasts as the sages, who nourish Israel like nursing breasts.

sources.quote: עַל שָׁדַיִם סֹפְדִים. יְטַפְּחוּ עַל לִבָּם
sources.says: Rashi says they beat on their hearts.

sources.quote: הֶסְפֵּד עַל לֵב, דִּכְתִיב: ״עַל שָׁדַיִם סוֹפְדִים״
sources.says: The Talmud says a eulogy is done by striking the heart, citing this verse.

sources.quote: עַל חַכְמֵי סַנְהֶדְרָאוֹת, שֶׁהֵם כְּשָׁדַיִם הַמֵּינִיקִים יִסְפְּדוּ
sources.says: Rashi cites a midrash: they mourn the sages of the Sanhedrin, who are like nursing breasts.

32:14.headline: Caves for wild animals, or ruins laid bare?
32:14.body: Radak says the towers will become caves where wild animals live. Rashi reads מערות from 'raze it, raze it' (Psalms 137:7): the place will lie in ruins.

sources.quote: יהיו עוד למערות שידורו בה חיות השדה
sources.says: Radak says they will become caves where wild animals live.

sources.quote: מְעָרוֹת לָשׁוֹן ״עָרוּ עָרוּ״
sources.says: Rashi says מערות comes from 'raze it, raze it'.

sources.quote: יִהְיֶה בְּתוֹךְ חֻרְבּוֹת
sources.says: Rashi says it will be among ruins.

32:14.headline: Wild donkeys, or Ishmael?
32:14.body: Metzudat Zion and Radak say פראים are wild donkeys, who will be glad to graze in the ruins. Rashi reads it as Ishmael, whom Genesis 16:12 calls a פרא אדם, a wild man.

sources.quote: פראים. חמור הבר
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says פראים are wild donkeys.

sources.quote: פרא למוד מדבר
sources.says: Radak says the wild donkey is used to the desert.

sources.quote: לְתַאֲוַת יִשְׁמָעֵאל וּלְמִרְעֶה אֱדוֹם וַחֲיָלוֹתָיו
sources.says: Rashi says it will be for the desire of Ishmael and the pasture of Edom and its armies.

32:15.headline: Not Mount Carmel here, but rich farmland
32:15.body: Radak and Metzudat Zion say כרמל here is land of fields, vineyards and fruit trees. The desert will become farmland, and the farmland will grow as thick as a forest.

sources.quote: לכרמל. כן יקרא מקום שדות וכרמים
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says a place of fields and vineyards is called כרמל.

sources.quote: מה שהוא מדבר יהיה כרמל שהוא מקום זרע ושדות תבואה ועצי מאכל
sources.says: Radak says what is desert will become כרמל, a place of sowing, grain fields and fruit trees.

sources.quote: והכרמל ליער יחשב. ברוב עצים
sources.says: Radak says the farmland will be like a forest in its many trees.

32:17.headline: Getting others to give is greater than giving
32:17.body: Rabbi Elazar reads מעשה הצדקה as 'the making of charity', getting others to give. From this he says that one who gets others to give is greater than one who gives.

sources.quote: גָּדוֹל הַמְעַשֶּׂה יוֹתֵר מִן הָעוֹשֶׂה – שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: ״וְהָיָה מַעֲשֵׂה הַצְּדָקָה שָׁלוֹם
sources.says: Rabbi Elazar says one who causes others to give is greater than one who gives, citing this verse.

32:19.headline: It will hail, but only on the forest
32:19.body: Rashi and Radak say וברד is not the noun 'hail' but a verb, 'and it will hail', as its vowels show. Radak says the hail will fall on the forest and spare the crops.

sources.quote: עַל כָּרְחֲךָ אֵין ׳בָּרַד׳ זֶה שֵׁם דָּבָר
sources.says: Rashi says this ברד cannot be a noun.

sources.quote: חציו קמץ וחציו פתח והוא פעל עבר
sources.says: Radak says its vowels mark it as a verb.

sources.quote: כשיברד יפול הברד ביער שלא יזיק לצמחים
sources.says: Radak says when it hails, the hail will fall on the forest and not harm the crops.

32:19.headline: Which city is brought low?
32:19.body: Rashi says it is the capital of Persia, which will fall. Metzudat David says it is Jerusalem, rebuilt on low ground because it will be safe without a hilltop.

sources.quote: מֶטְרוֹפּוֹלִין שֶׁל פָּרַס
sources.says: Rashi says the city is the capital of Persia.

sources.quote: בנין העיר תשפל להבנות במקום שפל ועמוק ועכ״ז יהיו בטוחים מן האויב
sources.says: Metzudat David says the city will be built in a low place and still be safe from enemies.

32:20.headline: Sowing by all waters: fields, or charity and Torah?
32:20.body: Radak says wherever they sow, they will find water. The Talmud reads sowing as charity and water as Torah: happy is Israel when they busy themselves with both.

sources.quote: על כל מקום מים כי בכל מקום שתזרעו תמצאו מים
sources.says: Radak says wherever you sow you will find water.

sources.quote: וְאֵין זְרִיעָה אֶלָּא צְדָקָה
sources.says: The Talmud says sowing means charity.

sources.quote: וְאֵין מַיִם אֶלָּא תּוֹרָה
sources.says: The Talmud says water means Torah.

32:20.headline: Sending out the ox's foot: a source in the law of damages
32:20.body: Radak says the plenty will be so great that oxen and donkeys are let loose to graze. The Talmud uses this phrase to show that an animal 'sent out', in the Torah's law of damages, means damage done by its feet.

sources.quote: עד שישלחו השורים והחמורים לרעות בשדות
sources.says: Radak says they will send the oxen and donkeys to graze in the fields.

sources.quote: ״וְשִׁלַּח״ – זֶה הָרֶגֶל, וְכֵן הוּא אוֹמֵר: ״מְשַׁלְּחֵי רֶגֶל הַשּׁוֹר וְהַחֲמוֹר״
sources.says: The Talmud says 'and he sent' means damage by the foot, and cites this verse.

33:4.headline: Locusts, or pools of water that make things pure?
33:4.body: Ibn Ezra and Radak say גבים is the Aramaic word for locusts, while Rashi reads it as water pits. The Talmud uses the pools: as a pool makes a person pure, the ten tribes' goods became fair to take once they fell into foreign hands.

sources.quote: גבים. תרגום ארבה בארמית
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says גבים is how Aramaic translates the word for locust.

sources.quote: גֵּבִים. כְּמוֹ ״לַחְשֹׂף מַיִם מִגֶּבֶא״
sources.says: Rashi says it is like "to scoop water from a pit" in Isaiah 30:14.

sources.quote: מָה גֵּבִים הַלָּלוּ מַעֲלִין אֶת הָאָדָם מִטּוּמְאָה לְטׇהֳרָה
sources.says: The Talmud says that just as these pools raise a person from impurity to purity, so Israel's money in foreign hands became clean.

33:6.headline: Six words, six orders of the Mishnah
33:6.body: Resh Lakish maps six words of this verse onto the six parts of the Mishnah, from אמונת, Seeds, to ודעת, Purities. He adds that even so, the fear of God is the treasure.

sources.quote: ״אֱמוּנַת״ — זֶה סֵדֶר זְרָעִים. ״עִתֶּיךָ״ — זֶה סֵדֶר מוֹעֵד
sources.says: Resh Lakish says אמונת is the order of Seeds and עתיך is the order of Festivals.

sources.quote: וַאֲפִילּוּ הָכִי, ״יִרְאַת ה׳ הִיא אוֹצָרוֹ״
sources.says: He ends that even with all of this, the fear of God is the treasure.

33:6.headline: Whose treasure is the fear of God: ours, or God's?
33:6.body: Radak says the fear of God is a person's treasure, which stands by him in hard times. The Talmud reads "His treasure" as God's: the only thing God keeps in His treasury is the fear of heaven.

sources.quote: ויראת ה' שהיא אוצרו של אדם
sources.says: Radak says the fear of God is a person's treasure.

sources.quote: אֵין לוֹ לְהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא בְּבֵית גְּנָזָיו אֶלָּא אוֹצָר שֶׁל יִרְאַת שָׁמַיִם
sources.says: Rabbi Chanina, citing Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, says God has nothing in His treasury but a store of the fear of heaven.

33:10.headline: When God "rises", He keeps His word
33:10.body: קום can mean standing up. Maimonides says that when it is said of God it means making something hold: now I will carry out my promise and my threat.

sources.quote: כלומר כעת אקיים את דברי והבטחתי ואיומי
sources.says: Maimonides says "Now I will rise" means "now I will fulfil my word, my promise and my threat".

33:11.headline: Pregnant with chaff: a word Ibn Ezra knows from Arabic
33:11.body: חשש is rare. Ibn Ezra says it is chaff, as in Arabic, "the language of Kedar", and Radak explains the image: their plans were the pregnancy, their deeds the birth, and both came to nothing.

sources.quote: חשש. כאשר היא בלשון קדר כמוץ
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says חשש means chaff, as the word is used in Arabic.

sources.quote: מִין מוֹץ; דָּבָר שֶׁנּוֹחַ לִדָּלֵק
sources.says: Rashi says it is a kind of chaff that catches fire easily.

sources.quote: וקורא המחשבה הריון והמעשה לידה
sources.says: Radak says the verse calls their thinking a pregnancy and their action a birth.

33:12.headline: Cut thorns, because cut thorns burn fastest
33:12.body: Rashi says כסוחים means cut, the word Onkelos uses for pruning in Leviticus 25:4. Radak says the verse picks cut thorns because thorns still growing hold water and burn slowly, so the plague will strike all at once.

sources.quote: ״לֹא תִזְמֹר״ תַּרְגּוּם אוֹנְקְלוֹס ״לָא תִכְסָח״
sources.says: Rashi says Onkelos translates "do not prune" with this same word.

sources.quote: ואמר כסוחים לפי שהקוצים שאינם כרותים אלא מחוברים הם למים ולא ידלקו במהרה
sources.says: Radak says it says cut thorns because thorns still attached are full of water and do not burn quickly.

33:13.headline: The "far" are the lifelong faithful; the "near" have just returned
33:13.body: Radak takes far and near as places around the Assyrian camp. Rashi and the Targum read them as people: the far served God from youth, and the near have just come back to Him.

sources.quote: הַמַּאֲמִינִים בִּי וְעוֹשִׂים רְצוֹנִי מִנְּעוּרֵיהֶם
sources.says: Rashi says the far ones are those who have believed and done God's will since their youth.

sources.quote: בַּעֲלֵי תְּשׁוּבָה שֶׁנִּתְקָרְבוּ אֵלַי מֵחָדָשׁ
sources.says: Rashi says the near ones are penitents who have newly come close.

sources.quote: שְׁמָעוּ צַדִיקַיָא דִנְטָרוּ אוֹרַיְתָא מִלְקָדְמִין
sources.says: The Targum says the far ones are the righteous who kept the Torah from the start.

33:15.headline: Isaiah's six rules for life, and how to shut your eyes
33:15.body: The Talmud says Isaiah set all the commandments on the six in this verse. Rabbi Chiya bar Abba says the last one, shutting one's eyes to evil, means not staring at women washing clothes.

sources.quote: בָּא יְשַׁעְיָהוּ וְהֶעֱמִידָן עַל שֵׁשׁ
sources.says: The Talmud says Isaiah came and set the commandments on six, quoting this verse.

sources.quote: זֶה שֶׁאֵין מִסְתַּכֵּל בְּנָשִׁים בְּשָׁעָה שֶׁעוֹמְדוֹת עַל הַכְּבִיסָה
sources.says: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba says this is one who does not look at women while they stand washing clothes.

33:17.headline: Which king in his beauty? Hezekiah, God, and a daily haircut
33:17.body: Radak says the king is Hezekiah, while Rashi and the Targum say it is God's presence. The Talmud learns from this verse that a king must have his hair cut every day.

sources.quote: מלך ביפיו. הוא חזקיהו
sources.says: Radak says the king in his beauty is Hezekiah.

sources.quote: שֶׁתִּזְכֶּה לִרְאוֹת זִיו שְׁכִינָתוֹ שֶׁל מָקוֹם
sources.says: Rashi says the righteous will merit to see the splendor of God's presence.

sources.quote: מֶלֶךְ מִסְתַּפֵּר בְּכׇל יוֹם
sources.says: The Talmud says a king cuts his hair every day, citing this verse.

33:18.headline: Counting towers: a tax man, or a scholar of 300 laws?
33:18.body: Radak says this is the tax officer who counted the tall houses in each town, since they paid more tax. The Talmud reads it about scholars who counted every letter of the Torah and knew 300 laws about a tower floating in the air.

sources.quote: שהיה סופר המגדלים אשר בעיר ועיר כי אותם הבתים הגבוהים היו חשובים ונותנים יותר במס
sources.says: Radak says he counted the towers in each city, because tall houses paid more tax.

sources.quote: שֶׁהָיוּ סוֹפְרִים כׇּל אוֹתִיּוֹת שֶׁבַּתּוֹרָה
sources.says: The Talmud says "the one who counts" refers to those who counted all the letters of the Torah.

sources.quote: שֶׁהָיָה סוֹפֵר שְׁלֹשׁ מֵאוֹת הֲלָכוֹת פְּסוּקוֹת בְּמִגְדָּל הַפּוֹרֵחַ בָּאֲוִיר
sources.says: Rabbi Yitzchak says "counting the towers" means reciting 300 laws about a tower floating in the air.

33:19.headline: A strange word for a strange tongue: foreign, or fierce?
33:19.body: Rashi reads נועז like לועז, "speaking a foreign tongue" (Psalms 114:1). Ibn Ezra calls it a strange word with no family, and Radak reads it from עז, "fierce".

sources.quote: אֶת עַם נוֹעָז. כְּמוֹ ״לוֹעֵז״
sources.says: Rashi says נועז is like לועז, a people whose language is not Hebrew.

sources.quote: והיא מלה זרה אין לה משפחה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it is a strange word with no family.

sources.quote: והאומר כי הנו"ן תחת למ"ד לא דבר נכונה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says those who think the נ stands for ל are wrong.

sources.quote: את עם נועז. כמו עז והוא נפעל
sources.says: Radak says it is from עז, strong or fierce.

33:20.headline: A tent that will never be packed up
33:20.body: יצען appears only here, and Ibn Ezra says it has no relative. Rashi reads "will not be moved", and Radak's father reads it from יצע, bedding: a tent never taken down and folded away.

sources.quote: יצען. אין לו ריע
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the word has no partner anywhere else.

sources.quote: בַּל יִצְעָן. בַּל יִסַּח
sources.says: Rashi says it means it will not be moved.

sources.quote: ופי' אהל שלא יורד ולא יהיה מצע לעולם אלא לעולם יהיה פרוש ונטוי
sources.says: Radak, citing his father, says it is a tent that is never taken down to become bedding, but stays spread out.

34:4.headline: Rolled up like a scroll, or wiped out as the book foretold?
34:4.body: Rashi reads ונגלו as rolling: the light is rolled away like a scroll, leaving the wicked in the dark. The Targum reads it as being wiped out from under the sky, as written about them in the book.

sources.quote: כְּאִלּוּ נִגְלַל הַשֶּׁמֶשׁ וְהָאוֹר כִּגְלִילַת סֵפֶר
sources.says: Rashi says it will be as if the sun and the light were rolled up like a scroll.

sources.quote: וְיִתְמְחוּן מִתְּחוֹת שְׁמַיָא כְּמָא דַאֲמִיר עֲלֵיהוֹן בְּסִפְרָא
sources.says: The Targum says they will be wiped out from under the heavens, as was said of them in the book.

34:5.headline: Why God's sword strikes in heaven first
34:5.body: Rashi says God's sword first kills the nations' princes above, since no nation falls until its angel in heaven falls. Ibn Ezra reads "the host of heaven" in the verse before the same way, as each nation's helper above.

sources.quote: שֶׁאֵין כָּל אֻמָּה לוֹקָה עַד שֶׁיִּלְקֶה שַׂר שֶׁלָּהּ בַּמָּרוֹם
sources.says: Rashi says no nation is struck until its prince on high is struck.

sources.quote: שאלה הדברים רמז לכל עזר שיש לו לכל גוי במשטר שמים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says these words hint at the helper each nation has in the rule of the heavens, as in Daniel.

34:5.headline: The people of my ban, my war, or my net?
34:5.body: חרם usually means something doomed to destruction, and Ibn Ezra reads it that way. Rashi reads "the people of my war", from a word the Mishnah uses for wartime, and Metzudat Zion also offers "my net".

sources.quote: שיש לי חפץ להיות חרם לעשות משפט בהם
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says God wants them to be a doomed people and to judge them.

sources.quote: עַם מִלְחַמְתִּי, לְשׁוֹן מִשְׁנָה
sources.says: Rashi says it means the people of my war, using a word from the Mishnah.

sources.quote: מלשון חרם ושממה, או הוא ענין רשת
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means destruction, or else a net.

34:6.headline: Why Bozrah suffers with Edom: it once gave Edom a king
34:6.body: Rashi says Bozrah is a town of Moab, punished with Edom because it gave Edom its king Jobab (Genesis 36:33). Ibn Ezra rejects those who say Bozrah is Constantinople, since that city is not even a thousand years old.

sources.quote: מֵאֶרֶץ מוֹאָב הִיא, אֲבָל לְפִי שֶׁהֶעֱמִידָה מֶלֶךְ לֶאֱדוֹם
sources.says: Rashi says Bozrah is in Moab, but because it set up a king for Edom it is struck with them.

sources.quote: יש אומר שהוא קושטנטינה, וזה לא יתכן כי אין לה היום אלף שנים שנוסדה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says some claim it is Constantinople, but that cannot be, since that city was founded less than a thousand years ago.

34:10.headline: "From generation to generation": the long war with Amalek
34:10.body: Rashi hears in מדור לדור Moses' words about Amalek, "from generation to generation" (Exodus 17:16). He traces the war from Moses to Saul, to Mordechai, and to the Messiah.

sources.quote: מִדּוֹרוֹ שֶׁל מֹשֶׁה לְדוֹרוֹ שֶׁל שָׁאוּל, וּמִשָּׁם לְדוֹרוֹ שֶׁל מָרְדְּכַי
sources.says: Rashi says the curse runs from Moses' generation to Saul's, and from there to Mordechai's.

sources.quote: בקמץ הלמ"ד ולית כותיה
sources.says: Radak notes that this לדור is pointed with a qamatz and has no match elsewhere.

34:11.headline: The "stones of emptiness" from the first verses of Genesis
34:11.body: תהו and בהו are the "unformed and void" of Genesis 1:2. The Talmud uses this verse to say בהו are wet stones sunk in the deep, while Radak sees a builder's line and plumb weight used here to unbuild.

sources.quote: בֹהוּ — אֵלּוּ אֲבָנִים הַמְפוּלָּמוֹת הַמְשׁוּקָּעוֹת בַּתְּהוֹם
sources.says: The Talmud says בהו are moist stones sunk in the deep, from which water comes, citing this verse.

sources.quote: כי מי שבונה נוטה קו ואבן העופרת שהיא המשקולת
sources.says: Radak says a builder stretches a line and hangs a lead weight, and here they are used for ruin.

sources.quote: בהו. ענין ריקות
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says בהו means emptiness.

34:11.headline: The ינשוף is named for the dusk it flies in
34:11.body: Radak says the ינשוף is a bird that flies, or cries out, at night. So its name comes from נשף, twilight.

sources.quote: והוא עוף שהוא עף בלילה, או אותו שהוא צועק בלילה, ולפיכך נקרא ינשוף מן נשף
sources.says: Radak says it is a bird that flies or cries at night, and so it is called ינשוף, from נשף.

34:13.headline: Not grass but a courtyard: a home for ostriches
34:13.body: חציר usually means grass. Here Ibn Ezra, Radak and Metzudat Zion read it as חצר, a courtyard, so the ruined city becomes a yard for ostriches.

sources.quote: חציר. כמו חצר
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says חציר here is the same as חצר, a courtyard.

sources.quote: חציר. כמו חצר, וכן ישיש וישש
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says חציר is like חצר, just as ישיש and ישש are the same word.

sources.quote: ותרגם יונתן כמו מקום אתרא לבת נעמא
sources.says: Radak notes the Targum translates it as a place for the ostrich.

34:14.headline: A hairy goat, or a demon that looks like one?
34:14.body: שעיר means a hairy goat, and Metzudat Zion says here it is a demon that looks like a goat to those who believe in it. Ibn Ezra and Radak think it may simply be a wild animal of the desert.

sources.quote: כן נקרא השד כי נראה כשעיר למי שמאמין בו
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the demon is called this because it appears like a goat to one who believes in it.

sources.quote: ושעיר. כדמות שעירים ברים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it is like wild goats.

sources.quote: ואפשר שהיא חיה מהחיות המדבר
sources.says: Radak says it may be one of the animals of the desert.

34:14.headline: Lilith: a demon, or a creature of the night?
34:14.body: לילית appears only here, and Rashi and Metzudat Zion say it is a demon. Ibn Ezra and Radak say it is a night creature, a bird or beast named for לילה, night.

sources.quote: לִּילִית. שֵׁם שֵׁדָה
sources.says: Rashi says Lilith is the name of a female demon.

sources.quote: לילית. היא אם השדים
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says she is the mother of the demons.

sources.quote: לילית. העוף שיעוף בלילה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it is the bird that flies at night.

sources.quote: וכן לילית חיה שצועקת בלילה או עוף שעף בלילה
sources.says: Radak says it is an animal that cries at night or a bird that flies at night.

34:16.headline: Which "book of the LORD" should we search?
34:16.body: Rashi says it is Genesis, where every creature came to the ark and none was missing. Radak says it is this prophecy itself, his father says the Torah's list of animals, and Ibn Ezra says it is God's written decrees.

sources.quote: קִרְאוּ מֵעַל סֵפֶר בְּרֵאשִׁית
sources.says: Rashi says to read from the book of Genesis, where all creatures gathered for the flood.

sources.quote: דרשו מעל ספר ה' והוא הספר הזה
sources.says: Radak says the book of the LORD is this very book.

sources.quote: פירש ספר ה' זה ספר תורת משה רבינו
sources.says: Radak says his father explained it as the Torah of Moses, with its list of animals and birds.

sources.quote: רמז לגזרות שמים שהם כתובים באצבע אלהים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it hints at heaven's decrees, written by God's finger.

35:1.headline: "Glad over them", or just "glad"?
35:1.body: The word ends in an unusual ם. Rashi reads it as 'they will rejoice over them', over the fall of Edom; Ibn Ezra and Metzudat Zion say the ם simply stands for the extra נ in verbs like ישמעון.

sources.quote: יששום. ישישו עליהם
sources.says: Rashi says it means they will rejoice over them.

sources.quote: הן ישושו על מפלתם של גבורי שעיר
sources.says: Rashi says they will rejoice over the fall of the mighty men of Seir, that is, Edom.

sources.quote: ישושום. המ״ם במקום נו״ן הנוספת בפעלים כגון ישמעון יזכרון
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the ם takes the place of the extra נ found in verbs like ישמעון.

sources.quote: יש אומרים שהמלה חסרת בי"ת, וכן הוא ישושו בם, ואין זה נכון
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says some read 'rejoice in them', but that is not right.

35:2.headline: "The glory of Lebanon" is the Temple
35:2.body: Rashi says Lebanon here means the Temple. The Talmud says Solomon planted golden trees in it that bore fruit; they withered when the nations entered, and God will bring them back, as this verse says.

sources.quote: הלבנון. בית המקדש
sources.says: Rashi says Lebanon is the Temple.

sources.quote: בשעה שבנה שלמה בית המקדש, נטע בו כל מיני מגדים של זהב
sources.says: The Talmud says Solomon planted golden fruit trees in the Temple.

sources.quote: וכשנכנסו גוים להיכל יבש, שנאמר: ״ופרח לבנון אומלל״, ועתיד הקדוש ברוך הוא להחזירן
sources.says: The Talmud says they withered when the nations entered, and God will restore them.

35:3.headline: The vowels tell who is being strengthened
35:3.body: Here חזקו is in the heavy verb form, so Rashi says it means 'strengthen others'. In the next verse, חזקו in the light form means 'be strong yourselves'.

sources.quote: חזקו לשון משקל כבד, ופתרונו: חזקו את אחרים
sources.says: Rashi says חזקו here is the heavy form and means 'strengthen others'.

sources.quote: חזקו אל תיראו זה נקוד ׳חזקו׳ לשון ׳קל׳: חזקו אתם מאליכם
sources.says: Rashi says the חזקו of the next verse is the light form: be strong yourselves.

35:4.headline: Hasty hearts: impatient for redemption, or panicked?
35:4.body: נמהרי לב are people whose hearts rush. Rashi says they are eager for the redemption and pained that it is late; Radak says they are frightened by the troubles of exile.

sources.quote: לנמהרי לב. שממהרים את הגאלה ומצרים על אחורה
sources.says: Rashi says they are those who hurry the redemption and grieve that it is late.

sources.quote: אותם שהיו נבהלים בלבם בצרות גדולות מן הגלות
sources.says: Radak says they are those whose hearts are alarmed by the great troubles of exile.

35:5.headline: Opened eyes: new sight, or new understanding?
35:5.body: Maimonides says the verb פקח always means opening the mind, not restoring the body's sight. Rashi likewise says the blind and deaf here are Israel.

sources.quote: משמשת רק במשמעות של גילוי הבחנה, לא של התחדשות של ראייה חושית
sources.says: Maimonides says פקח is used only for gaining discernment, not for new physical sight.

sources.quote: ועל ישראל הוא אומר, שקראם עורים וחרשים
sources.says: Rashi says the verse speaks of Israel, whom it calls blind and deaf.

35:7.headline: Grass, or a courtyard for reeds?
35:7.body: חציר usually means grass, and Metzudat Zion reads it so. Ibn Ezra and Radak read it as חצר, a courtyard: the jackals' den becomes a home for reed and rush.

sources.quote: חציר. דשא
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says חציר means grass.

sources.quote: חציר. כמו חצר
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says חציר is like חצר, a courtyard.

sources.quote: חציר. כמו חצר, כמו שפירשנו למעלה
sources.says: Radak says חציר is like חצר, as he explained earlier.

35:9.headline: The "breaker" among the beasts
35:9.body: פריץ comes from פרץ, to break through. Rashi says it is the wild boar; Radak says it is the beast that breaks the ways of beasts and comes where people live; the Targum reads an oppressive ruler.

sources.quote: אין לך פריץ בחיות כחזיר הבר
sources.says: Rashi says no beast breaks through like the wild boar.

sources.quote: אפילו הפריץ שבחיות שפורץ מנהג החיות שהולך למקום שבני אדם מצויין
sources.says: Radak says it is the beast that breaks the habit of beasts and goes where people are.

sources.quote: ושלטון מעיק
sources.says: The Targum renders it as an oppressive ruler.

35:10.headline: Joy forever, or the joy of long ago?
35:10.body: עולם can mean forever or long ago. Ibn Ezra reads joy forever; Rashi reads the joy Israel once had leaving Egypt, and the Talmud reads the crowns Israel wore at Sinai, which God will set back on their heads.

sources.quote: ושמחת נצח על ראשם
sources.says: Ibn Ezra reads it as everlasting joy on their heads.

sources.quote: ושמחת עולם. שמחה אשר מעולם, שהיתה להם כבר בדרך יציאתן ממצרים
sources.says: Rashi says it is the joy of old, which they had when they left Egypt.

sources.quote: עתיד הקדוש ברוך הוא להחזירן לנו
sources.says: The Talmud says God will give the Sinai crowns back to Israel.

sources.quote: שמחה שמעולם על ראשם
sources.says: The Talmud reads the verse as 'the joy from long ago on their heads'.

35:10.headline: Does joy catch them, or do they catch joy?
35:10.body: ישיגו means 'they will overtake'. Ibn Ezra and Metzudat David read it as joy chasing the people down; Ibn Ezra also reports others who say the people will chase joy and catch it.

sources.quote: ששון ושמחה ישיגו. אותם, ויש אומרים כי הם ירדפו אחרי הששון וישיגוהו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says joy will overtake them, and some say they will chase joy and reach it.

sources.quote: ישיגו. כאלו ירדפו אחריהם וישיגום
sources.says: Metzudat David says it is as if joy pursues them and catches them.

36:2.headline: The Washers' Field, where laundry was spread to dry
36:2.body: שדה כובס means "the washer's field". Rashi, following the Targum, says the launderers spread out clothes there. Metzudat David adds that they dried them in the sun.

sources.quote: שֶׁשּׁוֹטְחִין שָׁם הַכּוֹבְסִים אֶת הַבְּגָדִים
sources.says: Rashi says it is where the launderers spread out the clothes.

sources.quote: השדה שמכבסים שם הבגדים ושוטחים שמה מול השמש לנגבה
sources.says: Metzudat David says clothes were washed there and spread in the sun to dry.

36:3.headline: The "reminder": royal record keeper, or court clerk?
36:3.body: מזכיר means "one who reminds". Rashi says he wrote the royal records. He also gives a second reading: he reminded the king which case came first.

sources.quote: כּוֹתֵב הַזִּכְרוֹנוֹת בְּסִפְרֵי דִּבְרֵי הַיָּמִים
sources.says: Rashi says he wrote the records in the books of the chronicles.

sources.quote: הַמַּזְכִּיר אֵיזֶה דִּין בָּא לְפָנָיו רִאשׁוֹן
sources.says: Rashi also says he reminded which case came first, so it would be judged first.

sources.quote: הָאֶחָד מְסַדֵּר וּמַזְכִּירוֹ וְהַסּוֹפֵר כּוֹתֵב
sources.says: Rashi says the reminder sets things in order and the scribe writes them down.

36:5.headline: "Mere words of the lips": empty talk, or prayer?
36:5.body: The Assyrian mocks Hezekiah's "words of the lips". Ibn Ezra reads it as boasting: his strength is only talk. Radak says the words of the lips are Hezekiah's prayers, which the Assyrian thinks cannot win a war.

sources.quote: חשבת בלבך שדבר שפתים יצילך, וזו הוא התפלה
sources.says: Radak says the words of the lips mean prayer, which Hezekiah hoped would save him.

sources.quote: כי גבורתך בדבור היא לבדה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means your strength is only in speech.

36:8.headline: Not "mix in" but "make a bet"
36:8.body: התערב can mean to mingle. Rashi and Metzudat Zion say it comes from ערבון, a pledge: the Assyrian dares Hezekiah to bet he can find riders for 2,000 horses.

sources.quote: בְּדָבָר זֶה, אִם תּוּכַל לְקַיְּמָן. לְשׁוֹן ׳עֵרָבוֹן׳
sources.says: Rashi says it means to pledge on whether you can do this, from the word for a pledge.

sources.quote: מל׳ ערבון ומשכון
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it comes from a pledge and a security, as when two people bet.

36:12.headline: A crude word written, a polite one read aloud
36:12.body: The written word חראיהם is a coarse word for dung. Rashi cites the sages: where the text is crude, readers say a polite word instead, here צואתם.

sources.quote: וְלָשׁוֹן נָאֶה תִּקְּנוּ סוֹפְרִים לִקְרוֹתוֹ צוֹאָתָם
sources.says: Rashi says the scribes set a polite word, צואתם, to be read in its place.

sources.quote: מִקְרָאוֹת הַכְּתוּבִים לִגְנַאי קוֹרִין אוֹתוֹ לְשֶׁבַח
sources.says: Rashi quotes the rule that verses written coarsely are read in a decent way.

sources.quote: מל׳ חור ונקב
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the word comes from a hole or opening.

36:12.headline: A rare, coarse word for urine
36:12.body: שיניהם appears only in this story. Metzudat Zion says it means urine, close to the word שתן. Rashi glosses it as מימי רגליהם, "water of their feet".

sources.quote: הוא מי רגלים והוא קרוב מל׳ שתן
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means urine and is close to the word שתן.

sources.quote: שִׁינֵיהֶם. מֵימֵי רַגְלֵיהֶם
sources.says: Rashi explains it as "water of their feet".

36:14.headline: The same word Eve used of the serpent: "deceived"
36:14.body: ישא here means to mislead, not to lift. Metzudat Zion links it to Eve's words "the serpent deceived me". Rashi on Genesis makes the same link from the other side.

sources.quote: ענין הסתה ופתוי כמו הנחש השיאני
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means luring, as in "the serpent deceived me" in Genesis 3:13.

sources.quote: הִטְעַנִי, כְּמוֹ אַל יַשִּׁיא אֶתְכֶם חִזְקִיָּהוּ
sources.says: Rashi on Genesis explains the serpent's deceit with this very verse.

36:16.headline: "Make a blessing with me" means bring a peace gift
36:16.body: ברכה usually means a blessing. Rashi and Metzudat Zion say it is a gift of peace, as when Jacob told Esau "take my blessing". The Assyrian asks the city to surrender.

sources.quote: צְאוּ אֵלַי לְשָׁלוֹם וּבָרְכוּנִי, וְהָבִיאוּ אֵלַי תְּשׁוּרַת שָׁלוֹם
sources.says: Rashi says it means come out to me in peace and bring me a peace gift.

sources.quote: ענין מנחה ותשורת שלום כמו קח נא את ברכתי
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means a gift of peace, as in Genesis 33:11.

sources.quote: וּלְשׁוֹן ׳בְּרָכָה׳ נוֹפֵל בִּתְשׁוּרָה שֶׁהִיא לְהַקְבָּלַת פָּנִים
sources.says: Rashi says the word for blessing is used for a gift brought when greeting someone.

37:3.headline: The birthing stool: a labor with no strength to deliver
37:3.body: Rashi and Metzudat Zion say משבר here is the seat a woman sits on to give birth. Hezekiah compares the crisis to a birth where the child cannot come out.

sources.quote: הַדּוֹמָה לְאִשָּׁה הַיּוֹשֶׁבֶת עַל הַמַּשְׁבֵּר, וְאֵין כֹּחַ לַוָּלָד לָצֵאת
sources.says: Rashi says it is like a woman on the birthing seat when the child has no strength to come out.

sources.quote: משבר. מקום מושב היולדת
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says משבר is where a woman in labor sits.

37:3.headline: A day of rebuke, or of the enemy's proof?
37:3.body: תוכחה usually means rebuke. Rashi gives an Old French word for proof: the enemies use their success to 'prove' that their own gods are stronger.

sources.quote: הָאוֹיְבִים מוֹכִיחִים בְּהַצְלָחָתָם
sources.says: Rashi says the enemies prove their point by their success.

sources.quote: ותוכחה. ענין תוכחות וברור דברים
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the word means arguing and making a case.

37:9.headline: The same word twice, with two meanings
37:9.body: וישמע appears twice in this verse. Rashi says the first means 'he heard the news' and the second means 'he accepted': the king took the advice to turn and fight Cush first.

sources.quote: אֵין ׳וַיִּשְׁמַע׳ הַשֵּׁנִי כְּמוֹ ׳וַיִּשְׁמַע׳ הָרִאשׁוֹן
sources.says: Rashi says the second וישמע does not mean the same as the first.

sources.quote: הָרִאשׁוֹן לְשׁוֹן ׳שְׁמוּעָה׳, וְהַשֵּׁנִי לְשׁוֹן ׳קַבָּלָה׳
sources.says: Rashi says the first means hearing a report and the second means accepting.

37:24.headline: "The height of its end": Sennacherib aims at heaven itself
37:24.body: Isaiah writes מרום קצו, 'its highest end', where Kings writes מלון קצו, 'its lodging'. The Talmud says the two words show his plan: first destroy the dwelling below, then the dwelling above.

sources.quote: כְּתִיב ״מְרוֹם קִצּוֹ״, וּכְתִיב ״מְלוֹן קִצּוֹ״
sources.says: The Talmud notes one verse says 'height of its end' and the other 'lodging of its end'.

sources.quote: בַּתְּחִלָּה אַחְרִיב דִּירָה שֶׁל מַטָּה, וְאַחַר כָּךְ אַחְרִיב דִּירָה שֶׁל מַעְלָה
sources.says: The Talmud says he planned to destroy the dwelling below first, then the dwelling above.

37:24.headline: "Lebanon" here means the Temple
37:24.body: Sennacherib boasts he climbed to the far reaches of Lebanon. Rashi says Lebanon here is the Temple, and the Targum also reads it as their sanctuary.

sources.quote: יַרְכְּתֵי לְבָנוֹן. בֵּית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ
sources.says: Rashi says 'the far reaches of Lebanon' means the Temple.

sources.quote: וְאַף אֵיחוּד בֵּית מַקְדַשֵׁהוֹן
sources.says: The Targum renders it 'and I will also seize their Temple'.

37:27.headline: Stubble, or grain struck by blight?
37:27.body: Rashi says שדמה is the stubble left in the ground after harvest, and gives the Old French word. Metzudat Zion notes that the same verse in Kings reads שדפה, blight, since מ and פ can swap.

sources.quote: הַנִּשְׁאָר בַּקַּרְקַע, שָׁרְשֵׁי הַקָּצִיר
sources.says: Rashi says it is what stays in the ground, the roots left after harvest.

sources.quote: הוא כמו ושדפ׳ הנאמר במ״ב כי בומ״ף מתחלף
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it is like שדפה in Kings, because the letters ב, ו, מ, פ can swap.

37:33.headline: A siege ramp of packed earth, not thrown stones
37:33.body: Rashi says a סוללה is a mound of earth poured against the wall and pressed hard, so attackers can climb it. He heard others say it means hurled stones, but rejects that.

sources.quote: עַל שֵׁם שֶׁסּוֹלְלִים וְכוֹבְשִׁין אוֹתָהּ בְּמַקָּבוֹת כְּדֵי שֶׁיִּתְקַשֶּׁה
sources.says: Rashi says it is named for packing it down with hammers so it hardens.

sources.quote: אֲבָל אֵין בַּאֲבָנִים לְשׁוֹן ׳שְׁפִיכָה׳ וְלֹא לְשׁוֹן ׳סְלִילָה׳
sources.says: Rashi says stones are not 'poured' or 'packed', so the stone reading does not fit.

sources.quote: הוא צבור העפר ששופכים מול העיר ועולים בה להלחם
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it is a pile of earth poured against a city to climb and attack.

37:38.headline: Nisroch's name hides a plank from Noah's ark
37:38.body: Rashi reads the god's name נסרך as נסר, a plank, and cites the Talmud: Sennacherib worshipped a plank from Noah's ark.

sources.quote: נֶסֶר מִתֵּיבָתוֹ שֶׁל נֹחַ
sources.says: Rashi says Nisroch was a plank from Noah's ark.

39:2.headline: A rare word the Talmud reads three different ways
39:2.body: Rashi links בית נכתה to the spices carried in Genesis 37:25, so it is the king's spice storehouse. In the Talmud, Rav says it means his wife served the guests drinks, Shmuel says his treasury, and Rabbi Yochanan says his weapons.

sources.quote: בֵּית גְּנָזָיו שֶׁל בְּשָׂמִים
sources.says: Rashi says it is the house where he stored his spices.

sources.quote: אִשְׁתּוֹ הִשְׁקְתָה עֲלֵיהֶם. וּשְׁמוּאֵל אָמַר: בֵּית גְּנָזָיו הֶרְאָה לָהֶם
sources.says: Rav says his wife served them drinks; Shmuel says he showed them his treasury.

sources.quote: וְרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן אָמַר: זַיִן אוֹכֵל זַיִן הֶרְאָה לָהֶן
sources.says: Rabbi Yochanan says he showed them weapons that could defeat other weapons.

39:2.headline: Which 'good oil': the holy anointing oil, or balsam?
39:2.body: Rashi gives two views of השמן הטוב: the holy anointing oil, or balsam oil. He adds that balsam grew in Jericho, and that יריחו, Jericho, is named for its scent, ריח.

sources.quote: יֵשׁ פּוֹתְרִים: שֶׁמֶן הַמִּשְׁחָה
sources.says: Rashi says some explain it as the anointing oil.

sources.quote: וְגָדֵל בִּירִיחוֹ, לְכָךְ נִקְרָא יְרִיחוֹ עַל שֵׁם הָרֵיחַ
sources.says: Rashi says balsam grew in Jericho, and so the town is named for the smell.

39:6.headline: Nothing will be left, because he held nothing back
39:6.body: Hezekiah showed them everything: 'there was not a thing' (דבר) he did not show. Now 'not a thing' (דבר) will be left, and Rashi calls this measure for measure.

sources.quote: מִדָּה כְּנֶגֶד מִדָּה, כְּנֶגֶד ״לֹא הָיָה דָבָר״
sources.says: Rashi says the punishment is measure for measure, matching 'there was not a thing'.

sources.quote: לֹא הָיָה דָבָר. אַף סֵפֶר תּוֹרָה
sources.says: Rashi says that 'not a thing' he did not show included even the Torah scroll.

4:1.headline: Seven here means many, not an exact count
4:1.body: Radak says שבע is not a real count of seven women. Scripture uses seven to mean 'a lot', because time runs in weeks of seven days.

sources.quote: ושבע, אינו לחשבון מכוון אלא כן דרך המקרא לזכור שבע ושבעה לחשבון רב לפי שכל ימי העולם שבועות
sources.says: Radak says seven is not an exact number; Scripture uses seven for a large number because the world's days run in weeks.

sources.quote: הטע' רוב בעבור ימי השבוע
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says seven means many, after the days of the week.

4:2.headline: The 'sprout of the LORD': the Messiah, the survivors, or real crops?
4:2.body: The Targum and Radak read צמח as the Messiah, a branch of David's line. Ibn Ezra thinks it means the righteous who survive in Jerusalem, and he cites a teacher who took it literally, as God blessing plants and fruit.

sources.quote: ופירוש צמח ה' משיח בן דוד
sources.says: Radak says the sprout of the LORD is the Messiah, son of David.

sources.quote: יְהֵי מְשִׁיחָא דַייָ לְחֶדְוָה וְלִיקָר
sources.says: The Targum translates the sprout of the LORD as the Messiah of the LORD.

sources.quote: והנכון בעיני שהם צדיקי ירושלם שימלטו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it most likely means the righteous of Jerusalem who escape.

sources.quote: ור' משה הכהן פירש צמח כמשמעו, שהשם יתן ברכה בצמח ובפרי
sources.says: Ibn Ezra reports that Rabbi Moshe HaKohen read it plainly, as God blessing plants and fruit.

4:4.headline: A word for scrubbing, used for dried blood
4:4.body: ידיח is the word used for rinsing the offerings in the Temple. Malbim says it means hard scrubbing, so the verse washes the filth but scrubs the blood, because murder is harder to clean than other sin.

sources.quote: לְשׁוֹן רְחִיצָה בִּלְשׁוֹן מִשְׁנָה וּבַמִּקְרָא
sources.says: Rashi says it is a word for washing, both in the Mishnah and in Scripture.

sources.quote: וכן פה תפס בצואה רחיצה ובדם הדחה
sources.says: Malbim says the verse pairs washing with the filth and scrubbing with the blood.

4:6.headline: The Talmud tries to measure a sukkah from this verse
4:6.body: Rabbi Zeira reads 'a סכה for shade by day' as a rule for the festival hut: up to twenty cubits high you sit in the shade of its roof, above that only in the shade of its walls. The Talmud pushes back that the verse is about the days of the Messiah.

sources.quote: עַד עֶשְׂרִים אַמָּה אָדָם יוֹשֵׁב בְּצֵל סוּכָּה
sources.says: Rabbi Zeira says that up to twenty cubits a person sits in the shade of the sukkah's roof.

sources.quote: הָהוּא לִימוֹת הַמָּשִׁיחַ הוּא דִּכְתִיב
sources.says: The Talmud answers that this verse was written about the days of the Messiah.

4:6.headline: A rainstorm, or a stream of fire on the wicked?
4:6.body: Metzudat Zion reads זרם as rushing water, so the shelter keeps off the storm. Rashi reads it as fire pouring from the river of fire onto the wicked.

sources.quote: מזרם. ענין שטיפת ומרוצת המים
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means a rush of flowing water.

sources.quote: אֵשׁ הַמְּקַלַּחַת מִנְּהַר דִּינוּר עַל הָרְשָׁעִים
sources.says: Rashi says it is fire pouring from the river of fire onto the wicked.

40:1.headline: "Comfort, comfort": a double comfort for a double sin
40:1.body: The word is said twice. The midrash says Israel sinned double and was punished double, so it is comforted double; Ibn Ezra says the repeat means quickly, moment after moment.

sources.quote: חָטְאוּ בְּכִפְלַיִם
sources.says: The midrash says Israel sinned double.

sources.quote: וּמִתְנַחֲמִים בְּכִפְלַיִם, דִּכְתִיב (ישעיה מ, א): נַחֲמוּ נַחֲמוּ
sources.says: The midrash says Israel is comforted double, as it says "comfort, comfort".

sources.quote: וטעם פעמים דרך מהירות או רגע אחרי רגע
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the word is said twice to show speed, or comfort moment after moment.

40:2.headline: Her sin is "accepted": forgiven, or fully paid off?
40:2.body: Rashi reads נרצה as "appeased": God is reconciled. Ibn Ezra and Radak read it as "paid in full", like a hired worker who finishes his day: her punishment is complete.

sources.quote: נִרְצָה. נִתְפַּיֵּס
sources.says: Rashi says נרצה means appeased.

sources.quote: כי נרצה. נשלם ותם, כמו עד ירצה כשכיר יומו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means completed, like a hired worker finishing his day.

sources.quote: נשלם ענשה כמו אז תרצה הארץ את שבתותיה
sources.says: Radak says her punishment is complete, as the land "completes" its sabbaths.

40:6.headline: "All its kindness is like a flower": kindness, or strength?
40:6.body: חסד usually means kindness. Rashi says a mortal's promise of kindness withers like a flower, since he may die before he keeps it; the Targum reads the word as "their strength".

sources.quote: לְפִיכָךְ אִם אָמַר לַעֲשׂוֹת חֶסֶד הֲרֵי הוּא כְּצִיץ הַשָּׂדֶה
sources.says: Rashi says if a person promises kindness, it is like a flower of the field.

sources.quote: שֶׁאֵין בְּיָדוֹ לְקַיֵּם שֶׁמָּא יָמוּת
sources.says: Rashi says he may not be able to keep it, for he may die.

sources.quote: וְכָל תּוּקְפְהוֹן כְּמוֹצָא דְחַקְלָא
sources.says: The Targum renders it "all their strength is like the chaff of the field".

40:9.headline: Why is Zion's herald a feminine word here?
40:9.body: Here the bearer of good news is feminine, מבשרת; elsewhere Isaiah uses the masculine מבשר. Rashi says if Israel deserves it the news comes strong and fast, and if not it comes weakly and late; Ibn Ezra says the feminine just means a group.

sources.quote: זָכוּ – קַל כְּזָכָר, לֹא זָכוּ – תַּשׁ כִּנְקֵבָה, וּמְאַחֵר פְּעָמָיו עַד הַקֵּץ
sources.says: Rashi says if they merit, the herald is swift like a male; if not, weak like a female, and slow until the end.

sources.quote: הטעם על עדה ולא נקבה ממש
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the word means a community, not an actual woman.

40:11.headline: "His flock": a shepherd cares more for sheep he owns
40:11.body: Radak's father noticed the word "his": a shepherd pities his own flock more than one he guards for pay. Ibn Ezra also says God is not like a hired shepherd.

sources.quote: דקדק במלת עדרו שהעדר שהוא שלו חומל עליו יותר מן העדר שישמור בשכירות
sources.says: Radak says his father stopped on the word עדרו: a man pities his own flock more than one he keeps for hire.

sources.quote: והטעם איננו כרועה שכיר
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says God is not like a hired shepherd.

40:11.headline: עלות: nursing ewes, pregnant ewes, or the little lambs?
40:11.body: Rashi says the עלות are nursing ewes; Ibn Ezra says pregnant ones; Metzudat Zion says the young themselves, from עולל, "infant". Radak joins them: the mothers are named after their young.

sources.quote: הַצֹּאן הַמְּנִיקוֹת
sources.says: Rashi says they are the nursing sheep.

sources.quote: עלות. הם ההרות
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says they are the pregnant ones.

sources.quote: עלות. קטנות והוא מל׳ עולל ויונק
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says they are the little ones, from the word for infant.

sources.quote: ונקראו האמות עלות על שם בניהם שהם קטנים
sources.says: Radak says the mothers are called עלות after their small young.

40:12.headline: Measuring the waters "in his שעל": a hand, or a step?
40:12.body: Metzudat Zion says שעל is a closed hand, and Radak adds that this is a figure, since God has no hand. Rashi first reads it as "his walk", from משעול, a path.

sources.quote: בשעלו. באגרופו
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means in his fist.

sources.quote: ופירוש שעלו אגרופו, והוא עד"מ כי אין לו יד ואגרוף
sources.says: Radak says it means his fist, but as a figure of speech, since God has no hand.

sources.quote: בְּשָׁעֳלוֹ. בַּהֲלִיכָתוֹ
sources.says: Rashi first reads it as "in His walking".

sources.quote: דָּבָר אַחֵר: ׳שַׁעַל׳ שֵׁם כְּלִי הוּא
sources.says: Rashi's second reading: שעל is the name of a vessel.

40:12.headline: שליש: the earth measured in thirds, or a lost unit?
40:12.body: Rashi says God measured the earth in thirds: desert, settled land, and seas. Menachem, cited by Rashi, says it is a vessel, and Ibn Ezra admits we no longer know the old measures.

sources.quote: שְׁלִישׁ מִדְבָּר, שְׁלִישׁ יִשּׁוּב, שְׁלִישׁ יַמִּים וּנְהָרוֹת
sources.says: Rashi says a third is desert, a third settled land, a third seas and rivers.

sources.quote: וּמְנַחֵם פֵּרֵשׁ שֶׁהוּא שֵׁם כְּלִי
sources.says: Rashi reports that Menachem read it as the name of a vessel.

sources.quote: לכן לא נדע היום איך יהיו המדות הקדמונים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says we do not know today what the ancient measures were.

40:13.headline: "Who measured God's רוח?": the wind, prophecy, or God's will?
40:13.body: Maimonides says רוח here means will: who can know the plan of God's will? Rashi reads it as the holy spirit in the prophets' mouths, and Rav Saadia, cited by Ibn Ezra, read it as the wind, with "God" as the answer.

sources.quote: הוא גם שם הכַּוונה והרצון
sources.says: Maimonides says רוח is also a word for intention and will.

sources.quote: מי הוא היודע את סדר רצונו
sources.says: Maimonides reads the verse: who knows the order of His will?

sources.quote: אֶת רוּחַ הַקֹּדֶשׁ בְּפִי הַנְּבִיאִים
sources.says: Rashi reads it as the holy spirit in the mouths of the prophets.

sources.quote: אמר הגאון כי לא הזכיר הרוח עם השלשה המוסדים, ואמר כי השם תשובה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra reports that the Gaon read it as the element wind, with God's name as the answer, and disagrees.

40:15.headline: Nations like a "מר" from a bucket: the bitter last drop
40:15.body: Rashi says it is the bitter drop that drips from the bottom of a bucket, and Ibn Ezra says the word has no parallel. Maimonides uses the verse to show how small people are next to the rest of creation.

sources.quote: כְּטִפָּה מָרָה הַמְטַפְטֶפֶת מִשּׁוּלֵי הַדְּלִי
sources.says: Rashi says it is like a bitter drop dripping from the bottom of the bucket.

sources.quote: כטיפה הנופלת מהדלי, ואין רע לו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it is a drop falling from the bucket, and the word has no companion.

sources.quote: אל תטעה בנפשך לחשוב שהגלגלים והמלאכים לא נוצרו אלא בשבילנו
sources.says: Maimonides warns against thinking the heavens and angels were made only for us, citing this verse.

40:20.headline: המסכן: the skilled man, the poor man, or the steward?
40:20.body: Rashi reads "the expert", who knows which wood will last. Metzudat Zion and Radak read "the poor man", who cannot afford gold and picks good wood instead; Ibn Ezra brings a third view, "the steward".

sources.quote: הַמְסֻכָּן. הַמְּלֻמָּד
sources.says: Rashi says המסכן means the trained one.

sources.quote: המסכן. העני והדל
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means the poor man.

sources.quote: אבל הענין שלא יוכל לעשות בזהב ובכסף יבחר לו עץ טוב שלא ירקב
sources.says: Radak says the poor man who cannot make an idol of gold or silver chooses wood that will not rot.

sources.quote: יש אומרים כי המסכן כמו סוכן
sources.says: Ibn Ezra reports a view that it means a steward, like סוכן.

40:22.headline: God "sits" above the earth: not seated, but unchanging
40:22.body: ישב means to sit, but also to stay. Maimonides says here it means God endures forever, steady over the turning world; Radak says it is a figure of speech, since God has no place.

sources.quote: הקיים לעד היציב על הקפת הארץ
sources.says: Maimonides reads it as the One who endures forever, steady over the circuit of the earth.

sources.quote: ואמר היושב דרך משל כי אין לו מקום יתעלה
sources.says: Radak says "sits" is a figure of speech, for God has no place.

40:22.headline: The "circle of the earth": Ibn Ezra sees a round earth
40:22.body: חוג comes from מחוגה, a compass for drawing circles. Ibn Ezra says the verse shows the earth is round, not square, though he adds the proofs already show it.

sources.quote: חוּג. לְשׁוֹן ״מְחוּגָה״
sources.says: Rashi says חוג comes from מחוגה, the compass for circles.

sources.quote: והנה לעד כי הארץ עגולה לא רבועה, ואם אין צורך לפסוק
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says this is a witness that the earth is round, not square, though the verse is not needed for that.

40:28.headline: "God of the world": Radak reads אלהים as judge
40:28.body: Radak says the word אלהים, said of God, means judge, as in a law in Exodus. So the exiles should not think God ignores them: He judges the whole world.

sources.quote: אלהי שופט כמו עד שאלהים יבא דבר שניהם
sources.says: Radak says אלהי here means judge, as in the verse where a case comes before the judges.

sources.quote: ר"ל שופט העולם ומשגיח בו
sources.says: Radak says it means the judge of the world, who watches over it.

40:31.headline: Those who hope "exchange" strength, like a felled tree regrowing
40:31.body: חלף usually means to pass or to swap. Radak and Ibn Ezra read it as renewal, like Job's tree that is cut down and sprouts again: new strength comes before the old runs out.

sources.quote: כמו העץ אם יכרת ועוד יחליף והוא ענין התחדשות
sources.says: Radak says it is like a tree that is cut down and sprouts again: renewal.

sources.quote: קודם תום הכח הראשון, יבא כח אחר מהשם להם
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says before their first strength runs out, new strength comes from God.

40:31.headline: Wings like eagles, the bird that grows young again
40:31.body: אבר is a wing feather. Radak cites Rav Saadia: every ten years the eagle flies close to the heat, drops into the sea, sheds its feathers, and grows new ones as if young again.

sources.quote: אֵבֶר. כָּנָף
sources.says: Rashi says אבר means a wing.

sources.quote: כתב רבינו סעדיה כי הנשר יעלה לעשר שנים גבוה מאד על פני רקיע השמים
sources.says: Radak cites Rav Saadia: every ten years the eagle flies very high toward the sky.

sources.quote: ויתחדש אחר כן ויעלה אבר וישוב לימי עלומיו
sources.says: Radak says the eagle is then renewed, grows feathers, and returns to its youth.

41:7.headline: A goldsmith for an idol, or Abraham refining people
41:7.body: In the plain reading, the צורף is the goldsmith who covers the idol in gold. A midrash Rashi brings reads the verse about Abraham, who refined people and brought them close to God.

sources.quote: אֶת צֹרֵף. הַמְּרַקְּעוֹ בְּזָהָב
sources.says: Rashi explains the צורף as the one who plates the idol in gold.

sources.quote: זֶה אַבְרָהָם, שֶׁהוּא צוֹרֵף אֶת הַבְּרִיּוֹת לְקָרְבָן אֶל הַשְּׁכִינָה
sources.says: In the midrash Rashi brings, the צורף is Abraham, who refines people to bring them near to God’s presence.

41:7.headline: The anvil, or Abraham striking all the kings at once
41:7.body: Radak says פעם is the anvil the smith hammers on. The midrash in Rashi hears פעם as “one time”: Abraham struck down all the kings at once.

sources.quote: ופירוש פעם הסדן שמכין עליו
sources.says: Radak says פעם is the anvil that is struck.

sources.quote: זֶה אַבְרָהָם, שֶׁהָלַם כָּל הַמְּלָכִים הָאֵלֶּה פַּעַם אַחַת
sources.says: In the midrash Rashi brings, this is Abraham, who struck all these kings at one time.

42:1.headline: Who is "my servant"? Israel, the Messiah, or the prophet
42:1.body: The commentators do not agree. Rashi says it is Jacob, meaning Israel, Radak and the Targum say the Messiah, and Ibn Ezra thinks it is the prophet speaking of himself.

sources.quote: הֵן עַבְדִּי יַעֲקֹב אֵינוֹ כְּמוֹתְכֶם
sources.says: Rashi says the servant is Jacob, who is not like the idol worshippers.

sources.quote: הן עבדי. זהו מלך המשיח
sources.says: Radak says the servant is the king Messiah.

sources.quote: הָא עַבְדִי מְשִׁיחָא אֶקְרְבִינֵהּ
sources.says: The Targum renders it "here is my servant the Messiah".

sources.quote: והנכון בעיני שהוא הנביא, והוא מדבר בעד נפשו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the best reading is that the servant is the prophet, speaking about himself.

42:4.headline: He won't "run": he won't be crushed, like the cracked reed
42:4.body: ירוץ looks like "run", but Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Metzudat Zion read it as "be crushed", from רצוץ in verse 3. The servant who will not break a cracked reed or snuff out a dim wick will not himself grow dim or be crushed.

sources.quote: וְלֹא יָרוּץ. כְּמוֹ ׳לֹא יֵרָצֵץ׳
sources.says: Rashi says ירוץ means "will not be crushed".

sources.quote: ולא ירוץ. גופו, מפעלי הכפל, מגזרת רצוץ
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says ירוץ comes from the same root as רצוץ, "crushed", in the verse before.

sources.quote: ירוץ. מל׳ רציצה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says ירוץ comes from crushing.

sources.quote: לא יכהה מאורו ולא ירוצץ
sources.says: Metzudat David says he will not lose his light and will not be crushed.

42:5.headline: Two words for breath: נשמה for people, רוח for animals
42:5.body: Radak and Ibn Ezra say נשמה in this verse is given to people and רוח to the other living creatures. Rashi reads רוח differently, as a spirit of holiness.

sources.quote: אמר נשמת בעבור האדם ואמר רוח בעבור שאר בעלי החיים
sources.says: Radak says נשמה is said for people and רוח for the other living creatures.

sources.quote: ורוח. לחיות ההולכים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says רוח is for the animals that walk the earth.

sources.quote: וְרוּחַ. קְדוּשָׁה
sources.says: Rashi says רוח here means holiness.

42:6.headline: ואצרך: "I formed you" or "I will guard you"?
42:6.body: Rashi reads it from יצר, to form: "when I formed you", this was My plan. Radak and Metzudat Zion read it as "I will guard you" from harm.

sources.quote: וְאֶצָּרְךָ. כְּשֶׁיְצַרְתִּיךָ
sources.says: Rashi says ואצרך means "when I formed you".

sources.quote: ואצרך. ענין שמירה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says ואצרך means guarding.

sources.quote: ואצרך. אשמרך מן הגוים שלא ירעו לך
sources.says: Radak says it means God will guard Israel so the nations do not harm them.

42:6.headline: "A light to the nations": Rashi says the nations are Israel's tribes
42:6.body: Metzudat David reads it as opening the eyes of all the nations to know God. Rashi says each tribe of Israel is called a nation by itself, as in "a nation and a company of nations".

sources.quote: להאיר עיני הגוים כולם לדעת שה׳ הוא האלהים
sources.says: Metzudat David says it means to open the eyes of all the nations to know that the Lord is God.

sources.quote: כָּל שֵׁבֶט קָרוּי גּוֹי לְעַצְמוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says each tribe is called a nation by itself.

42:8.headline: The one name in the Bible that is truly a proper name
42:8.body: Ibn Ezra says this name of God is the only true proper name in Scripture. Radak says it belongs to God alone, unlike the word "god" that idol worshippers give their idols.

sources.quote: כי אין במקרא שם עצם [לבדו] רק זה לבדו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says there is no proper name in Scripture except this one alone.

sources.quote: הוא שמי המיוחד לי לא כשם הפסילים
sources.says: Radak says this is the name that belongs to God alone, not like the names of idols.

sources.quote: הוּא מְפֹרָשׁ בִּלְשׁוֹן אַדְנוּת וְכֹחַ
sources.says: Rashi says the name is explained as meaning lordship and power.

42:11.headline: "Those who dwell in the rock": the dead rising from graves
42:11.body: Radak reads these as people in towers built on rocks, who see the returning exiles from afar. Rashi and the Targum read them as the dead, who will come out of their graves and sing.

sources.quote: יֹשְׁבֵי סֶלַע. הַמֵּתִים שֶׁיִּחְיוּ
sources.says: Rashi says those who dwell in the rock are the dead who will come back to life.

sources.quote: יְשַׁבְּחוּן מֵיתַיָא כַּד יִפְקוּן מִבָּתֵּי עַלְמֵיהוֹן
sources.says: The Targum says the dead will give praise when they come out of their graves.

sources.quote: המגדלים הבנוים על הסלעים ועל ההרים
sources.says: Radak says it means the towers built on rocks and mountains.

42:14.headline: The "silent" half of Ezekiel's mysterious word חשמל
42:14.body: החשיתי means "I kept silent". Maimonides reports that the sages read Ezekiel's word חשמל as "sometimes silent, sometimes speaking", and took the silent half from this verse.

sources.quote: פעמים חשות, פעמים ממללות
sources.says: Maimonides quotes the sages explaining חשמל as "sometimes silent, sometimes speaking".

sources.quote: את (מובן) השתיקה הם גזרו מ"הֶחֱשֵׁיתִי מֵעוֹלָם"
sources.says: Maimonides says the sages took the meaning "silence" from this verse, "I have kept silent for ages".

sources.quote: החשיתי. ענין שתיקה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says החשיתי means keeping silent.

42:14.headline: ואשאף: panting like a woman in labor, or swallowing enemies whole
42:14.body: Ibn Ezra compares the sun that "pants" back to where it rises. Radak and Metzudat Zion read it as swallowing: God will swallow all His enemies at once.

sources.quote: אשאף יחד. כטעם שואף זורח
sources.says: Ibn Ezra compares "panting to where it rises" in Ecclesiastes.

sources.quote: אשאף. ענין בליעה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says אשאף means swallowing.

sources.quote: אשומם ואבלעם יחד כל אויבי
sources.says: Radak says God will lay waste and swallow all His enemies together.

sources.quote: וְאֶתְאַוֶּה לְהַשְׁמִיד הַכֹּל יָחַד
sources.says: Rashi says it means God longs to destroy all His enemies together.

42:16.headline: "I have done them": the future told in past tense?
42:16.body: Rashi and Radak say prophecy often speaks of the future as if it were already done. Metzudat David reads it as a real past: God already did such things when Israel left Egypt.

sources.quote: לְשׁוֹן נְבוּאָה לְדַבֵּר עַל הֶעָתִיד כְּאִלּוּ עָשׂוּי
sources.says: Rashi says this is the way of prophecy, to speak of the future as if it were done.

sources.quote: עשיתים. עבר במקום עתיד
sources.says: Radak says the past tense stands in for the future.

sources.quote: מאז כשיצאו ממצרים עשיתי כאלה
sources.says: Metzudat David says God did such things back when Israel left Egypt.

42:19.headline: כמשלם: one who is perfect, or one who has paid in full
42:19.body: Ibn Ezra, Radak and Metzudat David read it from שלם, "whole": the perfect, righteous one. Rashi reads it as "paid in full": whoever was blind has already borne his suffering and leaves clean.

sources.quote: מגזרת שלם, וכן המשולם הוא הצדיק
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the word comes from שלם, whole, and the משולם is the righteous one.

sources.quote: כמשולם. השלם במדות
sources.says: Metzudat David says it means the one who is whole in character.

sources.quote: וַהֲרֵי הוּא כִּמְשֻׁלָּם כָּל תַּגְמוּלָיו וְיוֹצֵא נָקִי
sources.says: Rashi says he is like one paid back in full for his deeds, who goes out clean.

42:20.headline: פקח means opening the mind, not just the eyes or ears
42:20.body: Maimonides says the verb פקח is used only for coming to understand, never for physical sight returning. He reads "ears open, yet he does not hear" this way, next to "they have eyes to see and did not see".

sources.quote: משמשת רק במשמעות של גילוי הבחנה, לא של התחדשות של ראייה חושית
sources.says: Maimonides says פקח means only the uncovering of understanding, not new physical sight.

sources.quote: פָּקוֹחַ אָזְנַיִם וְלֹא יִשְׁמָע
sources.says: Maimonides lists this verse among his examples.

sources.quote: הלא יש להם אזנים פתוחות להבין מצות ה׳
sources.says: Metzudat David says they have open ears to understand God's commands.

42:22.headline: בחורים: young men, or holes in the ground?
42:22.body: בחורים usually means young men, and Rashi's first reading keeps that: all their young men are in despair. A second reading in Rashi, and Radak and Ibn Ezra, read it as "in holes": they hide in caves and are trapped there.

sources.quote: בַּחוּרֵיהֶם פַּחֵי נֶפֶשׁ כֻּלָּם. תוספת: דָּבָר אַחֵר: הָפֵחַ בַּחוּרִים כֻּלָּם – יָשִׂימוּ אֶת עַצְמָם בְּפַחֵי הָאֲדָמָה וּבְחוֹרִים
sources.says: Rashi says their young men are all in despair; an added reading says they will hide in pits in the ground and in holes.

sources.quote: כמו על חור פתן אומר כי בחורים אשר התחבאו שם יפיחו אותם אויביהם
sources.says: Radak says בחורים means in holes, like a snake's hole, where the enemy will trap those who hid.

sources.quote: בחורים. מגזרת חור פתן
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says בחורים comes from חור, hole, as in "the snake's hole".

42:23.headline: "Backward" here means what is still to come
42:23.body: לאחור usually means backward or behind. Rashi, following the Targum, says that throughout Scripture it means the end, what will happen later.

sources.quote: וְכֵן כָּל ׳לְאָחוֹר׳ שֶׁבַּמִּקְרָא: עָתִיד לִהְיוֹת הוּא
sources.says: Rashi says every לאחור in Scripture is about what will happen in the future.

sources.quote: יְקַבֵּל וִיסַבַּר לְסוֹפָא
sources.says: The Targum renders לאחור as "for the end".

sources.quote: וישמע מה שעתיד להיות בסוף הימים זהו לאחור
sources.says: Radak says לאחור means what will happen at the end of days.

43:3.headline: How Egypt became Israel's ransom
43:3.body: כפר is a ransom, a price paid to free someone. Rashi says Egypt's firstborn died while Israel, God's firstborn, was saved. Radak says Cush, Seba and Egypt fell to Assyria in Israel's place.

sources.quote: כפרך. ענין פדיון
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the word means a ransom.

sources.quote: שֶׁבְּכוֹרֵיהֶם מֵתוּ וְאַתָּה, בְּנִי בְּכוֹרִי, נִצַּלְתָּ
sources.says: Rashi says Egypt's firstborn died while Israel, God's firstborn, was saved.

sources.quote: כוש וסבא ומצרים נתנם האל כופר לישראל
sources.says: Radak says God gave Cush, Seba and Egypt as a ransom for Israel.

43:6.headline: The north wind is told "give", the south only "don't hold back"
43:6.body: God speaks to the winds. Rashi says the north wind is weak and needs a push, so it is told "give". The south wind is strong, so it is only told not to hold back.

sources.quote: מִתּוֹךְ שֶׁהָרוּחַ צְפוֹנִית חַלָּשָׁה צְרִיכָה חִזּוּק
sources.says: Rashi says the north wind is weak and needs strengthening, so the verse says "give".

sources.quote: ואמר תני תכלאי הביאי בלשון נקבה לפי שהרוח בלשון נקבה
sources.says: Radak says the commands are in the feminine because the word for wind is feminine.

43:7.headline: "For My glory" means "because I willed it"
43:7.body: Ibn Ezra reads it plainly: made to bring honor to God's name. Maimonides says God's "glory" here is His own will. Everything was made only because God wanted it.

sources.quote: ולכבודי. להיות כבוד לשמי
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means to bring honor to God's name.

sources.quote: כלומר: כל מה שמיוחס לעשייתי, עשיתיו דווקא בשל רצוני ותו לא
sources.says: Maimonides says it means: all that I made, I made only because of My will.

43:10.headline: "Before Me no god was formed" troubled the commentators
43:10.body: Read plainly, the verse could hint that God too was formed. Radak says this was hard for the commentators, and some read נוצר as "formed things": no other god made anything. Ibn Ezra calls the plain worry blind.

sources.quote: הדבר הזה קשה למפרשים בעבור שאמר לפני ואחרי
sources.says: Radak says the commentators found this hard, since God has no before or after.

sources.quote: לפיכך פירשו מקצתם נוצר כמו יצר
sources.says: Radak says some read נוצר as "formed" in the active sense.

sources.quote: ועורי לב יחשבו שיצא מדברי הנביא שהשם נוצר חלילה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says only the blind of heart think the prophet means God was formed.

43:11.headline: Why "I, I" twice? Because God does not change
43:11.body: God says אנכי, "I", twice in a row. Radak says the doubling adds force. Ibn Ezra says it means God stays the same, unlike the changing heavens and earth, so He can save at any time.

sources.quote: הטעם אני אנכי פעמים, שלא אשתנה, כהשתנות צבאות מעלה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says God says "I" twice because He does not change as the heavenly hosts do.

sources.quote: אנכי אנכי. הכפל לחזק
sources.says: Radak says the doubling is for emphasis.

43:14.headline: Bars, runaways, oars, or wind-driven ships?
43:14.body: בריחים gets four readings. Ibn Ezra says the gate bars of Babylon, Radak says runaways, and Rashi brings the Targum's oars. Metzudat Zion reads it as ships, named for the wind, רוח, that drives them.

sources.quote: והורדתי בריחים. בריחי בבל
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says these are the bars of Babylon's gates.

sources.quote: אוריד יושבי בבכל ממעלותם ויברחו להם בבא כורש
sources.says: Radak says the people of Babylon will flee when Cyrus comes.

sources.quote: ׳מְשׁוֹטִין׳ הוּא עֵץ שֶׁמַּנְהִיג אֶת הַסְּפִינָה
sources.says: Rashi brings the Targum's "oars", the wood that steers a ship.

sources.quote: ענינו כמו ספינות ע״ש שכל מהלכם הוא ע״י הרוח
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means ships, named for the wind that moves them.

43:14.headline: Ships of their song, or ships of their wailing?
43:14.body: רנה can be a joyful song or a loud cry. The Targum reads the ships of their glory. Metzudat Zion and Radak read the cry of wailing as the Chaldeans flee.

sources.quote: בִּסְפִינַי תּוּשְׁבַּחְתְּהוֹן
sources.says: The Targum reads "in the ships of their praise".

sources.quote: ענין קול צעקה ויללה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means a cry of wailing.

43:17.headline: Snuffed out like a flax wick, with a last leap
43:17.body: דעכו means they went out, like a flame. Metzudat Zion says the word is about leaping, because a flame jumps as it dies. Radak and Ibn Ezra say it simply means put out.

sources.quote: ע״ש שבעת הכבוי קופצת השלהבת
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the word means leaping, because the flame jumps as it goes out.

sources.quote: וטעמו כבו וכן ידעך נרו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means "went out", as in Proverbs 20:20.

43:18.headline: Which "former things" should Israel stop recalling?
43:18.body: Rashi says the miracles in Egypt, since the new rescue will be greater. Radak brings the sages' reading: the "former things" are the rule of foreign empires, and the "ancient things" are the Exodus.

sources.quote: הַנִּסִּים הַלָּלוּ שֶׁאֲנִי מַזְכִּיר לָכֶם שֶׁעָשִׂיתִי בְּמִצְרַיִם
sources.says: Rashi says these are the miracles God did in Egypt.

sources.quote: ורז"ל פי' אל תזכרו ראשונות זהו שיעבוד מלכיות
sources.says: Radak reports the sages' reading that the former things are the rule of the empires.

43:22.headline: Tired of God, or never toiling for Him?
43:22.body: יגעת בי can mean "you grew weary of Me" or "you toiled for Me". Rashi says Israel quickly tired of God's service. Radak says Israel never even called on God, let alone toiled for Him.

sources.quote: נִלְאֵיתֶם מַהֵר בַּעֲבוֹדָתִי
sources.says: Rashi says they quickly grew tired of serving God.

sources.quote: ופי' כי יגעת כי תאמר שיגעת בי לא עשית
sources.says: Radak says if you claim you toiled for Me, you did not.

43:24.headline: You did not "buy" (קנית) Me "cane" (קנה)
43:24.body: The verse sets קנית, bought, next to קנה, a sweet-smelling cane used in incense. Rashi says it was plentiful in Israel, so no one had to pay for it. Radak says it came from far away and had to be bought, which is why the verse says "buy".

sources.quote: קנה. הוא קנה בושם
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it is a fragrant cane.

sources.quote: ואמר בקנה לא קנית לפי שלא היה הקנה בארץ ישראל כי אם על ידי קנין
sources.says: Radak says the verse uses "buy" because the cane only came to Israel by purchase.

sources.quote: לְפִי שֶׁהָיְתָה מְצוּיָה בְּאַרְצְכֶם הַרְבֵּה
sources.says: Rashi says it was plentiful in their land, so there was no need to buy it.

43:24.headline: I did not make you serve Me, but you made Me serve
43:24.body: Verse 23 says לא העבדתיך, "I did not burden you". Verse 24 turns the same verb around: העבדתני, "you burdened Me". Radak points out the reversal, and Rashi says Israel's sins made God a servant to idol worshippers.

sources.quote: והנה הדבר הזה להפך כי אני לא העבדתיך ואתה העבדתני
sources.says: Radak says this reverses the last verse: I did not burden you, but you burdened Me.

sources.quote: אַתֶּם גְּרַמְתֶּם לִי לִהְיוֹת שַׁמָּשׁ לְעוֹבְדֵי פְּסִילִים
sources.says: Rashi says you caused Me to become a servant to idol worshippers.

sources.quote: שבתי בעיני הגוים כעבד שאין לו כח
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says God looked to the nations like a slave with no power.

43:27.headline: Who is "your first father" who sinned?
43:27.body: Rashi says Abraham, who asked God "how will I know". Radak says Adam. Ibn Ezra says Jeroboam, the king Israel chose without God.

sources.quote: בְּאָמְרוֹ ״בַּמֶּה אֵדַע״
sources.says: Rashi says it is Abraham, when he asked "how will I know" in Genesis 15:8.

sources.quote: והנה אביך הראשון חטא והוא אדם הראשון
sources.says: Radak says the first father is Adam.

sources.quote: הוא ירבעם, שבחרו ישראל למלך
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it is Jeroboam, whom Israel chose as king.

44:2.headline: "From the womb" hints at Jacob gripping his brother's heel
44:2.body: God says He formed Jacob "from the womb". Ibn Ezra hears a hint of Jacob grabbing Esau's heel before birth, and Radak says the God who was with Jacob in the womb will be with his children in exile.

sources.quote: ויצרך מבטן, רמז ליעקב, כטעם בבטן עקב את אחיו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says "formed you from the womb" hints at Jacob, who grabbed his brother's heel in the womb.

sources.quote: ומי שהיה עם אביכם בבטן יהיה עמכם בגלות
sources.says: Radak says the One who was with your father in the womb will be with you in exile.

44:3.headline: "My spirit": God's goodwill, or the spirit of prophecy?
44:3.body: Metzudat Zion says רוחי here means God's will or favor. The Targum reads "my holy spirit", and Radak says Israel in exile is thirsty for prophecy, which had stopped.

sources.quote: רוחי. ענין רצון
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says רוחי here means will or favor.

sources.quote: כֵּן אֶתֵּן רוּחַ קוּדְשִׁי עַל בְּנָךְ
sources.says: The Targum renders it: so I will put my holy spirit on your children.

sources.quote: שישראל צמאים בגלות לדבר הנבואה שפסקה זה כמה שנים
sources.says: Radak says Israel in exile thirsts for prophecy, which had stopped many years before.

44:13.headline: "The glory of a man": Rashi reads it as his wife
44:13.body: The idol is made "like the glory of man, to sit in a house". Rashi and the Targum say a man's glory is his wife, who sits at home; Ibn Ezra says the phrase just repeats "the form of a man".

sources.quote: הִיא הָאִשָּׁה, שֶׁהִיא תִּפְאֶרֶת בַּעְלָהּ
sources.says: Rashi says the glory of man is the wife, who is her husband's glory.

sources.quote: כְּתוּשְׁבְּחַת אִתְּתָא לְמִיתַּב בְּבֵיתָא
sources.says: The Targum renders it "like the beauty of a woman, to sit in the house".

sources.quote: יש אומרים נקבה, ואין צורך רק הטעם כפול
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says some read it as a woman, but there is no need: the verse repeats itself.

44:14.headline: "Rain makes it grow", or "its trunk grows"?
44:14.body: גשם usually means rain. Ibn Ezra says it can mean "body", as in Aramaic, so the tree's trunk grows; Radak prefers rain and says God's rain still grows a tree planted for an idol.

sources.quote: וגשם. גוף, גם כן תרגום ארמית
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says גשם means body, as in Aramaic.

sources.quote: והנכון לפרשו כמשמעו, וכן תרגם יונתן ומטרא ירבי
sources.says: Radak says the right reading is the plain one, rain, as the Targum has it.

sources.quote: שאף על פי שהוא נוטע העץ לשם עכו"ם הגשם יגדל אותו
sources.says: Radak says even though he plants the tree for an idol, the rain still makes it grow.

44:16.headline: "I have seen the fire", or "I feel relief"?
44:16.body: The man warming himself says ראיתי אור, "I have seen the fire". Ibn Ezra brings Rav Saadia, who reads ראיתי as "I feel relief", though Ibn Ezra keeps the plain meaning.

sources.quote: ראיתי. כמשמעו, ורב סעדיה נ"ע אמר כי טעמו רָוַחְתִּי
sources.says: Ibn Ezra reads it plainly, and reports that Rav Saadia took it to mean "I feel relief".

44:18.headline: Their eyes are "plastered" shut. Who did it?
44:18.body: טח means to smear, like plastering a house wall. Ibn Ezra says God smeared their eyes; Radak adds it may be their own evil urge that covers their mind.

sources.quote: טח. ענין מריחה ומשיחה וכן וטח את הבית
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says טח means smearing, as in plastering a house.

sources.quote: והוא פועל יוצא, והפועל הוא השם
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the verb has an object, and the one who smears is God.

sources.quote: או יהיה הטח יצרם הרע הגובר על שכלם
sources.says: Radak says the one who smears may be their evil urge, which overpowers their mind.

44:20.headline: "Shepherd of ashes": a half-burned god, or a bad friendship
44:20.body: Rashi says the fool takes as his shepherd an idol whose other half became ash. In a second reading, רעה comes from רע, "friend": he joins himself to a worship that is ash.

sources.quote: הַשּׁוֹטֶה הַזֶּה הָיָה אוֹמֵר שֶׁהוּא לוֹ לְרוֹעֶה וּלְמְפַרְנֵס
sources.says: Rashi says the fool would say the idol was his shepherd and provider.

sources.quote: רוֹעֶה אֵפֶר לְשׁוֹן ׳רֵיעוּת׳
sources.says: Rashi's second reading takes רועה from friendship.

sources.quote: כאדם שירעה אפר, שיזיק ולא יועיל
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says he is like someone grazing on ash, which harms and does not help.

44:24.headline: Rashi: God chose Jacob while the twins still fought in the womb
44:24.body: God calls Himself the one who formed Israel "from the womb". Rashi takes this back to Rebecca's pregnancy, when the twins struggled inside her, and says God helped and chose Jacob from then.

sources.quote: מֵאָז ״וַיִּתְרוֹצְצוּ הַבָּנִים בְּקִרְבָּהּ״
sources.says: Rashi points to the moment the children struggled inside Rebecca.

sources.quote: הָיִיתִי לְךָ לְעֶזְרָה וּבְחַרְתִּיךָ
sources.says: Rashi says God was Jacob's help and chose him from then.

44:24.headline: Written "who was with me?", read "by myself"
44:24.body: The word is read מֵאִתִּי, "by Myself", but written מי אתי, "who was with Me?". The midrash joins the two: no one, not even an angel, was God's partner in making the world.

sources.quote: מִי אִתִּי כְּתִיב, מִי הָיָה שֻׁתָּף עִמִּי בִּבְרִיָּתוֹ שֶׁל עוֹלָם
sources.says: The midrash says the written form is "who was with Me": who was My partner in creating the world?

sources.quote: מי אתי כתיב לומר מי היה שותף עמי בבריאתו של עולם
sources.says: Radak repeats the midrash on the written form.

sources.quote: וכתוב מי אתי והנה הוא כמו לבדי
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the written form means the same as "alone".

44:27.headline: "The deep" that dries up is Babylon
44:27.body: God tells "the deep" to dry up. Rashi and the Targum say this is Babylon; Radak gives two reasons: the city was full of water, and it lay in a low valley.

sources.quote: הָאוֹמֵר לְבָבֶל: הִתְיַבְּשִׁי
sources.says: Rashi says this is God telling Babylon to dry up.

sources.quote: דַּאֲמַר עַל בָּבֶל תֶּחְרוֹב
sources.says: The Targum renders it: who said of Babylon, it will be laid waste.

sources.quote: היא בבל המשיל אותה למצולת ים לשני דברים האחד שהיא מלאה מים והשני לפי שהיתה בקעה
sources.says: Radak says Babylon is compared to the deep because it was full of water and lay in a valley.

45:1.headline: Was the Persian king Cyrus God's "anointed"?
45:1.body: Rashi says 'anointed' can mean anyone raised to greatness, so here it is Cyrus. The Talmud asks whether Cyrus was really the Messiah, and reads the verse as God speaking to the Messiah, complaining to him about Cyrus.

sources.quote: למשיחו. כל שם גדלה קרויה ׳משיחה׳
sources.says: Rashi says any title of greatness is called 'anointing'.

sources.quote: וכי כורש משיח היה? אלא אמר ליה הקדוש ברוך הוא למשיח: קובל אני לך על כורש
sources.says: The Talmud asks if Cyrus was the Messiah, and answers that God said to the Messiah: I complain to you about Cyrus.
