sources.quote: וכאן ננקד למשיחו בזרקא ולכורש ננקד במאריך להפרישו ולנתקו מעם למשיחו
sources.says: Rashi says the chant marks here separate 'His anointed' from 'Cyrus', which supports this reading.

45:2.headline: City walls, winding roads, or mountains?
45:2.body: The Targum reads הדורים as city walls, which go around the city. Rashi and Metzudat Zion also read crooked roads, like the sages' word for winding intestines; Ibn Ezra reports others who read mountains.

sources.quote: על שם שסובבת החומה את העיר. ויש לפרש הדורים: אורחות מקלקלות אישר לפניו
sources.says: Rashi says the Targum reads walls, since a wall goes around a city, and that it may also mean crooked paths made straight.

sources.quote: והדורים. ר״ל דרך מעוקם ומסובב ובדרז״ל הדורא דכנתא
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means a crooked, winding road, like the sages' term for the coiled intestines.

sources.quote: ויש אומר מגזרת הדר, והטעם הרים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says some derive it from הדר, 'splendor', and read it as mountains.

45:7.headline: God "forms" light but "creates" darkness: why a different verb?
45:7.body: Light and peace get the verbs יוצר and עשה; darkness and evil get בורא. Maimonides, Ibn Ezra and Radak say this is because darkness and evil are not things at all, only the absence of light and of good.

sources.quote: התבונן כיצד לא אמר "עושה חשך" ולא אמר "עושה רע", כי אין הם דברים מצויים
sources.says: Maimonides says the verse does not say 'makes darkness' or 'makes evil', because they are not things that exist.

sources.quote: ובורא חשך. מגזרת בריאה כטעם גזירה, כי החשך איננו כלום רק העדר האור
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says בורא here means decreeing, since darkness is nothing but the absence of light.

sources.quote: ועל חשך ורע אמר בורא כי אינה דבר כי הסרת האור היא החשך
sources.says: Radak says the verse uses בורא for darkness and evil because they are not things; darkness is the removal of light.

45:7.headline: Why the morning prayer says "creates all", not "creates evil"
45:7.body: The blessing before the morning Shema quotes this verse but changes 'creates evil' to 'creates all'. The Talmud says the verse is written 'evil' and recited 'all', to use a gentler word.

sources.quote: אלא כתיב ״רע״ וקרינן ״הכל״ לישנא מעליא
sources.says: The Talmud says the verse is written 'evil' but in the prayer we say 'all', as a nicer way of speaking.

sources.quote: עושה שלום ובורא את הכל
sources.says: Rashi quotes the verse in its prayer form: 'makes peace and creates all'.

45:8.headline: "I created it", in the singular: what is "it"?
45:8.body: Ibn Ezra says 'it' is Cyrus. The Talmud notes the verse says 'it', not 'them', and learns that a day of rain is as great as the day heaven and earth were created.

sources.quote: אני יי בראתיו. הוי"ו סימן כורש
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the ו at the end of בראתיו points to Cyrus.

sources.quote: גדול יום הגשמים כיום שנבראו שמים וארץ
sources.says: The Talmud says a day of rain is as great as the day heaven and earth were created.

sources.quote: ״בראתים״ לא נאמר, אלא ״בראתיו״
sources.says: The Talmud notes the verse does not say 'I created them' but 'I created it'.

45:18.headline: The world was made to be lived in, so people must have children
45:18.body: The Talmud learns from this verse that the world was created so people would have children. So a man who is half slave, and can marry no one, must be set free.

sources.quote: והלא לא נברא העולם אלא לפריה ורביה, שנאמר: ״לא תוהו בראה לשבת יצרה״
sources.says: The Talmud says the world was created only for having children, citing this verse.

sources.quote: כופין את רבו ועושה אותו בן חורין
sources.says: The Talmud says his master is made to set him free.

sources.quote: לא תהו בראה. כי לשבת יצרה
sources.says: Rashi says God did not make the earth to stand empty, but to be lived in.

45:20.headline: Survivors of the nations, or their lowest?
45:20.body: פליטי usually means survivors, and Rashi reads it so: those left from Nebuchadnezzar's sword. Radak and Metzudat Zion read it as the lowest of the nations, the idol worshippers, since the nations also have wise people who know idols are empty.

sources.quote: פליטי הגוים. אשר נשארו מחרבו של נבוכדנצר
sources.says: Rashi says they are those who survived Nebuchadnezzar's sword.

sources.quote: פליטי. ענין פחות ושפל כמו פליטי אפרים
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says פליטי means the low and worthless, as in 'the fugitives of Ephraim'.

sources.quote: שאי אפשר שאין בגוים חכמים ומבינים כי הבל הוא עבודת הפסילים
sources.says: Radak says there must be wise people among the nations who understand idol worship is empty.

46:1.headline: Idols are called עצבים because they bring grief
46:1.body: עצב is a word for an idol, and the same letters mean sorrow. Metzudat Zion says idols get this name because they grieve the people who cry to them and get no answer.

sources.quote: כן יקראו הגלולים ע״ש שמעציבים לב עובדיהם צועקים אליהם ואינם נענים
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says idols are called this because they sadden their worshippers, who cry to them and are not answered.

46:3.headline: Babylon carries its gods; Israel's God carries Israel
46:3.body: Verse 1 uses עמוסות and נשא for idols loaded onto tired animals. Verse 3 uses the same words for Israel, carried by God since birth. The commentators point out the reversal.

sources.quote: וְלֹא כְּעוֹבְדֵי כּוֹכָבִים וּמַזָּלוֹת שֶׁהָיוּ עוֹמְסִים וְנוֹשְׂאִים אֶת אֱלֹהֵיהֶם
sources.says: Rashi says Israel is not like idol worshippers, who load and carry their gods.

sources.quote: אֲבָל אַתֶּם עֲמוּסִים וּנְשׂוּאִים בִּזְרוֹעוֹתַי
sources.says: Rashi has God say: but you are loaded and carried in my arms.

sources.quote: אלהי בבל היו נשואים, ואני אלהי ישראל נשאתי
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the gods of Babylon were carried, but the God of Israel does the carrying.

46:4.headline: שיבה is a later age than זקנה
46:4.body: The verse pairs זקנה, old age, with שיבה, gray hair. Radak says שיבה is older still, and cites the sages: sixty is זקנה and seventy is שיבה.

sources.quote: שיבה יותר מזקנה, וכן אמרו בן ששים לזקנה בן שבעים לשיבה
sources.says: Radak says שיבה is more than זקנה, as the sages said: sixty for old age, seventy for gray hair.

sources.quote: שיבה. הוא יותר מהזקנה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says שיבה is beyond זקנה.

46:6.headline: Pouring out gold, or treating it as cheap
46:6.body: Rashi and Metzudat Zion read הזלים as pouring, like flowing water. Radak reads it from זול, cheap: gold is costly, yet they spend it freely on idols.

sources.quote: מל׳ הזלה ושפיכה וכן יזלו מים
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means pouring out, as in waters flowing.

sources.quote: אף על פי שהזהב ביוקר הם עושים אותו לפסילים כזול
sources.says: Radak says though gold is costly, they use it for idols as if it were cheap.

46:6.headline: Bowing, then bowing lower
46:6.body: סגד and השתחוה both mean bowing. Radak and Metzudat Zion say סגד is the smaller bow, and השתחוה goes further, which is why the verse says “they bow, yes, they prostrate.”

sources.quote: ענין השתחואה אלא שקטנה הימנה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it is a kind of bowing, but less than full prostration.

sources.quote: ההשתחוואה יותר מהסגידה, לפיכך אמר אף
sources.says: Radak says prostration is more than סגידה, so the verse says “yes, even.”

46:12.headline: “Stout-hearted”: faithful Israel, or cruel Babylon?
46:12.body: אבירי לב means strong of heart, for good or bad. Rashi reads it as praise for Israel, who held fast to God. Radak reads it as blame for the Babylonians, who were hard and cruel to Israel.

sources.quote: אֲשֶׁר אִמַּצְתֶּם לְבַבְכֶם וְנִדְבַּקְתֶּם בִּי
sources.says: Rashi says these are the ones who strengthened their hearts and clung to God.

sources.quote: אמר לאנשי בבל שהם אבירי לב ואכזרים לישראל
sources.says: Radak says it is addressed to the people of Babylon, who were hard-hearted and cruel to Israel.

47:1.headline: Babylon is called a virgin because no one had conquered her
47:1.body: The verse calls Babylon a בתולה, a young unmarried woman. Radak says it means no enemy had ever ruled over her until now.

sources.quote: וקראה בתולה שהיתה עד עתה כבתולה שלא נבעלה, כלומר שלא שלטה יד אדם עליה
sources.says: Radak says she is called a virgin because until now no human hand had ruled over her.

47:2.headline: You grind grain, not flour, so why say “grind flour”?
47:2.body: Flour is what you get after grinding, so the phrase sounds odd. Ibn Ezra says the grain is called by what it will become.

sources.quote: קמח. לא יתכן, רק נקרא על שם סופו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says grinding flour is not possible, so the grain is named for what it ends up as.

47:2.headline: Uncover your hair, your veil, or your arms?
47:2.body: Radak says צמה is the hair a woman arranges by her temples, and Metzudat Zion says it is the veil over her face. Rashi says it is her arms and legs, kept bound and covered.

sources.quote: הצמה הוא השער שמתקנת אותו האשה על צדעיה מעל פניה ומכסאה אותו בצעיף
sources.says: Radak says the צמה is the hair a woman arranges at her temples and covers with a scarf.

sources.quote: הוא המסוה המכסה את הפנים
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it is the veil that covers the face.

sources.quote: זְרוֹעֵךְ וְשׁוֹקַיִךְ, דָּבָר הַמְצֻמָּת וְקָשׁוּר וּמְכֻסֶּה
sources.says: Rashi says it means her arms and legs, something bound and covered.

47:2.headline: Bare your leg, your hair, or the path through the river
47:2.body: Radak reads שבל as the leg, from שביל, a path, since the leg walks the path. Ibn Ezra reads it as hair falling over the cheeks, and Rashi as the paths under the water she must wade through into exile.

sources.quote: והרגל יקרא שובל מענין שביל שהוא הדרך
sources.says: Radak says the leg is called שובל, from שביל, a road.

sources.quote: הוא השיער היורד על הלחיים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it is the hair that hangs down over the cheeks.

sources.quote: גַּלִּי הַשְּׁבִילִים מִן הַמַּיִם שֶׁעֲלֵיהֶם, כִּי דֶּרֶךְ שָׁם תֵּצְאִי בַּגּוֹלָה
sources.says: Rashi says it means uncover the paths beneath the water, because that is the way she will go into exile.

47:8.headline: A city is widowed when its king dies
47:8.body: Babylon boasts she will never be a widow or lose her children. Radak explains that a city's king is like her husband and her people are like her children.

sources.quote: העיר אלמנה במות מלכה שהוא לה כמו בעל לאשה והיא שכולה במות עמה שהם כמו בנים לה
sources.says: Radak says a city is a widow when its king dies, since he is like her husband, and bereaved when its people die, since they are like her children.

sources.quote: [אלמנה]. הבעל הוא המלך
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the husband here is the king.

47:9.headline: Not your friends, but your spells
47:9.body: חבר usually means a friend or companion. Rashi and Radak say here it means spells, as in חובר חבר, “one who casts spells” (Deuteronomy 18:11).

sources.quote: לְשׁוֹן כְּשָׁפִים, כְּמוֹ ״וְחֹבֵר חָבֶר״
sources.says: Rashi says it is a word for witchcraft, as in “one who casts spells.”

sources.quote: מן וחובר חבר והוא ענין כשפים
sources.says: Radak says it comes from “one who casts spells” and means witchcraft.

47:11.headline: No one to beg for help, or no dawn coming
47:11.body: Rashi, following the Targum, reads שחרה as “seek”: you will not know whom to beg for rescue. Ibn Ezra and Radak read it as dawn: a night with no morning, or trouble that arrives as suddenly as daybreak.

sources.quote: אֶת פְּנֵי מִי תְשַׁחֲרִי לְמַלְּטֵךְ מִמֶּנָּה
sources.says: Rashi asks whose face she will seek to save her from it.

sources.quote: לא תדעי שחרה. כלילה שאין לו שחר, והטעם אור
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it is like a night that has no dawn, and שחר means light.

sources.quote: ולא תדעי עת בואה כמו השחר שבא בבקר ברגע
sources.says: Radak says she will not know when it comes, like dawn, which arrives in a moment.

47:13.headline: Stargazers who need a clear sky, or simply star experts
47:13.body: Rashi, following Menachem, links הברי to ברור, clear: astrologers sort out the stars' paths and need a clear sky to do it. Ibn Ezra says the word has no relative, simply means experts in the stars, and calls the “clear” reading far-fetched.

sources.quote: וְכֵן חִבְּרוֹ מְנַחֵם עִמָּהֶם, מְבָרְרֵי הֲלִיכַת הַמַּזָּלוֹת
sources.says: Rashi says Menachem grouped the word with “clear,” meaning those who sort out the paths of the stars.

sources.quote: אין רע לו, וטעמו חכמי שמי', הם חכמי המזלות, ויש מי שהוציאוהו מגזרת ברור
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the word has no relative and means sky experts, the astrologers, and notes some who derive it from “clear.”

sources.quote: וכתוב הוברו כלומר אשר חזו לך עד עתה, וקרי הוברי שחוזים עתה ושניהם ענין אחד
sources.says: Radak says the written form means those who saw for you until now, the spoken form means those who see now, and both say the same thing.

47:13.headline: The stargazers know only “some of what” will come
47:13.body: The verse says the astrologers tell “from what” will come, not simply “what.” Rashi and the sages cited by Radak read the small word מאשר as “some of”: they glimpse a little of the future, never all of it.

sources.quote: וְאֵין יוֹדְעִין כָּל הַבֵּרוּר, לְכָךְ נֶאֱמַר ׳מֵאֲשֶׁר׳
sources.says: Rashi says they do not know the whole of it, which is why the verse says מאשר.

sources.quote: שאמרו מאשר ולא כל אשר, כלומר מודיעים מקצת העתידות ולא כולם
sources.says: Radak cites the sages: “from what,” not “all that,” meaning they foretell some future events and not all.

48:1.headline: "From the waters of Judah" means from Judah's descendants
48:1.body: The verse says Israel came "from the waters of Judah". Rashi and Ibn Ezra read the waters as offspring, like water flowing from a bucket. Ibn Ezra compares "the spring of Jacob" in Deuteronomy 33:28.

sources.quote: שֶׁיָּצְאוּ וְנָזְלוּ מִמֵּי דָּלְיוֹ שֶׁל יְהוּדָה
sources.says: Rashi says they came out and flowed from the waters of Judah's bucket, as in Numbers 24:7.

sources.quote: וממי יהודה, כמו זרע
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the waters of Judah mean his seed.

sources.quote: כל מי שיצא ממעין יעקב. וכן ומימי יהודה יצאו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says "the spring of Jacob" means all who came from Jacob, like this verse.

48:4.headline: A forehead of bronze, and the bronze altar that atones for it
48:4.body: A bronze forehead is a face that will not blush. Radak says it means a brazen person who feels no shame. Rashi on Exodus says the altar was covered in bronze to atone for this very sin.

sources.quote: וכן מצחך הוא כנחושה שלא תבוש מפני
sources.says: Radak says the forehead is like bronze, so it will not feel shame before God.

sources.quote: לְכַפֵּר עַל עַזּוּת מֶצַח, שֶׁנֶּ' וּמִצְחֲךָ נְחוּשָׁה
sources.says: Rashi says the altar's bronze atones for a brazen forehead, citing this verse.

48:5.headline: An idol is called עצב because it brings grief
48:5.body: עצב is a word for an idol. It sounds like עצב, sadness. Metzudat Zion says the idol is named for the grief it causes: its worshippers call to it and get no answer.

sources.quote: כן יקרא העכו״ם ע״ש שמעציב לב עובדיו קורא אליו ואינו נענה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the idol is called this because it grieves its worshippers, who call and get no answer.

48:8.headline: A rebel "from the womb": since Egypt, or by nature?
48:8.body: Rashi says from the womb means since Israel's start as a people in Egypt. Radak agrees, and adds a second reading: some bad traits are part of how a person is born.

sources.quote: מִשֶּׁהָיִיתָ בְּמִצְרַיִם
sources.says: Rashi says it means since you were in Egypt.

sources.quote: או פירוש מבטן כי הרשע יש קצת ממדותיו בטבע יצירתו
sources.says: Radak also says it can mean that some of the wicked person's traits are in his nature from birth.

48:10.headline: "I chose you" or "I tested you" in the furnace?
48:10.body: Some read בחרתיך as בחנתיך, "I tested you". Ibn Ezra and Radak keep "I chose". Radak says refining is itself choosing: picking the silver out from the waste.

sources.quote: יש אומרים שהוא כמו בחנתיך, ואין רע לו, והנכון שהו' כמשמעו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra notes the reading "tested you", but says the plain sense, "chose", is right.

sources.quote: כי הצרוף הוא בחירת הכסף מהסיגים
sources.says: Radak says refining is choosing the silver out from the waste.

48:12.headline: Jacob is the name from his father, Israel the name from God
48:12.body: God says "Jacob, and Israel whom I called". Rashi and Metzudat David say Jacob was the name his father gave him, but God gave the name Israel.

sources.quote: מֵאִתִּי נִקְרֵאתָ יִשְׂרָאֵל
sources.says: Rashi says God is the one who named him Israel, in Genesis 32:29.

sources.quote: כי אביו קרא לו יעקב וה׳ קראו ישראל
sources.says: Metzudat David says his father called him Jacob and God called him Israel.

48:12.headline: God's seal אמת spells first, middle and last
48:12.body: The sages call אמת, truth, God's seal. Rashi explains: א is the first letter, מ the middle and ת the last, matching "I am first and I am last".

sources.quote: אמצעית לאותיות וראשון ואחרון על שם אני ראשון ואני אחרון
sources.says: Rashi says the letters of אמת are the middle, first and last of the alphabet, after this verse.

48:13.headline: "My hand" made the earth, "My right hand" the heavens
48:13.body: Ibn Ezra and Radak say "hand" here means the left hand. The earth is lower, so it gets the left, and the heavens get the right. Rashi adds that the world took one hand, but the Temple two.

sources.quote: אף ידי. השמאל, דרך משל
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says "my hand" is the left hand, as a figure of speech.

sources.quote: וזכר היד שהיא שמאל לארץ לפי שהיא נקלה כנגד השמים
sources.says: Radak says the left hand goes with the earth because it is lower than the heavens.

sources.quote: שֶׁהָעוֹלָם נִבְרָא בְּיָד אַחַת
sources.says: Rashi says the world was made with one hand, citing this verse, while the Temple is built with two.

48:13.headline: Heaven and earth made together, or standing ready together?
48:13.body: The sages read "they stand together" as proof that heaven and earth were made at once, like a pot and its lid. Maimonides cites it the same way. Ibn Ezra says the plain sense is that both stand ready like servants when God calls.

sources.quote: אלא שניהם לא נבראו אלא כאלפס וכסויה
sources.says: Radak brings Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai: both were made together, like a pot and its lid.

sources.quote: שהשמים והארץ נבראו יחד
sources.says: Maimonides cites the sages' reading that heaven and earth were created together.

sources.quote: ובעת שאקרא אליהם למלאות חפצי, יעמדו שניהם לפני כעבדים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says when God calls them to do His will, both stand before Him like servants.

48:15.headline: "I called him": named him, or raised him up
48:15.body: Radak says God called Cyrus by name, as in Isaiah 45:1. Rashi says calling here means raising someone to greatness, like the "called ones of the assembly".

sources.quote: קראתיו בשם, כמו שאומר למשיחו לכרש
sources.says: Radak says God called him by name, as in "to His anointed, to Cyrus".

sources.quote: וּקְרִיאָה זוֹ לְשׁוֹן ׳גִּדּוּל׳
sources.says: Rashi says this calling means raising to greatness, as in Numbers 1:16.

48:16.headline: "I was there": every prophet stood at Sinai
48:16.body: The prophet says "from the time it happened, I was there". Rashi brings the sages' reading: all the prophets stood at Mount Sinai and got their prophecies there. Ibn Ezra rejects the Gaon's reading that the soul exists before the body.

sources.quote: וְלָמַדְנוּ מִכָּאן שֶׁכָּל הַנְּבִיאִים עָמְדוּ בְּסִינַי
sources.says: Rashi says we learn from here that all the prophets stood at Sinai.

sources.quote: שֶׁכָּל הַנְּבִיאִים עָמְדוּ עַל הַר סִינַי, וְשָׁם נִמְסְרוּ לָהֶם הַנְּבוּאוֹת
sources.says: Rashi says all the prophets stood on Mount Sinai, and their prophecies were handed to them there.

sources.quote: אמר הגאון מכאן רמז כי הנשמה קודם הגוף, ולא אמר כלום
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the Gaon found here a hint that the soul exists before the body, and rejects it.

48:16.headline: "And His spirit": His angel, or by His spirit?
48:16.body: God "sent me, and His spirit". Metzudat Zion and Radak say רוח here is an angel. Radak reports that Saadia read it as "with His spirit", and Rashi brings the Targum's "and His word".

sources.quote: ורוחו. ומלאכו
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means His angel.

sources.quote: והגאון רב סעדיה פירש כמו ברוחו
sources.says: Radak reports that Saadia read it as "with His spirit".

sources.quote: וּכְעַן ה׳ אֱלֹהִים שְׁלָחַנִי וּמֵימְרֵיהּ
sources.says: Rashi brings the Targum: God sent me, and His word.

48:19.headline: Like the sand's grains, or like the fish of the sea?
48:19.body: כמעתיו is a rare word. Radak says it is the grains of sand, small like coins. Rashi says the fish of the sea. Ibn Ezra hears the word for innards, מעים, pointing to fish.

sources.quote: ומעותיו הם אבני החול שהם צרורות קטנות והם כדמות מעות
sources.says: Radak says they are the grains of sand, tiny pebbles shaped like coins.

sources.quote: כְּדָגֵי הַיָּם לָרֹב
sources.says: Rashi says it means as many as the fish of the sea.

sources.quote: ומלת כמעותיו רמז למעי הדגים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the word hints at the innards of fish.

48:20.headline: "Flee Babylon" means hurry, not run in fear
48:20.body: ברחו usually means flee. Radak says they did not leave in fear. They left proudly and singing, so the word here means to go quickly.

sources.quote: אין זה בריחה מפחד כי ביד רמה יצאו ובקול רנה אלא פירושו מהירות ההליכה
sources.says: Radak says this is not fleeing in fear, since they left openly and singing; it means going fast.

sources.quote: ענין מהירות ההליכה ועם היה מבלי פחד
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means walking fast, even without fear.

49:1.headline: The prophet's name was chosen to mean salvation
49:1.body: Rashi says that while the prophet was still in the womb, God planned to call him ישעיה. The name holds the word ישועה, 'salvation', because he would foretell rescue and comfort.

sources.quote: לִהְיוֹת שְׁמִי יְשַׁעְיָה, לְהִנָּבֵא יְשׁוּעוֹת וְנֶחָמוֹת
sources.says: Rashi says God planned the name Yeshayahu before birth, so that he would prophesy salvations and comfort.

sources.quote: קרא שמי ישעיה לרמז שאנבא ישועות
sources.says: Metzudat David says the name was given as a hint that he would prophesy salvations.

49:2.headline: A polished arrow, or a chosen one?
49:2.body: Rashi and Metzudat Zion say ברור means polished, scraped clean of rust. The Targum translates it בחיר, 'chosen'.

sources.quote: לְחֵץ בָּרוּר. מְמוֹרָט
sources.says: Rashi says a ברור arrow is a polished one.

sources.quote: ברור. נקי מן החלודה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means clean of rust.

sources.quote: כְּגִיר בְּחִיר
sources.says: The Targum renders it 'like a chosen arrow'.

49:2.headline: A sword for those near, an arrow for those far
49:2.body: Radak asks why the prophet calls himself both a sword and an arrow. A sword strikes people close by, meaning Israel, and an arrow reaches far, meaning the nations.

sources.quote: ואמר חרב חדה כנגד ישראל שהם קרובים אליו, ובחרב יכה אדם לקרוב ולא לרחוק, ואמר חץ כנגד האומות שהם רחוקים
sources.says: Radak says the sharp sword stands for Israel, who are near, and the arrow for the nations, who are far.

sources.quote: לירות בלשוני למרחוק לאומות
sources.says: Radak says the arrow means shooting his words far off, to the nations.

49:3.headline: Why God calls the prophet himself 'Israel'
49:3.body: God tells the prophet, 'You are my servant, Israel'. Ibn Ezra and Metzudat David say God counts this one man as worth all of Israel.

sources.quote: או אתה ישראל שאתה נחשב בעיני ככל ישראל, והוא הנכון
sources.says: Ibn Ezra gives two readings: the prophet is of Israel's seed, or he counts in God's eyes as all Israel. He prefers the second.

sources.quote: הרי אתה לפני ככל המון ישראל
sources.says: Metzudat David says the prophet is before God like the whole people of Israel.

49:5.headline: Written 'not', read 'to him': will Israel be gathered?
49:5.body: The word is written לא, 'not', but read aloud as לו, 'to him'. Rashi follows the reading, that Israel will return to God, while Radak reads the written form as a question.

sources.quote: לוֹ יֵאָסֵף. אֵלָיו יָשׁוּב בִּתְשׁוּבָה
sources.says: Rashi says Israel will come back to God in repentance.

sources.quote: וכתוב ולא יאסף באל"ף ופירוש הכתוב בתמיה
sources.says: Radak says the word is written with an aleph, and the written form is meant as a question.

sources.quote: והגאון אמר לא יאסף לא ימות, כי מנהגו לפרש כדרך קרי וכדרך כתיב
sources.says: Ibn Ezra reports that the Gaon explained both the read and the written forms, taking the written one as 'he will not die'.

49:6.headline: Hearts under siege, ruined places, or exiles?
49:6.body: Rashi says ונצורי are hearts surrounded by the urge to sin, like a city under siege. Ibn Ezra says it means ruins, and the Targum says the exiles of Israel.

sources.quote: שֶׁלִּבָּם מֻקָּף יֵצֶר הִרְהוּרֵי עֲבֵירָה כְּעִיר נְצוּרָה
sources.says: Rashi says their hearts are surrounded by sinful thoughts like a besieged city.

sources.quote: ונצורי ישראל. חרבות
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the word means ruins.

sources.quote: וְגַלְוַת יִשְׂרָאֵל לַאֲתָבָא
sources.says: The Targum renders it 'to bring back the exiles of Israel'.

49:7.headline: Loathed by the nations, or loathing them?
49:7.body: Rashi reads it as one whom the nations loathe. Ibn Ezra gives that reading and also another: the prophet himself loathes every nation.

sources.quote: לְמִי שֶׁהַגּוֹי מְתַעֲבוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says it means the one whom the nation loathes.

sources.quote: או יהיה למתעב גוי שהנביא יתעב כל גוי
sources.says: Ibn Ezra offers a second reading, that the prophet loathes every nation.

49:7.headline: One extra letter: the princes stood and also bowed
49:7.body: Rabbi Elazar says kings will stand and princes will bow. Rabbi Zeira answers that the verse says 'princes, and they will bow', with an extra ו, so both groups did both.

sources.quote: מְלָכִים — בְּקִימָה, וְשָׂרִים — בְּהִשְׁתַּחֲוָיָה
sources.says: Rabbi Elazar says kings stand and princes bow.

sources.quote: הַשְׁתָּא דִּכְתִיב ״שָׂרִים וְיִשְׁתַּחֲווּ״ — הָא וְהָא עֲבוּד
sources.says: The Talmud says that because the verse is written 'princes, and they will bow', both groups did both.

49:8.headline: A time of favor: when you pray, or when you obey?
49:8.body: Rashi says עת רצון is a time of prayer, when Israel seeks God's favor. Radak and the Targum say it is a time when Israel does God's will.

sources.quote: בְּעֵת תְּפִלָּה, שֶׁאַתָּה מִתְרַצֶּה וּמִתְפַּיֵּס לְפָנַי
sources.says: Rashi says it is a time of prayer, when you make peace with Me.

sources.quote: בעת שתעשה רצוני אני עניתיך
sources.says: Radak says God answers Israel at a time when they do His will.

sources.quote: בְּעִידַן דְאַתּוּן עָבְדִין רְעוּתִי
sources.says: The Targum renders it 'at the time when you do My will'.

49:8.headline: 'I will guard you' or 'I will shape you'?
49:8.body: Rashi and Radak read ואצרך as 'I will guard you'. The Targum uses אתקן, the same verb it uses for יוצרי, 'who formed me', in verse 5.

sources.quote: וְאֶצָּרְךָ. וְאֶשְׁמָרְךָ
sources.says: Rashi says it means 'I will guard you'.

sources.quote: שאשמרך מן הכליה
sources.says: Radak says God will guard Israel from destruction.

sources.quote: וְאֶתְקְנִינָךְ וְאֶתְּנִינָךְ
sources.says: The Targum renders it 'and I will establish you'.

sources.quote: דְאַתְקְנַנִי מִמְעַיִן
sources.says: In verse 5 the Targum uses the same verb for 'who formed me from the womb'.

49:8.headline: Raise up the land, or the righteous who lie in it?
49:8.body: Rashi says God will restore the land of Israel. The Targum, quoted by Radak, reads it as raising the righteous who lie in the dust.

sources.quote: אֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל, הַבְּחוּרָה לִי
sources.says: Rashi says it is the land of Israel, chosen by God.

sources.quote: ותרגם להקים ארץ לאקמא צדיקיא דשכבין בעפרא
sources.says: Radak notes the Targum renders it as raising the righteous who lie in the dust.

sources.quote: לַאֲקָמָא צַדִיקַיָא דְשָׁכְבִין בְּעַפְרָא
sources.says: The Targum says: to raise up the righteous who lie in the dust.

49:9.headline: Streams of water, or bare hilltops?
49:9.body: Rashi follows the Targum: שפיים are streams of water. Radak and Metzudat Zion say they are high places, where no one expects to find pasture.

sources.quote: תִּרְגֵּם יוֹנָתָן ״נַגְדִּין״, נַחֲלֵי מַיִם
sources.says: Rashi quotes the Targum's word, meaning streams of water.

sources.quote: ובכל שפיים. מקומות הגבוהים
sources.says: Radak says שפיים are high places.

sources.quote: כן נקראו המקומות הגבוהים
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says high places are called by this name.

49:12.headline: The land of Sinim is the far south
49:12.body: The Targum, quoted by Rashi, calls it 'the land of the south'. Radak and Metzudat Zion say it is named for the Sinites who live there, a people descended from Canaan.

sources.quote: מֵאֶרֶץ סִינִים. ״מֵאַרַע דָּרוֹמָא״
sources.says: Rashi quotes the Targum: from the land of the south.

sources.quote: כי הסינים שוכנים שם, והסינים הוא מבני כנען
sources.says: Radak says the Sinites live there, and they are descended from Canaan.

sources.quote: נקרא כן על שם היושבים שמה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the land is named after the people who live there.

49:14.headline: Why both 'left me' and 'forgot me'?
49:14.body: The Talmud asks if leaving and forgetting are not the same. Resh Lakish says a man who takes a second wife still remembers the first, but Zion feels God has both left her and forgotten her.

sources.quote: הַיְינוּ עֲזוּבָה, הַיְינוּ שְׁכוּחָה
sources.says: The Talmud asks whether 'left' and 'forgotten' mean the same thing.

sources.quote: אָדָם נוֹשֵׂא אִשָּׁה עַל אִשְׁתּוֹ רִאשׁוֹנָה, זוֹכֵר מַעֲשֵׂה הָרִאשׁוֹנָה. אַתָּה עֲזַבְתַּנִי וּשְׁכַחְתַּנִי
sources.says: Resh Lakish says a man who marries again still remembers his first wife, but Israel says God has left and forgotten her.

49:15.headline: Her baby, or the burnt offerings Israel brought?
49:15.body: Rashi says עולה means her infant, like עולל. The Talmud hears עולות, burnt offerings: God asks, would I forget the offerings you brought Me in the desert?

sources.quote: הֲתִשְׁכַּח אִשָּׁה עוּלָהּ. עוֹלָל שֶׁלָּהּ
sources.says: Rashi says עולה means her baby.

sources.quote: כְּלוּם אֶשְׁכַּח עוֹלוֹת אֵילִים וּפִטְרֵי רְחָמִים שֶׁהִקְרַבְתְּ לְפָנַי בַּמִּדְבָּר
sources.says: The Talmud has God ask whether He could forget the burnt offerings and firstborn animals Israel offered in the desert.

49:15.headline: 'Even these may forget': the golden calf is forgotten
49:15.body: Plainly, אלה are mothers, who may sometimes forget their children. The Talmud and the Targum read it as Israel's sin: even the golden calf will be forgotten, but God will not forget Sinai.

sources.quote: פעמים שגם אלה הנשים תשכחנה בניהן
sources.says: Radak says that sometimes even these women forget their children.

sources.quote: שֶׁמָּא לֹא תִּשְׁכַּח לִי מַעֲשֵׂה הָעֵגֶל? אָמַר לָהּ: ״גַּם אֵלֶּה תִשְׁכַּחְנָה״
sources.says: In the Talmud Israel asks if God will forget the golden calf, and He answers, 'even these will be forgotten'.

sources.quote: שֶׁמָּא תִּשְׁכַּח לִי מַעֲשֵׂה סִינַי? אָמַר לָהּ: ״וְאָנֹכִי לֹא אֶשְׁכָּחֵךְ״
sources.says: Israel then asks if God will forget Sinai, and He answers, 'I will not forget you'.

sources.quote: דִלְמָא לָא מִתְנַשֵׁי לִי יַת דַעֲבָדִית עֵגֶל דִדְהַב
sources.says: The Targum tells the same exchange, with Israel worried about the golden calf.

49:16.headline: Engraved on God's palms, or above the clouds?
49:16.body: Rashi and Radak read כפים as palms: Zion is engraved on God's hand, always in view. Saadia, quoted by Radak, and a second reading in Rashi take כפים as clouds.

sources.quote: כְּאִלּוּ אַתְּ חֲקוּקָה עַל כַּפִּי לִרְאוֹתֵךְ וּלְזָכְרֵךְ תָּמִיד
sources.says: Rashi says it is as if Zion were engraved on God's palm, to see and remember always.

sources.quote: מֵעַל עַנְנֵי כָּבוֹד
sources.says: Rashi's second reading: above the clouds of glory.

sources.quote: פירש רב סעדיה ז"ל כמו עננים
sources.says: Radak reports that Saadia explained כפים as clouds, then says the plain meaning is correct.

sources.quote: אֲבָל אֲנִי אֶעֱשֶׂה לָךְ דָּבָר שֶׁנִּרְאֶה לְעוֹלָם
sources.says: The Talmud has God say He will make Israel a sign that is always seen, citing this verse.

49:17.headline: Your children hurry home, or were quicker to forget?
49:17.body: Rashi says Zion's children will hurry to return. Metzudat David reads it as a rebuke: Zion's children forgot their land faster than God would.

sources.quote: מִהֲרוּ בָּנָיִךְ. לָשׁוּב
sources.says: Rashi says the children hurry to return.

sources.quote: יותר מהרה שכחו בני ציון את ארצם משאשכח אני
sources.says: Metzudat David says Zion's children forgot their land more quickly than God would forget.

49:20.headline: 'Come close' here means 'move over'
49:20.body: גשה usually means 'come near'. In this crowded city, Metzudat Zion says it means 'move away for my sake', and Rashi says 'go to the other side for me'.

sources.quote: גשה לי. התרחק בעבורי
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means 'move away for me'.

sources.quote: הִתְקָרֵב לְצַד אַחֵר בִּשְׁבִילִי
sources.says: Rashi says it means 'move to another side for my sake'.

49:24.headline: A righteous captive, or a captor in the right?
49:24.body: Rashi says the captive is righteous Jacob, held by Esau. Radak says the nations mean they took Israel by right, and in the next verse God answers that the captor is no righteous man but a tyrant.

sources.quote: מַלְקוֹחַ שִׁבְיוֹ שֶׁל יַעֲקֹב הַצַּדִּיק
sources.says: Rashi says the captives are those of Jacob the righteous.

sources.quote: ועוד כי הוא שבי צדיק כי בצדק ובמשפט לקחו
sources.says: Radak says the nations claim they took the captive justly.

sources.quote: ומה שתאמרו צדיק אינו כי אם עריץ
sources.says: Radak says God answers that the captor is not righteous but a tyrant.

49:25.headline: An odd form: 'your opponent' built like a verb
49:25.body: יריבך looks like 'he will quarrel with you'. Radak says it is a noun, 'the one who quarrels with you', with an extra י, and Ibn Ezra calls it a strange word.

sources.quote: יריבך. שם תאר והיו"ד נוספת כיו"ד יקום
sources.says: Radak says it is a noun with an added yod.

sources.quote: והכלל שהי' מלה זרה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra lists several views and concludes it is a strange word.

49:26.headline: Those who taunt you, or those who count you?
49:26.body: Rashi links מוניך to hurting with words: those who taunt you. Ibn Ezra cites others who read it as 'those who count you', since Israel is compared to sheep.

sources.quote: אוֹנָאַת דְּבָרִים, הַמְקַנְתְּרִים אוֹתָךְ בְּגִדּוּפֵיהֶם
sources.says: Rashi says it means hurtful words: those who provoke you with insults.

sources.quote: ואחרים אמרו סופריך, כמו על ידי מונה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra cites others who say it means those who count you, as a shepherd counts sheep.

5:1.headline: A vineyard in a corner, or on a horn
5:1.body: Metzudat Zion reads קרן as a corner of the land. Radak reads it as a horn: the Land of Israel sits higher than all lands, as a horn rises highest on the body.

sources.quote: בקרן. פנה וזויות וכן על קרנות המזבח
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says קרן means a corner, as with the corners of the altar.

sources.quote: וקרא ארץ ישראל קרן לפי שהיא גבוהה מכל הארצות, והקרן גבוה מכל הגוף
sources.says: Radak says the Land of Israel is called a horn because it is higher than all lands, as the horn is the highest part of the body.

5:2.headline: A word with no relatives, explained from Arabic and Aramaic
5:2.body: Ibn Ezra says ויעזקהו has no related word in Tanach and reads it, from Arabic, as “fenced it in.” Rashi ties it to the Aramaic עזקא, “ring”: a fence all the way around, while Radak also offers “dug it.”

sources.quote: והנכון שאין למלה הזאת אח, רק תמצא בלשון קדר, וטעמו כמו גדר ומשוכה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the word has no sibling and is found in Arabic, meaning a fence or hedge.

sources.quote: סִיְּגוֹ וּגְדָרוֹ סָבִיב, מֻקָּף כְּמִין טַבַּעַת, דִּמְתַרְגְּמִינָן ״עִיזְקָא
sources.says: Rashi says it means fenced all around like a ring, from the Aramaic עיזקא.

sources.quote: ויעזקהו. פירוש חפרו, מדברי רבותינו ז"ל מצאום יושב ועוזק תחת הזתים
sources.says: Radak reads it as “dug it,” from a word the sages use for digging under olive trees.

5:2.headline: The choice vine adds up to 606 commandments
5:2.body: A שורק is a choice vine, and Radak says it gives good grapes without pips. The sages also count the letters of שורק as 606, the commandments Israel received beyond the seven given to all of Noah’s children.

sources.quote: ואמר כי נקרא שורק הגפן שמוציא ענבים טובים שאין בהם חרצן
sources.says: Radak says the vine is called שורק because it bears good grapes without pips.

sources.quote: נְטַעְתִּים שׂוֹרֵק, שֵׁשׁ מֵאוֹת וָשֵׁשׁ מִצְווֹת כְּמִנְיַן שׂוֹרֵק הוֹסַפְתִּי עֲלֵיהֶם, עַל שֶׁבַע מִצְווֹת שֶׁנִּצְטַוּוּ בְּנֵי נֹחַ
sources.says: Rashi says God planted them as a שורק: 606 commandments, the number of שורק, added to the seven given to Noah’s descendants.

5:2.headline: A watchtower in the vineyard, or the winepress
5:2.body: Ibn Ezra reads מגדל as a watchtower, a place for the guard to sit. Rashi says it is the winepress, where the grapes are pressed.

sources.quote: ויבן מגדל בתוכו. מקום לשבת השומר
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the מגדל is a place for the watchman to sit.

sources.quote: וַיִּבֶן מִגְדָּל בְּתוֹכוֹ. גַּת לַעֲצוֹר עֲנָבִים
sources.says: Rashi says the מגדל is a winepress for pressing grapes.

5:6.headline: Thorns, or the worm that splits stone
5:6.body: Menachem ben Saruq and Metzudat Zion take שמיר ושית as kinds of thorns. Rashi reads שמיר as the tough worm that splits stone, which Solomon used to build the Temple.

sources.quote: שמיר ושית. שמות מיני קוצים
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says שמיר and שית are names of kinds of thorns.

sources.quote: מִינֵי קוֹצִים פָּתַר בָּהֶם מְנַחֵם בֶּן סָרוּק (מחברת מנחם: שמר), וַאֲנִי אוֹמֵר: שָׁמִיר לְשׁוֹן תּוֹלַעַת חָזָק הוּא הַמְבַקֵּעַ אֲבָנִים, שֶׁבּוֹ בָּנָה שְׁלֹמֹה אֶת בֵּית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ
sources.says: Rashi says Menachem read them as thorns, but he reads שמיר as a strong worm that splits stones, used by Solomon to build the Temple.

5:6.headline: No rain from the clouds, or no word from the prophets
5:6.body: Radak reads it plainly: God will hold back the rain from their land. Rashi follows the Targum: the clouds are the prophets, who receive prophecy from above as clouds receive rain.

sources.quote: ומשל ועל העבים אצוה יתפרש כמשמעו שאמנע ברכתי מארצם
sources.says: Radak says it means what it says: God will withhold his blessing of rain from their land.

sources.quote: הַנְּבוּאָה נִמְשְׁלָה לְמָטָר, שֶׁהֶעָבִים מְקַבְּלִין אוֹתָהּ מִן הַשָּׁמַיִם, כָּךְ הַנְּבִיאִים מְקַבְּלִין הַנְּבוּאָה מִפִּי הַקְּדוּשָׁה
sources.says: Rashi says prophecy is compared to rain: as clouds receive rain from heaven, prophets receive prophecy from God.

5:6.headline: God “commands” the clouds: how the Bible speaks about nature
5:6.body: Maimonides stops on this verse as an example of a pattern. The Bible describes ordinary nature, like rain falling or not, as God’s own command.

sources.quote: על ענייני הטבע הנוהגים תמידית, א) כמו התמוססות השלג כשהאוויר מתחמם, וגעישת מי הים כשהרוח סוערת, נאמר: "יִשְׁלַח דְּבָרוֹ וְיַמְסֵם" (תהילים קמז,יח), "וַיֹּאמֶר וַיַּעֲמֵד רוּחַ סְעָרָה וַתְּרוֹמֵם גַּלָּיו" (שם קז,כה). ב) ועל ירידת הגשם נאמר: "וְעַל הֶעָבִים אֲצַוֶּה מֵהַמְטִיר
sources.says: Maimonides lists this verse among cases where regular natural events, like rainfall, are described as God’s command.

5:7.headline: Hoping for justice and finding its sound-alike
5:7.body: God hoped for משפט, justice, and found משפח, sin piled on sin or a skin sore, and for צדקה, righteousness, but heard צעקה, a cry. Rashi and Radak point out that each pair sounds almost alike.

sources.quote: וְהִנֵּה מִשְׂפָּח – אֲסִיפַת חֵטְא עַל חֵטְא, כְּמוֹ ״מֵהִסְתַּפֵּחַ״ (שמואל א כו:יט), ״סְפָחֵנִי נָא״ (שמואל א ב:לו). דָּבָר אַחֵר: לְשׁוֹן נֶגַע, וּלְפִי שֶׁהוּא לָשׁוֹן נוֹפֵל עַל הַלָּשׁוֹן בִּקְרִיאָתוֹ, דּוֹמֶה ׳מִשְׁפָּט׳ לְ׳מִשְׂפָּח׳, וְכֵן ׳צְעָקָה׳ לִ׳צְדָקָה׳, נָפַל בּוֹ רוּחַ הַקֹּדֶשׁ בְּפִי הַנָּבִיא
sources.says: Rashi reads משפח as gathering sin upon sin or as a skin disease, and says the prophet chose it because it sounds like משפט, as צעקה sounds like צדקה.

sources.quote: פי' נגע, כמו ספחת, ולצחות הלשון סמך משפט אל משפט, וכן צעקה לצדקה מפני שהם קרובים להם באותיות
sources.says: Radak reads משפח as a skin sore and says it was set beside משפט, and צעקה beside צדקה, because their letters are close.

5:8.headline: Twenty-two cries of woe to match twenty-two of happiness
5:8.body: Here begins a run of הוי, “woe,” cries. Rashi notes that Psalms says אשרי, “happy,” 22 times about those who keep the Torah, and Isaiah answers with 22 הוי for the wicked.

sources.quote: עֶשְׂרִים וּשְׁנַיִם ״אַשְׁרֵי״ נֶאֱמַר בְּסֵפֶר תְּהִלִּים עַל מְקַיְּמֵי הַתּוֹרָה, וְעֶשְׂרִים וּשְׁנַיִם ״הוֹי״ אָמַר יְשַׁעְיָה עַל הָרְשָׁעִים
sources.says: Rashi says Psalms has 22 “happy” for those who keep the Torah, and Isaiah said 22 “woe” about the wicked.

5:12.headline: The harp that puts every other instrument to shame
5:12.body: The נבל has more strings than the כנור. Rashi says it is called נבל because it puts every other instrument to shame (מנבל).

sources.quote: נִימִין יְתֵרוֹת יֵשׁ בְּנֵבֶל מִן הַכִּנּוֹר, וְלָמָּה נִקְרָא שְׁמוֹ נֵבֶל? שֶׁמְּנַבֵּל כָּל מִינֵי כְּלֵי זֶמֶר
sources.says: Rashi says the נבל has more strings than the כנור and is named because it shames all other instruments.

5:17.headline: Lambs grazing as they are led, or as was promised
5:17.body: Metzudat Zion reads כדברם from the Aramaic for “lead”: the lambs graze as they always did. The sages, cited by Rashi, read it from דבר, “word”: as was spoken of them, the comfort promised to the righteous.

sources.quote: כדברם. כמנהגם כי וינהג תרגומו ודבר וכן אני אשימם דוברות בים (מ״א ה) שהוא ענין הנהגה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says כדברם means “as their custom,” because the Aramaic for leading is דבר.

sources.quote: וְרַבּוֹתֵינוּ דָּרְשׁוּ כְּדָבְרָם – כַּמְדֻבָּר בָּם, נֶחָמוֹת הַנִּדְבָּרוֹת לָהֶם
sources.says: Rashi says the sages read כדברם as “as was spoken about them,” the comfort promised to them.

5:18.headline: Sin starts as a thread and ends as a cart rope
5:18.body: The verse sets thin cords (חבלי השוא) beside a thick cart rope (עבות). Rashi and Radak cite the sages: the urge to do wrong starts thin as a thread and ends thick as a cart rope.

sources.quote: גּוֹרְרִים יֵצֶר הָרַע עֲלֵיהֶם מְעַט מְעַט בַּתְּחִלָּה בְּחַבְלֵי הַשָּׁוְא כְּחוּט שֶׁל קוּרֵי עַכָּבִישׁ, וּמִשֶּׁנִּתְגָּרֶה בָּהֶם מִתְגַּבֵּר וְהוֹלֵךְ עַד שֶׁנַּעֲשֶׂה כַּעֲבוֹת הָעֲגָלָה שֶׁקּוֹשְׁרִין בּוֹ אֶת הַקָּרוֹן לִמְשׁוֹךְ
sources.says: Rashi says people draw the evil urge to themselves little by little, first like a spider’s thread, until it becomes like a cart rope.

sources.quote: ובדברי רז"ל יצר הרע בתחילה דומה לחוט השער ולבסוף לעבות העגלה
sources.says: Radak cites the sages: the evil urge is first like a hair and in the end like a cart rope.

5:25.headline: Bodies like spit in the streets, or like cut branches
5:25.body: Rashi reads כסוחה as spit or vomit thrown out of the body, from סחי, “filth.” Radak reads it as “cut down,” from the Aramaic word for pruning a vine.

sources.quote: כְּרוֹק וְקִיא הַנִּיסָח מִתּוֹךְ גּוּפוֹ שֶׁל אָדָם, שֶׁהוּא מָאוּס. וּבִלְשׁוֹן חֲכָמִים קָרוּי סְחִי
sources.says: Rashi says it means like spit and vomit expelled from the body, called סחי by the sages.

sources.quote: ופירוש כרותה, תרגום לא תזמר לא תכסח
sources.says: Radak says it means cut down, as the Targum renders “do not prune” with תכסח.

50:2.headline: "I came and no one was there": to the prophets, or the synagogue?
50:2.body: Ibn Ezra says God 'came' through the prophets He sent. The Talmud reads it of the synagogue: when God comes and does not find ten men there, He is angry.

sources.quote: מדוע באתי. רמז לנביאים שהתנבאו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says 'I came' points to the prophets who prophesied.

sources.quote: בְּשָׁעָה שֶׁהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא בָּא בְּבֵית הַכְּנֶסֶת, וְלֹא מָצָא בָּהּ עֲשָׂרָה
sources.says: The Talmud says this is when God comes to the synagogue and does not find ten men.

50:3.headline: Darkening the sky, or the nations' heavenly princes?
50:3.body: Radak reads it plainly: God darkened the sky, as in the plague of darkness in Egypt. Rashi reads שמים as the heavenly hosts, the angels who stand over the nations, dressed in mourning when God punishes them.

sources.quote: צְבָא הַשָּׁמַיִם, שָׂרֵי הָעוֹבְדֵי כּוֹכָבִים וּמַזָּלוֹת
sources.says: Rashi says 'heavens' means the heavenly host, the princes of the idol-worshipping nations.

sources.quote: שהלבשתי להם השמים קדרות שהיה להם חשך שלשת ימים
sources.says: Radak says God dressed the sky in black for Egypt, with three days of darkness.

50:3.headline: A sky in mourning that never fully cleared
50:3.body: Ibn Ezra says the black sky is clouds, or an eclipse. The Talmud reads the verse as lasting: since the Temple was destroyed, the sky has never been seen fully clear.

sources.quote: הטעם על העבים, ויש אומרים על קדרות השמש
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it refers to clouds, and some say to a darkening of the sun.

sources.quote: מִיּוֹם שֶׁחָרַב בֵּית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ לֹא נִרְאֵית רָקִיעַ בְּטׇהֳרָתָהּ
sources.says: The Talmud says that since the Temple was destroyed the sky has not been seen in its purity.

50:10.headline: Who walks in darkness, and why?
50:10.body: Ibn Ezra prefers to read the one in darkness as the prophet, who has no honor in this world. The Talmud reads it as someone who missed synagogue: if he went for a good deed, he has light; if for his own affairs, he has none.

sources.quote: תאר לעבדו שהוא הנביא
sources.says: Ibn Ezra cites a reading that this describes God's servant, the prophet, and calls it correct.

sources.quote: אִם לִדְבַר מִצְוָה הָלַךְ — נוֹגַהּ לוֹ
sources.says: The Talmud says if he went to do a good deed, there is light for him.

50:11.headline: "You will lie down in sorrow" means you will die
50:11.body: Ibn Ezra and Metzudat Zion say 'lie down' here means death, as in 'David lay down with his fathers'. The Talmud has angels greet the wicked at death with these words.

sources.quote: בעצבון תמותון, כמו וישכב דוד
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means you will die in sorrow, as in 'David lay down'.

sources.quote: תשכבון. כן נקרא המיתה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says death is called lying down.

sources.quote: וְאַחַת אוֹמֶרֶת לוֹ: ״לְמַעֲצֵבָה יִשְׁכַּב״
sources.says: The Talmud says one band of angels greets a dying wicked man with 'he will lie down in sorrow'.

51:1.headline: צור: a rock, a mountain, a quarry, and so a source
51:1.body: Maimonides lists the meanings of צור: a mountain, a hard stone, a quarry, and from the quarry, the source of anything. Here the quarry you were cut from is Abraham, so follow his ways.

sources.quote: "צור" – מונח רב־משמעי
sources.says: Maimonides says צור is a word with several meanings.

sources.quote: ג) והוא שם המכרה שכורים ממנו אבני מחצב
sources.says: Maimonides says one meaning is a quarry that building stones are dug from, and he cites this verse.

sources.quote: הושאל מונח זה מן המשמעות האחרונה ל(משמעות של) מוצאו של כל דבר וראשיתו
sources.says: Maimonides says the word was then borrowed to mean the source and beginning of anything.

sources.quote: כאילו פירש שהצור שחֻצבתם ממנו הוא אברהם אביכם, ועל כן לכו בעקבותיו
sources.says: Maimonides says the rock you were cut from is Abraham, so walk in his footsteps.

sources.quote: חצבתם ממנו זה אברהם
sources.says: Radak says the rock you were cut from is Abraham.

51:2.headline: "I called him" may mean "I made him great"
51:2.body: Rashi and Metzudat Zion read קראתיו as "I made him great", like the leaders called קריאי העדה. The Targum reads it as "I brought him near to serve Me".

sources.quote: קְרָאתִיו – רִבִּיתִיו וְגִדַּלְתִּיו, לְשׁוֹן ״קְרִיאֵי הָעֵדָה״
sources.says: Rashi says קראתיו means I raised him up and made him great, as in "the called ones of the assembly".

sources.quote: קראתיו. ענין גדולה ורוממות
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says קראתיו means greatness and being raised up.

sources.quote: קָרֵיבְתֵּהּ לְפוּלְחָנִי
sources.says: The Targum renders it "I brought him near to My service".

51:4.headline: ארגיע: "I will give rest", or "I will act in a moment"
51:4.body: Rashi and Ibn Ezra read it as "I will give rest", like מרגוע. Ibn Ezra reports another reading from רגע, a moment, "I will do it at once", but says the first is right.

sources.quote: אַרְגִּיעַ. אָנִיחַ
sources.says: Rashi says ארגיע means "I will give rest".

sources.quote: ויאמר אחד מן המפרשים, כי ארגיע אעשה רגע בלא עיכוב, והראשון הוא הנכון
sources.says: Ibn Ezra reports one reading of "I will do it in a moment, without delay", but says the first reading is correct.

sources.quote: ארגיעה. מלשון מרגוע והשקט
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the word comes from rest and quiet.

51:6.headline: נמלחו: the sky wears out like rags, or churns like the sea
51:6.body: Rashi first reads it as worn out, like the rags called מלחים in Jeremiah. He also offers "churned", from sailors (מלחים) stirring the sea with oars, and Radak reads it as ruin, like a salt land.

sources.quote: נִתְבַּלּוּ, כְּמוֹ (ירמיהו לח:יב) ״בְּלוֹיֵי הַסְּחָבוֹת וְהַמְּלָחִים״
sources.says: Rashi says נמלחו means worn out, like the old rags in Jeremiah.

sources.quote: לָשׁוֹן אַחֵר: נִמְלָחוּ – נִתְבַּלְבְּלוּ, לְשׁוֹן מַלָּחֵי הַיָּם
sources.says: Rashi gives another reading: stirred up, from the sailors of the sea.

sources.quote: נמלחו. ענין השחתה, וכן ארץ מלחה לא תשב
sources.says: Radak says נמלחו means ruin, as in a salt land where no one lives.

51:9.headline: מחוללת: God slew the monster, or made it tremble
51:9.body: Rashi reads it from חלל, slain. Radak, Ibn Ezra and Metzudat Zion read it from חיל, shaking like a woman in labor, so God made Pharaoh tremble.

sources.quote: מְחוֹלֶלֶת. לְשׁוֹן הֶרֶג חָלָל
sources.says: Rashi says מחוללת means killing, from חלל, the slain.

sources.quote: מחוללת. מגזרת חיל כיולדה
sources.says: Radak says it comes from חיל, the shaking of a woman giving birth.

sources.quote: מחוללת. מגזרת חיל אחז
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it comes from חיל, as in "trembling seized".

sources.quote: מחוללת תנין. אשר הרעידה את פרעה
sources.says: Metzudat David says it means God made Pharaoh tremble.

51:9.headline: The sea monster God struck is Pharaoh
51:9.body: Radak, Ibn Ezra and Metzudat Zion say the תנין is Pharaoh, whom Ezekiel calls "the great sea monster" lying in his rivers. The Targum says Pharaoh and his army were strong like a sea monster.

sources.quote: תנין. זה פרעה, וכן אמר התנין הגדול הרובץ בתוך יאוריו
sources.says: Radak says the תנין is Pharaoh, called "the great monster lying in his rivers".

sources.quote: תנין. כן יקרא פרעה מלך מצרים
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says Pharaoh king of Egypt is called תנין.

sources.quote: ותנין. הוא פרעה וכן כתוב בספר יחזקאל התנין הגדול
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the תנין is Pharaoh, as Ezekiel writes "the great monster".

sources.quote: שֵׁיצֵיתִי פַּרְעֹה וּמַשִׁרְיָתֵהּ דַהֲווּ תַּקִיפִין כְּתַנִינָא
sources.says: The Targum says God destroyed Pharaoh and his army, who were strong like a sea monster.

51:14.headline: צעה: an exile on the move, or a frail human body
51:14.body: Radak and Metzudat Zion read צעה as one who wanders: the exiles will soon be set free. Rashi brings a midrash that reads it as a man who must empty his bowels to live, to show how weak the feared enemy really is.

sources.quote: צעה. הוא ענין טלטול הנוע ממקום למקום
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says צעה means wandering from place to place.

sources.quote: ולשון צועה הוא ענין טלטול ונוע ממקום למקום
sources.says: Radak says צועה means wandering from place to place.

sources.quote: אֲפִלּוּ נְקָבִין קָשִׁין עָלָיו, וְצָרִיךְ הוּא לְהִפָּתֵחַ בְּהִלּוּךְ הַמֵּעַיִם
sources.says: Rashi says even a blocked bowel is hard on a man, and he must open up to live.

sources.quote: אֲבָל הַלָּשׁוֹן רִאשׁוֹן מִדְּרַשׁ אַגָּדָה הוּא
sources.says: Rashi says that first reading comes from a midrash.

sources.quote: איך תפחד מבן אדם שימות והנה בעודו בחיים הוא דבר חלוש מאד
sources.says: Radak explains the midrash: why fear a mortal, who is very weak even while alive?

51:15.headline: רגע הים: God splits the sea, rebukes it, or calms it
51:15.body: Rashi, Radak and Metzudat Zion link רגע to "my skin cracked" in Job, so God splits the sea. The Targum reads "rebukes the sea", and Ibn Ezra prefers "calms", from מרגוע, rest.

sources.quote: רוגע. ענין בקוע כמו עורי רגע
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says רוגע means splitting, as in "my skin cracked".

sources.quote: רוגע. תרגם יונתן כמו גוער דנזיף בימא, ויש לפרשו כמו בוקע
sources.says: Radak says the Targum reads it as "rebukes the sea", and it can also mean "splits".

sources.quote: רֹגַע הַיָּם. לְשׁוֹן ״עוֹרִי רָגַע״
sources.says: Rashi says רוגע is the word in "my skin cracked" in Job.

sources.quote: דִנְזֵיף בְּיַמָא
sources.says: The Targum renders it "who rebukes the sea".

sources.quote: ויש אומרים מניח, אחר שהמו גליו, לשון מרגוע (ירמיהו ו' ט"ז), והוא הישר בעיני
sources.says: Ibn Ezra reports the reading "calms the sea after its waves roar", from מרגוע, rest, and says this seems right to him.

51:16.headline: "To plant the heavens": Israel, as many as the stars
51:16.body: Rashi follows the Targum: the heavens are the people promised to be as many as the stars, and the earth is the people promised to be like the dust. Maimonides reads heavens and earth here as a picture of Israel's restored kingdom.

sources.quote: לְקַיָּמָא עַמָּא דַּאֲמִיר עֲלֵיהוֹן דְּיִסְגּוֹן כְּכוֹכְבֵי שְׁמַיָּא
sources.says: Rashi quotes the Targum: to establish the people of whom it was said they will multiply like the stars of the sky.

sources.quote: שיהיו נטועים על אדמתם עם ישראל אשר עליהם נאמר ככוכבי השמים
sources.says: Metzudat David says Israel, compared to the stars, will be planted in their land.

sources.quote: כי הוא מתייחס תדיר בדבריו לשלטונה של המלכות כאילו היא עולם המיוחד לה, כלומר שמים וארץ
sources.says: Maimonides says Isaiah often speaks of the kingdom as if it were its own world, its own heavens and earth.

51:17.headline: קבעת: a kind of cup, or the dregs stuck at its bottom
51:17.body: The Targum renders it as a kind of cup. Rashi, Radak and Metzudat Zion read it as the dregs settled at the bottom, so Jerusalem drank the cup down to the last drop.

sources.quote: תִּרְגֵּם יוֹנָתָן: ״פַּיְלֵי״, וְהוּא שֵׁם כּוֹס. וְלִי נִרְאֶה: קֻבַּעַת – אֵלּוּ הַשְּׁמָרִים הַקְּבוּעִים בְּתַחְתִּית הַכְּלִי
sources.says: Rashi says the Targum takes it as a kind of cup, but he thinks it is the dregs settled at the bottom of the vessel.

sources.quote: קבעת. מלשון קבע והם השמרים הקבועים בתחתיות הכוס
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says קבעת means the dregs fixed at the bottom of the cup.

sources.quote: עד השמרים גם מצית אותה עד שלא נשאר בכוס אפילו טפה
sources.says: Radak says she drank to the dregs and drained it until not a drop was left.

sources.quote: קובעת. אין רע לו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the word has no match elsewhere.

51:17.headline: Cup of תרעלה: a drink that numbs, makes you shake, or kills
51:17.body: Rashi says תרעלה is a drink that dulls a person and saps his strength, as if he were wrapped and bound. Radak and Ibn Ezra read it as trembling, and Radak also offers deadly poison.

sources.quote: הוּא מַשְׁקֶה הַמְטַמְטֵם וּמַתִּישׁ כֹּחַ הָאָדָם כְּאָסוּר וְקָשׁוּר וּמְעֻטָּף
sources.says: Rashi says it is a drink that dulls a person and saps his strength, as if bound and wrapped.

sources.quote: התרעלה.  הרעדה, או פירושו סם המות
sources.says: Radak says it means trembling, or else deadly poison.

sources.quote: כמו רעדה שירעד האדם בראותה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it is like a trembling that seizes a person who sees it.

51:19.headline: "Two" troubles, yet the verse names four
51:19.body: Radak, Ibn Ezra and Metzudat David say the four words make two pairs: plunder goes with the sword, and breaking goes with famine. Rashi says the troubles came doubled, two by two.

sources.quote: כי השוד הוא החרב והשבר הוא הרעב
sources.says: Radak says plunder is the sword and breaking is the famine.

sources.quote: השוד הוא החרב, כי השוד לעולם עם החרב, והשבר הוא הרעב
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says plunder is the sword, since plunder always comes with the sword, and breaking is famine.

sources.quote: צָרוֹת כְּפוּלוֹת, שְׁתַּיִם שְׁתַּיִם
sources.says: Rashi says these are doubled troubles, two by two.

51:19.headline: "Who can I comfort you with?" No one has suffered like you
51:19.body: Rashi and Ibn Ezra explain that people take comfort when told that someone else went through the same thing. God says there is no other nation hurt like Jerusalem to point to.

sources.quote: מִי אָבִיא לָךְ לְנַחֲמֵךְ וְלוֹמַר: אַף אֻמָּה פְּלוֹנִית הִיא לָקְתָה דֻּגְמָתֵךְ
sources.says: Rashi says: whom can I bring to comfort you by saying that some other nation was struck like you?

sources.quote: כי האדם יתנחם כאשר יאמר לו מה שאירע לך כבר אירע כן לפלוני
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says a person is comforted when told that what happened to him already happened to someone else.

sources.quote: וכאומר הנה באמת לא קרה למי כמקרך
sources.says: Metzudat David says it means nothing like this has truly happened to anyone else.

51:20.headline: תוא, a wild ox, is תאו with two letters swapped
51:20.body: Radak and Metzudat Zion say תוא is the wild ox called תאו in Deuteronomy 14:5, with the letters reversed, like כבש and כשב. Jerusalem's children lie in the streets like a wild ox caught in a net.

sources.quote: ותוא היא החיה הנזכרת בתורה ותאו וזמר בהפוך האותיות כמו כבש וכשב והוא שור הבר
sources.says: Radak says תוא is the animal named in the Torah as תאו, with the letters swapped like כבש and כשב, and it is the wild ox.

sources.quote: כתוא. הוא שור הבר והוא בהפוך מן ותאו וזמר
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it is the wild ox, the reverse of תאו.

sources.quote: תּוֹא כְּמוֹ ״וּתְאוֹ וָזָמֶר״
sources.says: Rashi says תוא is like the תאו of Deuteronomy.

52:2.headline: Sit on your throne, or Jerusalem the captive?
52:2.body: The same letters can mean 'sit' or 'captivity'. Rashi reads 'sit on the throne'. Radak reads it as captivity, and notes that the Targum took it as sitting.

sources.quote: שבי. על הכסא
sources.says: Rashi says it means sit, on the throne.

sources.quote: שבי. כמו את השבי ואת המלקוח, ויונתן תרגם ענין ישב
sources.says: Radak compares it to 'the captives and the spoil', and notes that Jonathan's Targum translated it as sitting.

52:3.headline: 'Sold for nothing' can mean sold for worthless things
52:3.body: חנם usually means free, with no price paid. The Talmud and Rashi also read it as 'for worthless things': idol worship, or the urge to do wrong.

sources.quote: מכרתי אתכם לגוים, והטעם בלא כסף
sources.says: Ibn Ezra gives the plain sense: God sold them to the nations without money.

sources.quote: חנם נמכרתם״ – בעבודה זרה
sources.says: Rabbi Yehoshua reads 'sold for nothing' as sold for idol worship.

sources.quote: על עסקי חנם, הוא יצר הרע שאינו לכם לשכר
sources.says: Rashi says they were sold over worthless pursuits, the urge to do wrong, which pays them nothing.

52:3.headline: Not redeemed with silver, but what is the silver?
52:3.body: Plainly, God will free Israel without any price. Rashi says the price is repentance instead of money, while in the Talmud Rabbi Yehoshua reads 'silver' as repentance and good deeds, and says Israel will be freed even without them.

sources.quote: ולא בכסף תגאלו. אלא בתשובה
sources.says: Rashi says they will be redeemed not with money but with repentance.

sources.quote: ולא בכסף תגאלו״ – לא בתשובה ומעשים טובים
sources.says: Rabbi Yehoshua reads 'not with silver' as not through repentance and good deeds.

52:5.headline: Do the rulers boast, or make Israel howl?
52:5.body: Rashi reads the word as boasting: the rulers brag about their power. Radak takes it from ילל, to wail: the rulers make Israel howl under hard labor.

sources.quote: יהילילו. מתפארים לאמר
sources.says: Rashi says it means they boast.

sources.quote: שרשו ילל מענין יללה והוא מבנין הפעיל
sources.says: Radak says the root is the one for wailing, in a form that makes others wail.

sources.quote: יהילילו אותם בעבודתן הקשה
sources.says: Radak says the ruling nations make Israel wail with hard labor.

52:7.headline: How lovely are the messenger's feet: the root is debated
52:7.body: This form is rare. Ibn Ezra ties it to תאוה, 'a delight to the eyes' in Genesis 3:6, and rejects a root that starts with נ. Radak agrees on the root and says the sense is beauty.

sources.quote: מה נאוו מבניין נפעל, מגזרת וכי תאוה הוא
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the word comes from the same root as 'a delight to the eyes' in Genesis.

sources.quote: והאומר כי הנו"ן שורש, אינו אמת
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says whoever thinks the נ is part of the root is wrong.

sources.quote: שרשו אוה והאל"ף נחה והנו"ן לנפעל
sources.says: Radak gives the root as אוה and says the meaning is beauty.

52:9.headline: Ibn Ezra hears 'speak out' in the word, as in Arabic
52:9.body: פצחו, burst out, is a rare verb. Radak says it means raising the voice, and Ibn Ezra links it to clear speech, saying the language of Kedar, Arabic, uses it for speaking.

sources.quote: פצחו. לשון צחות, וכן בלשון קדר, הנה הוא כטעם דיבור
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it is a word of eloquence, and in the language of Kedar it means speech.

sources.quote: פצחו. ענינו הרמת קול
sources.says: Radak says it means raising the voice.

52:11.headline: Vessels of the Lord: Temple vessels, Torah, or weapons?
52:11.body: כלי can mean vessels or weapons. The Targum reads the vessels of the Temple, Ibn Ezra says Israel carries the Torah, and Radak says Israel's weapons on the way home will be God's kindness, not swords.

sources.quote: נטלי מני בית מקדשא
sources.says: The Targum says they carry the vessels of the Temple.

sources.quote: הם ישראל נושאי התורה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the carriers are Israel, who carry the Torah.

sources.quote: כלי זיין שלכם יהיו כלי ה' ולא חרב ולא חנית
sources.says: Radak says their weapons will be God's, not sword or spear.

52:12.headline: God walks behind as the rear guard who waits for stragglers
52:12.body: מאסף, the gatherer, is the name for the troop at the back of a marching camp. Rashi says it gets that name because it waits for the weak and those who stumble, so here God guards Israel from behind as well as leading in front.

sources.quote: ההולך אחרי המחנה קרוי מאסף, לפי שהוא ממתין את הנחלשים ואת הנכשלים
sources.says: Rashi says the one who walks behind the camp is called the gatherer because he waits for the weak and the stumbling.

sources.quote: לפי שהוא מאסף כל הנכשלים הנשארים באחרונה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says he gathers all the stragglers left at the back.

52:13.headline: My servant will prosper, or my servant will understand?
52:13.body: ישכיל usually means to act wisely. Radak reads 'will prosper', and Metzudat Zion explains that success looks like wisdom, while Ibn Ezra reads 'my servant will understand'.

sources.quote: ישכיל. יצליח, כמו ויהי דוד בכל דרכיו משכיל
sources.says: Radak says it means will prosper, as with David who succeeded in all his ways.

sources.quote: הוא ענין הצלחה כי המצליח בדבר נראה כאלו עשה מעשהו בהשכל
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means success, because one who succeeds looks as if he acted wisely.

sources.quote: והנה ישכיל עבדי. יבין עבדי
sources.says: Ibn Ezra reads it as 'my servant will understand'.

52:15.headline: Will he sprinkle the nations, or make them talk?
52:15.body: יזה usually means to sprinkle, as with blood, and Ibn Ezra reads it as shedding the nations' blood. Radak links it to dripping words, as in preaching, and reads that the nations will talk about him.

sources.quote: וטעם יזה. ישפוך דמיהם
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means he will shed their blood.

sources.quote: ענין דבור, כמו יטיף שהוא בענין הזיה
sources.says: Radak says it means speech, like the word for dripping that is also used for preaching.

sources.quote: כן יבדר עממין סגיאין
sources.says: The Targum translates it as 'he will scatter many nations'.

52:15.headline: Kings' mouths spring open, or snap shut?
52:15.body: קפץ can mean to spring open, as in leaping over hills, or to close, as in 'do not shut your hand'. Radak says both fit here: kings open their mouths to tell of his greatness, or cover them in awe.

sources.quote: ושניהם יכולים להתפרש על מלת יקפצו
sources.says: Radak says the word can mean opening or closing, and both readings fit.

sources.quote: יקפצו. יסגרו פיהם מרוב תמהון
sources.says: Rashi says they will shut their mouths in great amazement.

53:2.headline: Not a nursing baby but a young shoot on a tree
53:2.body: יונק usually means a baby that nurses. Here the commentators say it is a tender branch that "nurses" from the tree, as in Hosea 14:7.

sources.quote: ענף רך היוצא מהאילן
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it is a soft branch growing out of a tree.

sources.quote: כְּיוֹנֵק מִיּוֹנֶקֶת הָאִילָנוֹת
sources.says: Rashi says the people rose up on their own like a shoot from a tree.

sources.quote: כמו ילכו יונקותיו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra compares it to the spreading shoots in Hosea 14:7.

53:2.headline: "And we desired him" means we did not desire him
53:2.body: Read plainly, ונחמדהו says "and we desired him", which makes no sense here. Rashi reads it as a question, Radak says the earlier "not" counts twice, and Metzudat Zion says the "and" means "that".

sources.quote: הֵיאַךְ נֶחְמְדֵהוּ? וְנֶחְמְדֵהוּ תָּמוּהַּ הוּא
sources.says: Rashi reads it as a question of surprise: how could we desire him?

sources.quote: ולא היינו חומדים אותו אלא מתעבים אותו ולא שזכר עומד במקום שנים
sources.says: Radak says it means we did not desire him, because the word "not" serves twice.

sources.quote: הוי״ו היא במקום שי״ן
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the vav stands for "that": no look that we should desire him.

53:3.headline: Lowest of men, or a man others kept away from?
53:3.body: חדל means to stop or hold back. Radak gives two readings: he was the lowest of people, or people held back from joining him.

sources.quote: פחות שמבני אדם היה, או פירוש חדל הוא מאישים שלא היו מתחברים עמו
sources.says: Radak says it means either the lowest of people or someone people would not keep company with.

sources.quote: חדל להחשב עם אנשים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says he stopped being counted among people.

53:3.headline: Who is hiding their face from whom?
53:3.body: The phrase "like one hiding the face from him" can point either way. Rashi says the sufferer hid his own face in shame, while Radak says we hid our faces so as not to look at him.

sources.quote: כְּאָדָם מְנֻגָּע שֶׁמַּסְתִּיר פָּנָיו וְיָרֵא מְהַבִּיט
sources.says: Rashi says they hid their faces like a stricken man who is afraid to look up.

sources.quote: היינו כמסתרים פנים ממנו שלא היינו רוצים להביט בו
sources.says: Radak says the onlookers hid their faces because they did not want to look at him.

53:4.headline: Rashi: אכן means "but", which turns the verse around
53:4.body: אכן is often read as "surely". Rashi says it always means "but": the speakers admit they were wrong about why he suffered.

sources.quote: אָכֵן לְשׁוֹן ׳אֲבָל׳ בְּכָל מָקוֹם
sources.says: Rashi says אכן means "but" everywhere it appears.

53:5.headline: Wounded, or writhing in pain like a woman in labor?
53:5.body: Ibn Ezra takes מחלל from the root for a wound or a slain body. Radak and Metzudat Zion take it from the root for trembling and birth pains.

sources.quote: והוא מחולל. מגזרת חלל
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the word comes from חלל, a wound or one slain.

sources.quote: מענין חיל כיולדה
sources.says: Radak says it comes from the shaking of a woman giving birth.

sources.quote: מלשון חיל וחלחלה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means trembling and anguish.

53:5.headline: "Our peace", or "all of us"?
53:5.body: שלומנו looks like "our peace". Radak's first reading takes it from שלם, whole: the suffering meant for all of us fell on him.

sources.quote: שלומינו כמו כלנו, כמו הגלת שלומים
sources.says: Radak says it means "all of us", and also brings the reading "our peace".

sources.quote: שֶׁהוּא הָיָה מְיֻסָּר לִהְיוֹת שָׁלוֹם לְכָל הָעוֹלָם
sources.says: Rashi reads it as peace: he suffered so the whole world would have peace.

53:6.headline: Did God make the sin strike him, or accept his plea?
53:6.body: פגע can mean to strike or to plead. Rashi says God was won over through him, while Metzudat Zion says God made our sin hit him. Ibn Ezra brings both.

sources.quote: נֶעְתַּר עַל יָדוֹ וְנִתְרַצָּה עַל עֲוֹן כֻּלָּנוּ
sources.says: Rashi says God accepted prayer through him and forgave everyone's sin.

sources.quote: הפגיש בו לרעה להכותו
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says God made the sin meet him to strike him.

sources.quote: ויש אומרים מגזרת ואל תפגע בי
sources.says: Ibn Ezra notes that some read it as pleading, as in Jeremiah 7:16.

53:6.headline: Here "sin" means the punishment for sin
53:6.body: עון usually means sin. Ibn Ezra and Radak say that here it means the penalty a sin brings, as in Genesis 15:16.

sources.quote: במקום הזה כמו עונש
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says in this place the word means punishment.

sources.quote: פירוש עון עונש העון
sources.says: Radak says עון here is the punishment for the sin.

53:7.headline: Squeezed for money, like a ewe stripped of its wool
53:7.body: נגש is used for a creditor pressing for payment. Radak says the lamb led to slaughter stands for harm to the body, and the shorn ewe for losing one's money.

sources.quote: נגש בממון, כמו נגש את הכסף
sources.says: Radak says he was pressed for money, as in 2 Kings 23:35.

sources.quote: נלחץ ונדחק לקחת עשרו
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says he was squeezed so they could take his wealth.

sources.quote: ודמיון הרחל הוא לנגישת הממון שהוא בדמיון הגז
sources.says: Radak says the ewe stands for being squeezed for money, which is like shearing.

53:8.headline: "Land of the living" is the Land of Israel
53:8.body: Being cut off from the land of the living sounds like death. Rashi and Radak say the land of the living is the Land of Israel, so it means exile. Radak adds that exile felt like death.

sources.quote: וְגוֹלֶה מֵאֶרֶץ חַיִּים, הִיא אֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל
sources.says: Rashi says he was exiled from the land of the living, which is the Land of Israel.

sources.quote: ויש לפרש כי בגלות נחשב באמת כאלו נגזר מארץ חיים
sources.says: Radak also reads it as exile, which truly counted as being cut off from life.

53:8.headline: One plural word shows the servant is a whole people
53:8.body: The chapter speaks of one man. Then למו, "to them", appears. Metzudat Zion says this plural shows the whole nation is meant.

sources.quote: לכן אמר למו לגלות שעל הכלל ידבר
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the plural reveals that the passage speaks of the whole nation.

sources.quote: בעבור מלת למו שהוא כמו להם
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says למו means "to them" and builds his reading on it.

53:9.headline: "In his deaths", or a monument over his grave?
53:9.body: Radak reads במתיו as "his deaths", plural, for the many ways Jews were killed. Ibn Ezra brings a reading from במה, a raised structure set over a grave.

sources.quote: לשון רבים כי מיתות רבות יעשו לו
sources.says: Radak says it is plural because many kinds of death were done to him.

sources.quote: והטעם בנין שיושם על הקבר
sources.says: Ibn Ezra cites a view that it means a structure put over a grave.

53:9.headline: "The rich man" here means the ruler
53:9.body: עשיר normally means rich. Metzudat Zion says it means the ruler, since the rich usually rule. Radak keeps "rich": Jews were killed for their wealth.

sources.quote: ר״ל מושל כי על פי הרוב ימשול העשיר
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the word means a ruler, because the rich usually rule.

sources.quote: כי גם העשיר הורגים אותו בעבור עשרו
sources.says: Radak says even the rich man was killed for his wealth.

53:10.headline: אשם here is a payment to make up for a wrong
53:10.body: אשם can mean guilt or a guilt offering. Rashi says it is a payment you give to the one you wronged, like the gift the Philistines sent back with the ark.

sources.quote: אָשָׁם זֶה לְשׁוֹן ׳כֹּפֶר׳, שֶׁנּוֹתֵן אָדָם לְמִי שֶׁחָטָא לוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says אשם means a payment a person gives to someone he wronged, as in 1 Samuel 6:3.

sources.quote: ענין חטא ופשע
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means sin and wrongdoing.

53:11.headline: Who is made righteous: many nations, or God?
53:11.body: יצדיק צדיק can mean "the righteous one makes others righteous" or "he declares the Righteous One just". Radak says Israel will teach the nations, while Metzudat David says the servant accepts God's judgment as fair.

sources.quote: שהיה צדיק ויודע את ה' יצדיק בדעתו גוים רבים
sources.says: Radak says righteous Israel, knowing God, will make many nations righteous.

sources.quote: בדעתו יחשוב להצדיק את ה׳ הצדיק
sources.says: Metzudat David says in his mind he declares God, the Righteous One, to be just.

sources.quote: הָיָה שׁוֹפֵט עַבְדִּי מִשְׁפַּט אֱמֶת
sources.says: Rashi says the servant judged truly for all who came before him.

53:12.headline: He prayed for the very people who wronged him
53:12.body: The same verb as in verse 6 returns. Here Radak and Metzudat Zion read it as pleading: he prayed for those who sinned against him.

sources.quote: היה מתפלל בעבור הפשעים שהיו פושעים בו
sources.says: Radak says he prayed for the sinners who sinned against him.

sources.quote: ענין תחנה ובקשה
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the word means pleading and asking.

55:1.headline: The water the thirsty are called to is Torah
55:1.body: The verse invites the thirsty to come to the water. Rashi reads the water as Torah, and Maimonides notes that the sages often call wisdom 'water', citing this verse.

sources.quote: לכו למים. לתורה
sources.says: Rashi says 'come to the water' means come to the Torah.

sources.quote: והמים משל לתורה ולחכמה
sources.says: Radak says the water is a figure for Torah and wisdom.

sources.quote: וכך נפוץ אצלם כינוי החכמה בשם מים
sources.says: Maimonides says the sages commonly call wisdom 'water', and cites this verse.

55:2.headline: 'Eat what is good' means learn
55:2.body: Maimonides lists this verse as a place where eating stands for learning: wisdom keeps the soul alive the way food keeps the body alive. Radak says the 'good' to eat is the Torah.

sources.quote: הושאל לשון אכילה לחכמה וללימוד
sources.says: Maimonides says the word for eating is borrowed for wisdom and learning, and cites this verse.

sources.quote: ואכלו טוב. זה התורה
sources.says: Radak says the good they are told to eat is the Torah.

sources.quote: כי החכמה לנשמה כמאכל לגוף
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says wisdom is to the soul what food is to the body.

55:4.headline: A witness to the nations, or one who warns them?
55:4.body: עד usually means a witness. Radak says here it means one who warns, since a warning is given in front of witnesses, while the Targum translates it as 'a master'.

sources.quote: הן עד. מזהיר ומעיד בכם כמו העדותי בכם היום
sources.says: Radak says it means one who warns, as in 'I warn you today'.

sources.quote: הא רב לעממיא מניתה
sources.says: The Targum translates: I have appointed him a master over the peoples.

55:6.headline: God is always present, so when is He 'to be found'?
55:6.body: Ibn Ezra notes that God is everywhere at all times, so the phrase must mean before the decree is sealed. A midrash ties that to Yom Kippur, while the Targum reads it as 'while you are still alive'.

sources.quote: כי ידוע שהשם נמצא בכל מקום ובכל עת, הנה הטעם קודם חתום הגזרות
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says God is found everywhere always, so the meaning is before the decrees are sealed.

sources.quote: עד שלא אחתם גזר דין ביום הכפורים. לכך נאמר: דרשו ה' בהמצאו
sources.says: The midrash says God accepts repentance until He seals the decree on Yom Kippur, and that is why the verse says this.

sources.quote: תבעו דחלתא דיי עד דאתון חיין
sources.says: The Targum says: seek the Lord while you are alive.

55:8.headline: God's 'thoughts' share only a name with ours
55:8.body: Radak reads this as about forgiving: people hold a grudge, but God forgives fully. Maimonides reads it more deeply: God's knowing differs from ours in kind, as the heavens differ from the earth.

sources.quote: הנה אני מרבה לסלוח לא ככם
sources.says: Radak says God forgives much, unlike people.

sources.quote: שידיעתו שונה מידיעתנו באופן העצמי הזה, כמו שעצם השמים שונה מעצם הארץ
sources.says: Maimonides says God's knowledge differs from ours in its very nature, as heaven differs from earth, and cites this verse.

55:13.headline: The cypress that rises is Mordecai, 'chief of spices'
55:13.body: The sages read this verse as the Purim story, with the cypress as Mordecai. They link him to the 'chief spice' מר דרור, which the Aramaic calls מרי דכיא, a sound close to Mordecai.

sources.quote: יעלה ברוש זה מרדכי הצדיק שנקרא ראש לבשמים
sources.says: The Talmud passage says the cypress is Mordecai, who is called the chief of spices.

sources.quote: ואתה קח לך בשמים ראש מר דרור ומתרגמינן מרי דכיא
sources.says: It cites the spice מר דרור and its Aramaic translation מרי דכיא.

55:13.headline: The myrtle in place of the nettle is Queen Esther
55:13.body: Esther's Hebrew name was Hadassah, from הדס, myrtle. The sages read the verse as Purim: in place of the nettle, Vashti, rises the myrtle, Esther.

sources.quote: יעלה הדס זו אסתר הצדקת שנקראת הדסה
sources.says: The Talmud passage says the myrtle is Esther, who was called Hadassah.

sources.ref: Otzar Midrashim, Midrashim on Megilat Esther, Midrash on the Book of Esther 3
sources.quote: ותחת הסרפד זו ושתי הרשעה
sources.says: The midrash says the nettle is the wicked Vashti.

sources.quote: רבותינו דרשו: תחת הרשעים יעלו צדיקים
sources.says: Rashi reports that the sages read it as the righteous rising in place of the wicked.

56:5.headline: A 'hand and a name': here the hand means a place
56:5.body: יד usually means hand. Ibn Ezra and Metzudat Zion say here it means a place, as in Deuteronomy 23:13, and Radak adds that it is a place of honor, not a spot on the ground.

sources.quote: יד. מקום כמו ויד תהיה לך
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says יד means a place, as in 'you shall have a place' in Deuteronomy.

sources.quote: יד. מקום, כמו יד תהיה לך
sources.says: Ibn Ezra also says it means a place.

sources.quote: אבל זה אינו מקום גופני אלא במקום מעלה ושבח
sources.says: Radak says it is not a physical place but a place of rank and praise.

56:7.headline: 'My house of prayer': the Talmud learns that God prays
56:7.body: The verse says 'my prayer', not 'their prayer'. From this the Talmud learns that God Himself prays, and gives His prayer: that His mercy overcome His anger.

sources.quote: ״תפלתם״ לא נאמר, אלא ״תפלתי״, מכאן שהקדוש ברוך הוא מתפלל
sources.says: The Talmud says the verse does not say 'their prayer' but 'my prayer', so God prays.

sources.quote: יהי רצון מלפני שיכבשו רחמי את כעסי
sources.says: It gives God's prayer: may it be My will that My mercy conquer My anger.

56:10.headline: Mute dogs: watchdogs that a scrap of food can silence
56:10.body: A watchdog that cannot bark is useless. Radak cites a midrash that asks whether any dog is truly mute, and answers: this is a dog that goes quiet once it is thrown a scrap, and so were Israel's judges.

sources.quote: וכי יש כלב אלם אלא מה הוא אלמים
sources.says: Radak cites the midrash asking whether there is such a thing as a mute dog.

sources.quote: אדם משליך לו פרוסה סוכר את פיו כך היו דייני ישראל
